READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. There has been much discussion on the relationship of Isa. 14:12-21 to Satan. It seems to me that we must take seriously the historical context and specific literary statements of Isaiah and assert that originally this referred to the king of old Babylon (or kings of Assyria after Ashurbanipal). However, the king of old Babylon's problem, as all conscious creatures, was pride. If we go back to Gen. 3:5, we see this desire to be like God. Not only has sin affected the angelic world, but also the material world (cf. Daniel 4; 11:36; Ezek. 28:13ff; 2 Thess. 2:4). The king is a type of wicked leadership. Behind the wicked world leaders in the OT stood their national deities (cf. Dan. 10:13,20; also note Deut. 32:8 in the LXX). From the NT we understand that there is a personal force of evil known as Satan. The identification in this chapter with Satan was probably influenced by
    1. Jerome's Vulgate translating Isa. 14:12 as "Lucifer"
    2. Tertulian and Gregory the Great relating this passage to Luke 10:18
    3. This passage being used as a backdrop to both Dante's Inferno and Milton's Paradise Lost

    SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN

  2. I personally am feeling more and more uncomfortable using Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 as biblical texts for the origin and demise of an angelic tempter. I think our curiosity drives us to use contexts inappropriately. The Bible is silent on many issues that we are curious about. Systematic Theology must start with exegesis! In many ways the spiritual realm is purposefully clouded and concealed.

  3. For a similar context see Ezekiel 28 at www.freebiblecommentary.org, "Old Testament Studies," written commentaries.

  4. The Jewish Study Bible (p. 812) says of this poem "it describes the ignominious death of an Assyrian monarch of Isaiah's time, probably Sargon II, who was killed in battle in 705 B.C. It was later reinterpreted as predicting the death of a Babylonian monarch." I think Isaiah (or a disciple) may have used an earlier poem, or at least its imagery, to describe a series of arrogant eastern kings who were destroyed by YHWH.

  5. It is impossible to fit together all the historical allusions in this prophecy. Remember, Hebrew prophecy is a historical "pointer," not a detailed road map. Westerners misunderstand the OT's imagery, ambiguity, and hyperbole! See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic and G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible. Both books have been very helpful to me on this issue.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 14:2-3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:2-3 There is a "role-reversal" between Isa. 14:2 (servitude of Israel's enemies) and Isa. 14:3 (Israel's servitude, which is now over). The "role-reversal" plot is common in the OT. YHWH acts in unexpected ways to affirm the choice of Abraham's seed (cf. Genesis 12; 15; 17). The purpose of His special attention is not favoritism, but an eternal redemptive plan (cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3) for all humans made in His image (cf. Gen. 1:26-27).

As so often in Isaiah, there is a short-term focus and a long-term focus. The prophet merges these two horizons. A good example might be chapter 13, where old Babylon and Neo-Babylon's judgment are merged.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:4 "taunt"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:4 "taunt" This is the Hebrew Wisdom Literature term mashal (BDB 605), which is usually translated "proverb." However, the poetic structure of Isa. 14:3-21 is in the meter of a funeral dirge (i.e. chapter 47 and Lamentations).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WISDOM LITERATURE

▣ "against the king of Babylon" The peson identified by this title is uncertain. Please read "Contextual Insights," C, second paragraph of chapter 13. Notice how in Isa. 14:24, without any "oracle" formula, Assyria is addressed directly. After the fall of the city of Babylon to Assyria in 689 B.C., the Assyrian kings took the added throne title of "king of Babylon."

NASB  "the oppressor has ceased"
NKJV  "the golden city ceased"
NRSV  "his insolence has ceased"
NJB  "how did his arrogance end"
LXX  "the taskmaster has ceased"
JPSOA  "the oppression ended"
Peshitta  "the zealous one ceased"
REB  "how still his raging arrogance"

The MT has the word מדהבה (BDB 551, from an Aramaic root, cf. NKJV), but this is used only here in the OT. If the ד (d) is changed to ר (r), like the scroll of Isaiah in the Dead Sea Scrolls, then מרהבה (BDB 923) becomes "arrogant" or "insolent." The UBS Text Project gives this emendation a "C" rating (considerable doubt) rating.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:5 "The Lord has"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:5 "The Lord has" YHWH is the controller behind human history (cf. Isa. 14:22-23,24). He may be unseen to those who lack faith, but He is directing history for His coming of Messiah (first coming inaugurates the Kingdom) and the consummation of the age of righteousness (second coming).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING

SPECIAL TOPIC: THIS AGE AND THE AGE TO COME

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

▣ The "staff" (BDB 641) and "scepter" (BDB 986) were symbols of kingly power (cf. Isa. 14:6). They are used as imagery of YHWH's use of Assyria as His tool for judgment on His people in Isa. 10:5.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:7 "The whole earth is at rest and is quiet"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:7 "The whole earth is at rest and is quiet" The "rest" (BDB 628, KB 679, Qal PERFECT) refers to a time of peace from invasion. This same VERB is used in Isa. 14:3 (Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) to refer to the rest/peace of the covenant people. Here it refers to the whole ANE (i.e. "the whole earth"). See SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH

The fall of the Mesopotamian powers causes rest, quiet, and joy throughout the ANE. The oppressor is defeated (cf. Isa. 14:8).

▣ "They break forth into shouts of joy" Isaiah speaks often of the joy of deliverance (i.e. salvation, cf. Isa. 44:23; 49:13; 52:9; 54:1).

Here, it has an element of an eschatological joy (i.e. "the whole earth"). YHWH's will for mankind was rest, peace, abundance, and joy (cf. Genesis 1-2)!

entries.title: Isaiah 14:8 "no tree cutter comes up against us"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:8 "no tree cutter comes up against us" This can mean one of three things.

  1. Babylon exported many trees from Lebanon for her own building projects (literal)
  2. the enemy will not cut lumber to build siege equipment (literal)
  3. the land will prosper in peace (symbolic)

From Assyrian documents we learn cutting timber was common imagery for defeating foreign armies. In Isa. 10:33-34 this imagery is used of YHWH's action.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:9 "Sheol"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:9 "Sheol" Sheol is personified as preparing a welcoming gathering for the fallen kings. It (BDB 982) refers to the holding place of the dead. In the OT life after death is described as being a conscious existence, but with no joy; people being a mere shadow of their former selves with enforced equality in silence (cf. Isa. 14:10-11, Job 3:17-19; 10:21-22; 21:23-26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD? I. B.

NASB  "spirits of the dead"
NKJV  "the dead"
NRSV, JPSOA  "the shades"
TEV, NJB  "ghosts"
LXX  "mighty ones"
REB  "the ancient dead"
Peshitta  "mighty men"

The term (BDB 952 I, cf. Isa. 26:19) is used in poetry for

  1. dead kings, TEV, NJB
  2. dead warriors, LXX
  3. dead ancestors, REB
  4. the dead in general, NASB, NKJV

In historical texts it refers to the Rephaim, an ethnic group associated with the giants. In Canaanite mythology this term referred to dead kings, leaders, and military heroes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS

NASB, NKJV, REB  "leaders of the earth"
NKJV  "chief one of the earth"
TEV  "those who were powerful"
NJB, Peshitta  "rulers of the world"
JPSOA  "earth's chieftans"
LXX  "who have ruled the earth"

This is literally "rams" (BDB 800, cf. Ezek. 34:17). It referred to the leader of a flock and then metaphorically of human societies. This is obviously ANE hyperbole, refering to the known world of that day.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:11 The first two lines denote the lavish and extravagant lifestyle of the ANE kings. They lay on pillows and slept on soft beds.

The last two lines describe the new bed of the kings in Sheol/grave (i.e. worms). Even the monarchs who saw themselves as gods, will one day be in a bed of worms! Mortality is a leveler of all mankind (cf. Isa. 5:14). What a contrast!

▣ "worms" Here it is used literally as an idiom for death and imagery for the fear of death and transitoriness of all human life.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:12 "How you have fallen from heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:12 "How you have fallen from heaven" The VERB (BDB 656, KB 709, Qal PERFECT) denotes a settled condition. The question is, "Is this literal or figurative?" The VERB is used for a violent death (BDB 657, Isa. 14:2a). Isaiah uses it in Isa. 3:8; 8:15 for the destruction of a city. But the added phrase, "from heaven," is what causes commentators to assert an angelic being, as well as the similar words of Jesus in Luke 10:18.

NASB  "O star of the morning"
NKJV, Vulgate  "O Lucifer"
NRSV  "O Day Star"
TEV  "bright morning star"
NJB, LXX  "Day star"
REB  "Bright morning star"
JPSOA, NET  "O Shining One"
Peshitta  "O Reviler of the nations"

The Hebrew NOMINATIVE MASCULINE term is הילל (BDB 237, KB 245). This form is found only here in the OT. The VERBAL root, הלל can mean

  1. "shine," possibly referring to the new moon
  2. "be boastful" or "to praise," from which we get the Hallel psalms (i.e. praise psalms)

The KB mentions several options as to the origin of this root.

  1. from a Ugaritic root, hll
  2. from an Arabic root, the crescent of the new moon
  3. from a Hebrew root, uncertain, but probably refers to Venus the morning star ("son of the dawn")
  4. from the Latin, Lucifer referring to Venus (i.e. lit. "light-bearer")

The whole point of the title is that this heavenly light is quickly eclipsed by the morning light. Its splendor is brief! There is a new, brighter, and better light coming!

▣ "You" The next two lines of Isa. 14:12 obviously refer to an earthly king of Assyria or Babylon (cf. Isa. 14:16-17). The imagery of the poem (Isa. 14:4-21) is taken from Canaanite mythology (esp. Isa. 14:13-14), which is known from Ras Shamra Tablets dating from the fifteenth century B.C. found at the city of Ugarit.

The terms "star of the morning" (Helal) and "dawn" (Shabar) are both the names of deities in Canaanite mythology, as is a mountain of the gods in the north (Mount Zaphon, cf. Ps. 48:2). Also the title for deity, "Most High," is common in Ugaritic poems and refers to Ba'al Shamim ("Lord of heaven"). In Canaanite mytho-poetry Helal, a lesser god, tries to usurp power, but is defeated. This is behind Isaiah's imagery of an arrogant eastern potentate.

This description of a proud, arrogant Near Eastern king is extended from Isa. 14:8-11. Only Isa. 14:12, taken literally following the Vulgate, and a lack of knowledge of Ugaritic literature can use this context as referring to a rebellious angelic leader (i.e. Satan).

entries.title: Isaiah 14:13 "stars of God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:13 "stars of God" The title for Deity is El, אל (BDB 42), which was a common designation of deity throughout the ANE. This, too, could reflect the Canaanite mythology from Ugarit. See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, "The Langauge of Myth," pp. 219, 242.

The stars were viewed as angels/gods who controlled human destiny (i.e. Babylonian astral worship from Ziggurats). This person wanted total control over the earth.

▣ "I will sit on the mount of assembly
  In the recesses of the north This is a Babylonian and Canaanite symbol of deity's abode (cf. Ps. 48:2; Ezek. 28:14). The surprising thing is its location "in the recesses of the north." This mountain of the gods in the far north was part of Canaanite mythology (i.e. Mt. Saphon). See Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, p. 279. The Greek gods also lived on a mountain, Mount Olympus.

Remember, verses 13-14 are alleged statements of an ANE king.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:13-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:13-14 These two verses show the arrogance and pride of the ANE kings (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP).

  1. "I will ascend to. . .," BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERFECT
  2. "I will raise my throne. . .," BDB 926, KB 1202, Hiphil IMPERFECT
  3. "I will sit on. . .," BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERFECT
  4. "I will ascend above...," same VERB as #1
  5. "I will make myself like. . .," BDB 197, KB 225, Hiphil IMPERFECT

Arrogance and pride are the essence of the fallen human spirit. YHWH uniquely judges this human self-deification!

entries.title: Isaiah 14:14 "Most High"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:14 "Most High" This title Elyon, עליון (BDB 751 II; see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, B.), is used by

  1. Balaam in Num. 24:16 and is parallel to Shaddai (i.e. Almighty, BDB 994; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADDAI)
  2. Moses in his Song before his death in Deut. 32:8
  3. David in 2 Sam. 22:14 and in several Psalms
  4. in the Ras Shamra Tablets for the Canaanite High god

entries.title: Isaiah 14:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:15 Instead of going to the mountain in the far (BDB 438) north, he will go down to the depths (BDB 438), Sheol.

The term Sheol (BDB 982, see SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?, I. B.) is parallel to "the pit" (BDB 92, cf. Ezek. 31:16), which is another name for the grave (cf. Prov. 28:17). The same term is used in Isa. 14:19 and is parallel to tomb/sepulcher (cf. Isa. 14:18).

The JPSOA translation's footnote (p. 813) asserts that "to the recesses of the pit" (NASB) should be translated "to the bottom of the Pit." It bases this on Ezek. 32:21-32, where the lowest part of Sheol is reserved for those who did not receive a proper burial (cf. Isa. 14:19).

entries.title: Isaiah 14:16-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 14:16-19 This is the fourth strophe; it refers to the astonishment of the on-lookers in Sheol at the body of the dead King of Babylon. It is similar to Isa. 14:9-11.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:17 This verse denotes the aggressive deportation practices of both Assyria and Babylon. This population control mechanism is reversed by Cyrus II (Medo-Persia) in 538 B.C.

14:19
NASB  "like a rejected branch"
NASB margin  "like an abhorred branch"
NKJV  "like an abominable branch"
NRSV, REB, JPSOA  "like loathsome carrion"
NJB  "like a loathsome branch"
LXX  "like an abominable corpse"
Peshitta  "like an abominable person"
RSV, NEB  "like one untimely born"
NET  "like a shoot that is thrown away"

The MT has the NOUN "shoot" (BDB 666, KB 718 II), which the Aramaic Targums translated as "miscarriage" (BDB 664, RSV, "an untimely birth).

This is followed by "loathed" (BDB 1073, KB 1765, Niphal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE). This imagery refers to a rejected king as cast from his tomb.

The UBS Text Project, p. 31, gives "like a shoot" a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

This same term (BDB 666) is used in Isa. 6:13 of "the holy seed in the stump" and in Isa. 11:1 of the stem/shoot from Jesse, both of which refer to the Messiah, the true King. The kings of ANE are a "rejected branch"!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BRANCH OF THE LORD

▣ "Like a trampled corpse" This speaks of the humiliation of an improper burial (possible reference to Sargon II). Not only did the king miss the royal funeral, he missed burial altogether!

The term "trampled" (BDB 100, KB 115, Hophal PARTICIPLE) is also used in Isa. 14:25 (Qal IMPERFECT).

  1. It was imagery for YHWH's judgment (cf. Isa. 63:6, Qal IMPERFECT and 63:18, Polel PERFECT).
  2. The Psalms use it regularly for the covenant people's victory over enemies through YHWH's power and presence (cf. Ps. 44:5; 60:12; 108:13).
  3. A disobedient covenant people trample God's land (cf. Jer. 12:10; Polel PERFECT).

entries.title: Isaiah 14:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:20 Not only will the arrogant king be denied a proper burial, he will not be succeeded by a family member. He and his family will be cut off. His own country will not remember him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

entries.title: Isaiah 14:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:21 The king's descendants will be killed because of their father's sins. This reflects Exod. 20:5. The king and his wicked nation must not be allowed to prosper. YHWH wants the earth full, but not of unrighteousness.

▣ "with cities" This line of poetry is a rejection of the Assyrian King's attempt to dominate all of the ANE.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:22 "offspring and posterity"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:22 "offspring and posterity" These two terms refer to descendants.

  1. current children (BDB 630)
  2. the family tree or lineage (BDB 645)

Loss of descendants was seen as a great shame and curse in the ANE (cf. Isa. 47:9). It may even have been thought to affect one's afterlife.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:22-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 14:22-23 This forms a prose conclusion. It seems to me that Isa. 14:23 is related to Isa. 13:21-22, which is imagery to describe the total desolation of this nation, this king, and his city.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:23 "I will sweep it with the broom of destruction"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 14:23 "I will sweep it with the broom of destruction" YHWH is depicted as a wife/child cleaning the house by sweeping (BDB 370, KB 367, Pilpel PERFECT with waw). All the trash is removed. What a domestic, but powerful imagery (unique to Isaiah).

entries.title: Isaiah 14:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:24 This verse asserts that God's plans and purposes will be accomplished. His word is sure (cf. Isa. 46:11; 55:8-9; Job 23:13; Ps. 33:9; Acts 4:28).

▣ "The Lord of hosts has sworn" By the power and authority of Himself, YHWH states His plans and purposes (cf. Isa. 14:24; 45:23; 62:8; Deut. 1:8,35; 2:14; 4:31; 6:10,18,23; Jer. 51:14; Amos 4:2; 8:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

entries.title: Isaiah 14:24-27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:24-27 Most English translations make a paragraph change here. But notice there is no "oracle" marker, which implies that Isa. 13:1-14:27 is one literary unit dealing with the destruction of Assyria. See Contextual Insights, C.

There is only one causality in OT theology—YHWH (cf. 2 Chr. 20:6; Eccl. 7:14; Isa. 14:24-27; 43:13; 45:7; 54:16; Jer. 18:11; Lam. 3:33-38; Amos 3:6b). It is a literary and theological way to assert YHWH's sovereignty! The OT does not discuss secondary causes.

  1. angelic temptation
  2. human choices
  3. natural calamities
  4. diseases

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

entries.title: Isaiah 14:25 "to break Assyria in My land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:25 "to break Assyria in My land" This may refer to the plague which devastated 185,000 troops of Sennacherib in one night before the gates of Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:13-19:37, esp. 19:35-37; 2 Chronicles 32).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

▣ "his yoke will be removed from them" This is a recurrent theme (cf. Isa. 9:4; 10:27). Yoke, like "staff" or "rod," was imagery of foreign oppression.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:26-27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:26-27 This Assyrian king had a plan for world domination (Isa. 14:26), but YHWH had another plan (cf. Isa. 8:10), a plan for world redemption (Isa. 14:27)! Assyria, Babylon and Persia are tools in YHWH's plan and no one can withstand His hand.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Isaiah 14:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:28 Notice there is an "oracle" mentioned in Isa. 14:28-32 which deals with YHWH's judgment on Philistia (i.e. the Philistines), but this is not linked to the Assyrian-oriented strophe of Isa. 14:24-27.

This strophe (vv. 28-32) is a separate prophecy about YHWH's judgment of Philistia. It is not related to the oracle about Assyria in vv. 1-23.

▣ "In the year that King Ahaz died" In my OT SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY, three scholars give their proposed dates for Ahaz.

  1. John Bright, 735 ‒ 715 B.C.
  2. E. J. Young, 736 ‒ 728 B.C.
  3. R. K Harrison, 732/731 ‒ 716/715 B.C.

These dates (reign and co-reign, not necessarily death) could fit four aggressive Assyrian kings.

  1. Tiglath-Pileser III, 745 ‒ 727 B.C.
  2. Shalmaneser V, 727 ‒ 722 B.C.
  3. Sargon II, 722 ‒ 705 B.C.
  4. Sennacherib, 705 ‒ 681 B.C. (185,000 soldiers killed before the walls of Jerusalem in 701 B.C., cf. Isaiah 36-39; 2 Kings 18-19).

Number 3, Sargon II, died in battle away from home and did participate in a military campaign against Philistia.

entries.title: Isaiah 14:29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:29 Philistia is commanded not to rejoice (BDB 970, KB 1333, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense) because the evil empire has been defeated. Their short-term deliverance will not last!

▣ The last two lines of Isa. 14:29 are very ambiguous and uncertain. They seem to mean that things will go from bad to worse.

The phrase "flying serpent" is the NOUN "serpent" (BDB 977 I, cf. Isa. 30:6; Num. 21:6) plus the PARTICIPLE "flying" (BDB 733, KB 800, Polel PARTICIPLE), which denotes rapid movement (i.e. striking, sliding, darting).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERAPHIM

entries.title: Isaiah 14:30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:30 The first two lines refer to God's care for

  1. His covenant people who have been oppressed by Philistia (cf. Isa. 14:32c) or
  2. the needy of society; the MT uses the imagery "the first-born of the poor"

▣ "I will destroy. . .it will kill" These two lines of poetry describe YHWH's action "I," v. 30c, by the means of famine, the "it" of v. 30d. This is another example of OT theology whereby there are no secondary causes, only God's actions.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

entries.title: Isaiah 14:31 "Wail, O gate; cry, O city"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:31 "Wail, O gate; cry, O city" These two IMPERATIVES

  1. wail, BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil
  2. cry, BDB 277, KB 277, Qal

describe the overthrow of the five cities of the Philistines, each with its own king (city states).

▣ "Melt away, O Philistia, all of you" The VERB (BDB 556, KB 555, Niphal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE) describes the paralyzing fear which grips a population (cf. Exod. 15:15; Josh. 2:9,24; 1 Sam. 14:16).

Note this phrase refers to the destruction of the entire society (cf. Jeremiah 47 and Amos 1:6-8).

entries.title: Isaiah 14:31 "For smoke comes from the north"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:31 "For smoke comes from the north" The empires of the Fertile Crescent are to the east of Canaan, but because of the desert in between their armies, had to follow the Euphrates to its headwaters and then move south along the coastal plain. Therefore, "north" became an idiom of invasion, evil, and destruction.

  1. here it refers to Assyria
  2. in Jer. 4:6; 6:1,22; 10:22; 13:20; 15:12; 46:20,24; Ezek. 26:7 it refers to Neo-Babylon

▣ "there is no straggler in his ranks" This describes a new Mesopotamian invader. One is gone (cf. Isa. 14:29), but another one, a worse one (cf. Isa. 14:29c,d), is coming!

entries.title: Isaiah 14:32 "seek refuge"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:32 "seek refuge" See SPECIAL TOPIC: REFUGE (OT)

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Does Isaiah 13-14 refer to Babylon or Assyria?
  2. Are Isaiah 13 and 14 talking about a particular historical king or is the title used as a symbol of godless human government?
  3. Is Isaiah 14 a reference to Satan?
  4. Does this chapter mention demons or animals in Isa. 13:21-22; 14:23?
  5. Sum up the theological truth in one sentence.
  6. How is this prophecy used in the NT?

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 15:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
15:1 Notice how Isaiah's contextual marker of a new message or vision "oracle" (BDB 672 III) appears in Isa. 15:1. See note at Isa. 13:1 (cf. Isa. 14:28; 17:1; 19:1; 21:1,11,13; 22:1; 23:1; 30:6). This term denotes a divine revelation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "Moab" This is one of Israel's relatives from Lot and one of his two daughters after their flight from Sodom (cf. Genesis 19). Moab, Ammon, and Edom (i.e. the trans-Jordan nations) are first mentioned as receiving domination by Judah in Isa. 11:14.

Chapters 15-16 form a literary unit dealing with Moab's judgment (cf. Jeremiah 48; Ezek. 25:8-11; Amos 2:1-3; Zeph. 2:8-11). Moab is mentioned often in the book of Numbers because Israel had to travel through their land to get to Canaan. Moses was buried there (cf. Deuteronomy 34).

▣ "Surely in a night" This phrase is repeated twice and emphasizes the suddenness and completeness of the coming judgment of Moabite cities.

The two VERBS "devastated" (BDB 994, KB 1418) and "ruined" (lit. "cut off," BDB 198, KB 225) are both PERFECTS (there is a series of four PERFECT VERBS in v. 1), also denoting a complete destruction. Isaiah used the VERB "ruined" to describe himself in Isa. 6:5.

The Assyrian armies invaded Canaan/Palestine several times.

  1. Sargon II in 715 B.C.
  2. Sargon II in 711 B.C.
  3. Sennacherib in 701 B.C.

▣ "Ar" The term (BDB 786 I) can refer to a city (it is the general name for city in the Moabite language) or a region (i.e. Deut. 2:9,29).

Since Kir (BDB 885 II) also means "wall" (cf. LXX, i.e. walled city) in Hebrew, it is possible that Ar and Kir refer to the capital of Moab in parallel poetic lines.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS (locations mentioned in the literary unit of Isaiah 15-16)

 Isaiah was very familiar with the geographical area of the Trans-Jordan (east of Jordan).

  1. Cities
    1. Ar, Isa. 15:1
    2. Kir, Isa. 15:1 (Kir-hareseth, 16:7,11)
    3. Dibon, Isa. 15:2,9
    4. Nebo, Isa. 15:2
    5. Medeba, Isa. 15:2
    6. Heshbon, Isa. 15:4; 16:9
    7. Elealeh, Isa. 15:4; 16:9
    8. Jahaz, Isa. 15:4
    9. Zoar, Isa. 15:5
    10. Eglath-shelishiyah, Isa. 15:5 (lit. "the Third Eglath," cf. Jer. 48:34)
    11. Luhith, Isa. 15:5
    12. Horonaim, Isa. 15:5
    13. Eglaim, Isa. 15:8
    14. Beer-elim, Isa. 15:8
    15. Dimon (DSS, "Dibon"), Isa. 15:9
    16. Sela, Isa. 16:1
    17. Kir-hareseth, Isa. 16:7,11
    18. Sibmah, Isa. 16:8,9
    19. Jazer, Isa. 16:8,9
    20. Admah (Isa. 15:9 REB)?

  2. Water Courses
    1. water of Nimrim, Isa. 15:6
    2. brook of Arabim (possibly a "wadi of poplars"), Isa. 15:7
    3. waters of Dimon, Isa. 15:9
    4. fords of Arnon, 16:2

  3. The listing of these numerous cities and water courses are to emphasize a total destruction (the invader is unnamed and uncertain). There is a movement of refugees southward or to Judah (cf. Isa. 16:1-4).

  4. Isaiah 15-16 forms a literary unit related to YHWH's dealing with Moab, also note Jer. 48 and Ezek. 25:9-11.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: MOAB

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 15:2 "to the temple. . .even to the high places"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
15:2 "to the temple. . .even to the high places" This is a reference to Moabite places of worship of Chemosh (cf. Num. 21:29; Jer. 48:46). The temple of this Canaanite deity was possibly located near Dibon, Moab's capital. The worship of this god involved human sacrifice. Verse 9a (DSS has "Dybon," but the MT has "Dimon") mentions "blood," which may refer to

  1. human sacrifice
  2. military invasion

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHEMOSH

▣ "Dibon. . .Nebo. . .Medeba" There are also cities of Moab listed in the book of Numbers in relation to the Wilderness Wandering Period as Israel finally approached Canaan from the eastern side of the Jordan Rift Valley.

entries.title: Isaiah 15:2-3 wails. . .bald. . .beard cut off. . .mourning. . .girded with sackcloth. . .wailing"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
15:2-3 wails. . .bald. . .beard cut off. . .mourning. . .girded with sackcloth. . .wailing" These all refer to mourning rites of the ANE (cf. Isa. 22:12; Ezra 9:3; Job 1:20; Jer. 7:29; 16:6; 41:5; 47:5; 48:37; Ezek. 7:18; 27:31; Micah 1:16). The population tries to turn to their gods (cf. Isa. 15:2); they try to repent and seek help, but there is no help from lifeless idols!

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

entries.title: Isaiah 15:4 "Heshbon. . .Elealeh. . .Jahaz"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
15:4 "Heshbon. . .Elealeh. . .Jahaz" These are also cities on the eastern side of Jordan, close to and often identified with Moab (or Ammon, i.e. Mesha Stone, 9th century B.C.).

▣ "cry out" This is the VERB (BDB 277, KB 277, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) that was used in its Qal IMPERATIVE form in Isa. 14:31 (Philistia). Here it denotes Moab and in Isa. 15:5 it denotes YHWH or Isaiah. Note its use in Jer. 48:20,31.

▣
NASB  "the armed men"
NKJV, Peshitta  "the armed soldiers"
NRSV, LXX, JB  "the lions"
NJB  "warriors"
REB  "stoutest warriors"
JPSOA  "the shock troops"

The difference between "soldiers" (BDB 323 II) and "loins" (BDB 323) in Hebrew is vocalization, not a consonantal change.

▣ "His soul trembles within him" This VERB (BDB 438, KB 440, Qal PERFECT) appears only here. There are several Hebrew words translated "tremble." They denote fear and lack of action in the face of God's judgment. They characterize "holy war." This one may have been chosen for poetic reasons to sound like the VERB "cry out."

The term "soul" is nephesh and denotes air-breathing life on this planet. It is used as imagery for a human person.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

entries.title: Isaiah 15:5 "My heart cries out for Moab"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
15:5 "My heart cries out for Moab" The "my" in context must refer to YHWH Himself (cf. Isa. 15:9). Although it could be the prophet himself, cf. Isa. 16:9,11. YHWH hears the cries of Moab's people and is moved. They still receive judgment, but not from a thoughtless, uncaring God! They are even offered help/refuge in Isa. 16:1-4. What an amazing text!

The Septuagint changes the referent to "the heart of the region of Moab cries within her" (cf. NJB).

▣
NASB, NRSV, TEV, REB, JPSOA  "Eglath-shelishiyah"
NKJV, LXX, Peshitta  "like a three-year-old heifer" (from same root; KB 784)

This (BDB 722) seems to be a city (i.e. "third Eglath," cf. Jer. 48:34).

▣ "His fugitives" The MT has "her bars" (BDB 138, בריחה from בריה), but most translations change the vocalization to "his fugitives" from מברה (BDB 138).

entries.title: Isaiah 15:5-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 15:5-9 The Jewish Study Bible sees these verses as referring to Moabites fleeing to Edom (p. 815). This is possible because the exact location of these cities mentioned is uncertain, though all are east or southeast of the Jordan River.

entries.title: Isaiah 15:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 15:6 In the OT God controls the weather (cf. Deuteronomy 27-29). He brings abundance for covenant obedience, but withholds agricultural production in the face of evil, wickedness, and rebellion (i.e. the two ways, Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; 30:15,19; Psalm 1). Moab faces both invasion (cf. Isa. 15:9a) and lack of food.

entries.title: Isaiah 15:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
15:7 Moab was located on a major trade route from Egypt to Syria. She taxed all the caravans and became wealthy.

15:9
NASB, NRSV, NJB, REB  "A lion" (אריה, BDB 71, MT)
NKJV  "Lions"
JPSOA  "I drench it"
LXX  "I will remove the offspring"
Peshitta  "I will plot"
NEB  "a vision" (אראה)
DSS  "I give a drink" (ארוה)

the MT has "a lion for the remnant of the land." The UBS Text Project, p. 36, gave this a "C" rating (considerable doubt), but suggested it was an allusion to 2 Kgs. 17:25 (i.e. "YHWH sent lions").

This could be

  1. literal, God uses wild animals to judge (i.e. 1 Kgs. 13:24-28; 2 Kgs. 17:25)
  2. a symbol of the Assyrian army (cf. Isa. 5:29; Jer. 50:17)
  3. figurative of invasion from Judah (cf. Isa. 11:14, the lion [ruler] of Judah).

There are two ways to view this strophe.

  1. The JPSOA significantly changes the translation of this verse (esp. lines 2-4) to make it positive (cf. Isa. 15:5, "my").
     "For I pour added (water) on Dimon
     I drench it ‒ for Moab's refugees ‒ with soil (footnote, 'tears') for its remnant" (DSS)
  2. The LXX of Isa. 15:9, lines 2-4, are also very different, but decidedly negative.
     "For I will bring Arabs upon Remnon,
     and I will remove the offspring of Moab and Ariel
     and the remnant of Adama."

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 16:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:1 To whom is the tribute sent and from whom and why, are the contextual questions.

  1. the fleeing Moabites send a sacrificial gift to the Davidic ruler in Jerusalem to secure his aid, TEV, NRSV
  2. a reference to Messiah, cf. Isa. 16:5; Peshitta, Vulgate
  3. a message of continuing judgment and destruction even to the survivors of Moab, cf. Isa. 16:12

▣ "Send" The VERB (BDB 1018, KB 1511) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. It denotes a desperate, frantic action.

▣ "the tribute lamb" The MT has only "lambs" (BDB 503 III, PLURAL). Only NASB adds the ADJECTIVE "tribute" to its translation. As for the PLURAL vs. SINGULAR:

  1. PLURAL, NRSV, REB, JB, NET (UBS Text Project, p. 37, gives this a "C" rating)
  2. SINGULAR, MT, NJB, NASB, NKJV, TEV

Moab was known for its sheep (cf. 2 Kgs. 3:4).

The ancient versions have very different translations.

  1. LXX, "I will send as it were creeping animals on the land!"
  2. Peshitta, " I will send the son of the ruler of the land."
  3. JPSOA, "Dispatch a messenger to the ruler of the land."

▣ "From Sela" The basic meaning of the term (BDB 700) is "crag," "cliff" (cf. Jer. 51:25), but it came to designate a city in Edom, called Sela, or Petra (BDB 701 II, cf. 2 Kgs. 14:7; Isa. 42:11). However, Sela does not fit the context exactly so maybe another rock feature close to the border with Judea. It possibly simply denotes a southern route.

Where is not as important as from whom, to whom, and why.

▣ "to the mountain of the daughter of Zion" This is a figurative way of referring to YHWH's temple in Jerusalem (cf. Isa. 1:8; 10:32). This means that the lambs were given to be sacrificed to YHWH (cf. Ezra 7:17).

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 16:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:2 Moab is described as

  1. fleeing/fluttering birds, BDB 622 I, KB 672, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  2. scattered nestlings, BDB 1018, KB 1511, Pual PARTICIPLE

She is further identified as "the daughters of Moab," but this, like Isa. 16:14, refers to all the inhabitants of the land that remained alive.

▣ "at the fords of the Arnon" The Arnon River (wadi El-Mujib) flows into the middle of the Dead Sea on the eastern side. It was the geographical boundary between Ammon on the north and Moab on the south (extending to the Zered Brook [possible wadi El-Hesa]).

It is surprising that these fords (low water crossings) are not close to Judah's borders, but across the Dead Sea. Possibly a Judean military force had marched through Ammon to these fords. It is also possible that the phrase denotes a southern exodus from a northern invader.

entries.title: Isaiah 16:3 "Cast your shadow like night at high noon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:3 "Cast your shadow like night at high noon" This is metaphorical language for protection of a foreign refugee in Judah (cf. Deut. 23:16-17). It may be a specific historical reference to the Shekinah cloud of glory that followed the Israelites through this very land during the Wilderness Wandering Period. It was a cloud cover (shade and cool) in the daytime and pillar of fire at night. It symbolized YHWH's personal presence, provision, and protection.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW

entries.title: Isaiah 16:3-4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:3-4 These verses give

  1. the message (IMPERATIVES used as requests) which accompanied the lambs
  2. Isaiah's admonition for the Judeans to accept the Moabites. I think option #1 is best.
    1. "give advice," BDB 97, KB 112, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, written MASCULINE PLURAL, but to be read as FEMININE SINGULAR to agree with "advice" (BDB 420), which is FEMININE
    2. "make a decision," BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE
    3. "cast your shadow," BDB 1011, KB 1483, Qal IMPERATIVE (cf. Isa. 25:4; 32:2; Ps. 91:1)
    4. "hide the outcasts," BDB 711, KB 771, Piel IMPERATIVE
    5. "do not betray the fugitive," BDB 162, KB 191, Piel IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    6. "let the outcasts of Moab stay with you," BDB 157, KB 184, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    7. "be a hiding place to them," BDB 217, KB 241, Qal IMPERATIVE

Although Moab was a traditional enemy, there were close connections to the Davidic house (i.e. Ruth; 1 Sam. 22:3-5).

entries.title: Isaiah 16:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:4 There is a series of time conditions related to Moab's invasion after which the governmental authority of Judea will be extended to the whole area (cf. Isa. 16:5).

Here are the conditions.

  1. the extortioner (BDB 568) has come to an end (BDB 67, KB 79, Qal PERFECT)
  2. destruction (BDB 994, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) has ceased (BDB 477 I, KB 476, Qal PERFECT
  3. oppressors (BDB 942, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) have completely disappeared from the land (BDB 1070, KB 1752, Qal PERFECT)

entries.title: Isaiah 16:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:5 This verse describes the coming government from Judea (cf. Isa. 9:6-7; 11:3-5; see SPECIAL TOPIC: IMMANUEL'S PERSON AND REIGN).

  1. a throne will be established (PERFECT with waw) in lovingkindness (BDB 338, see SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS)
  2. a judge will sit (PERFECT with waw) on it in faithfulness (BDB 54) in the tent of David
  3. he will seek justice (BDB 1048, cf. Isa. 11:3,4)
  4. he will be prompt in righteousness ("righteousness," BDB 841, cf. Isa. 11:4,5, see SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS "prompt," BDB 555, usually means skilled in something, therefore, able to do it rapidly. Here it denotes a Davidic ruler who quickly acts in righteousness)

This verse is why the Peshitta and Vulgate view this context as Messianic.

entries.title: Isaiah 16:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:6 This begins a new strophe. Isaiah 16:1-5 is what YHWH hoped would happen, but Isa. 16:6 describes why it could not (compare Jer. 48:29).

  1. the pride of Moab
  2. excessive pride
  3. arrogance
  4. pride
  5. fury (BDB 720, "insolence")
  6. false, idle boasts (BDB 95 III, empty, imaginary pretensions, cf. Job 11:3; Jer. 48:30)

The Hebrew term "pride" (BDB 144) is repeated in different ways four times. Moab, like her idols, claims much, talks much, but cannot do anything!

entries.title: Isaiah 16:7-10 "Therefore"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:7-10 "Therefore" Here are the consequences.

  1. Moab shall wail because of her Ba'al worship (i.e. "raisin cakes"), Isa. 16:7,12
  2. fields wither and no harvest, Isa. 16:8-10 (cf. Isa. 15:6, another idiom for agricultural failure)

It is also possible that "raisin cakes" in this context refers to a luxurious lifestyle.

16:10 "wine" See SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM.

▣ "I have made the shouting to cease" This refers to YHWH-sent invaders who disrupted the harvest and its annual festivals.

The concept of the removal of "joy" is recurrent in this verse.

  1. gladness taken away, BDB 62, KB 74, Niphal PERFECT with waw
  2. joy taken away (assuming same VERB as #1)
  3. no cries (or songs) of joy, BDB 943, KB 1247, Pual IMPERFECT
  4. no jubilant shouting, BDB 929, KB 1206, Pola IMPERFECT
  5. shouting to cease, BDB 991, KB 1407, Hiphil PERFECT

entries.title: Isaiah 16:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:11 The question is who is speaking.

  1. YHWH (i.e. "My heart," lit. internal organs, מעה, BDB 588, KB 609, see SPECIAL TOPIC: INWARD PARTS, cf. Isa. 63:15; Jer. 31:20)
  2. the prophet
  3. Moab personified

Because of Isa. 16:12, Moab (#3) cannot be right. Because of Isa. 16:13 it could be #2, the prophet Isaiah, but because of Isa. 15:5,9, as well as the Messianic implications of Isa. 16:5, I think it is YHWH who grieves over the "what-could-have-been." YHWH loves humans made in His image, made for fellowship, yet they turn to false gods, false hopes!

The UBS Text Project, p. 38, gives a "C" rating to the "I," meaning YHWH is speaking.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣
NASB, REB   "Kir-hareseth"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, JPSOA   "Kir Heres"

The MT is reflected in NKJV, but it is a shortened form of the name in NASB (cf. Isa. 16:7; the city was simply referred to as "Kir" in Isa. 15:1).

entries.title: Isaiah 16:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:12 This verse can be understood in two ways.

  1. Moab brings offerings (Isa. 16:1) to Jerusalem (Isa. 16:5), but her pride refuses to fully embrace YHWH (Isa. 16:6). YHWH cares for them (Isa. 15:5; 16:11).
  2. Moab seeks help from her gods (i.e. "high place" and "sanctuary," Isa. 15:2; 16:12), but they are unable to respond.

entries.title: Isaiah 16:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
16:14 This describes the imminent (3 years) fate of prideful Moab!

Instead of abundant people, wealth, influence, and crops, Moab will be "very small and impotent"! The reversals in history are shocking and point fallen humanity to the promise and desire for stability and peace found only in Israel's God!

For a good brief discussion of "wage earners" (hired man), see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, p. 76.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 17:1 "Damascus"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:1 "Damascus" This was the capital of Aram/Syria. The invasion and destruction of Syria have been alluded to earlier in Isa. 7:16; 8:4; 10:9. It was an ancient city (cf. Gen. 14:15; 15:2) and an important city located on the northern and northeastern trade routes.

▣ Notice the synonymous parallelism of lines 2 and 3. Tiglath-pileser III partially destroyed Damascus in 732 B.C. It was rebuilt as a regional Assyrian capital. Remember all prophecy is hyperbolic (see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, pp. 99-102, and G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 110-117).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ISAIAH 17

  1. This context reflects the consequences of the alliance between Syria and Israel to rebel against Assyria. It is often called the Syro-Ephramatic War (735 B.C.)

  2. Syria and Israel tried to get Judah to join their coalition (cf. Isa. 7:1-8:23), but Ahaz refused and asked Assyria for help.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 17:2 "The cities of Aroer"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:2 "The cities of Aroer" This phrase is confusing.

  1. This is the name of a city, not a region.
  2. There are several cities that go by this name (BDB 792, which may refer to a "tree" or a "mountain crest," AB, vol. 1, p. 399). Three of the four possible sites are south of Syrian territory.
  3. The LXX leaves out the place name (as does REB).
  4. The Peshitta spells it Adoer.

It seems that Syria and Israel are linked together in this chapter. They had formed a political/military alliance against Assyria and tried to make Judah join. This co-alliance caused the Syro-Ephraimite war where these two northern nations invaded Judah (cf. Isa. 7:16; 8:4; 10:9) to force her to join their fight against Assyria.

Most of the references are to the Northern Ten Tribes called

  1. Israel/Jacob (Isa. 17:4)
  2. Samaria
  3. Ephraim (Isa. 17:3)

Syria was under Israelite control during the United Monarchy period.

Aroer is probably a reference to the fortress located on the Arnon River near Dibon.

entries.title: Isaiah 17:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:3 The walled fortified cities of Syria and Ephraim will disappear (BDB 991, KB 1407, Niphal perfect with waw). The JPSOA has a footnote that supports a textual emendation from "Ephraim" (BDB 68) אפרים to ארם "Aram" (BDB 78), which would be a true parallelism. But if the first strophe is about the Syro-Ephraimite War, then the parallelism is already there. I think Isa. 17:3 has an AB, BA poetic pattern (chiasim), as it is in the MT.

▣ "the remnant of Aram" This phrase could refer to

  1. the capital as the only place of Syrian power that remains (and it will fall, Isa. 17:6)
  2. when the capital falls most of the population will not survive

▣ Although the last two lines of Isa. 17:3 appear to be positive, they are not. Ephraim is destroyed in 3a, now Syria shares her fate (sarcastically, "glory," cf. Isa. 17:4). "Glory" could refer to the capital of Israel, "Samaria," which fell after an extended siege to Assyria under Sargon II in 722 B.C.

▣ "Declares the Lord of hosts" YHWH is in control of history, especially those events that affect His covenant people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS.

entries.title: Isaiah 17:4 "in that day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:4 "in that day" It is uncertain how the text which follows should be divided into poetic strophes. This phrase could denote the start of a new strophe (cf. Isa. 17:4, Isa. 17:7, Isa. 17:9, Isa. 17:11). It is difficult to know the difference between poetry and elevated prose (note paragraph divisions and poetic lines of different translations at the beginning of the chapter).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣
NASB   "fade"
NKJV, REB, Peshitta   "wane"
NRSV   "brought low"
TEV   "come to an end"
NJB   "dimimish"
JPSOA   "dwindle"
LXX   "failing"

This VERB (BDB 195, KB 223, Niphal IMPERFECT) originally referred to low hanging fruit or limbs, but the Niphal stem denoted that which was brought low or laid low (cf. Jdg. 6:6). The Qal stem is used in Isa. 19:6 and 38:14.

This is the first of several negative statements describing the fate of the Northern Ten Tribes.

  1. glory. . .will fade, Isa. 17:4
  2. fatness of his flesh will become lean, Isa. 17:4
  3. Jacob/Israel will be cut down, Isa. 17:5
  4. only a few olives left at the very top, Isa. 17:6

entries.title: Isaiah 17:5 "the valley of Rephaim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:5 "the valley of Rephaim" This refers to a fertile valley southwest of Jerusalem which is mentioned several times in the OT (cf. 2 Sam. 5:18,22; 23:13; 1 Chr. 11:15; 14:9; and here). It must have served as the origin of Isaiah's imagery of expected fruitfulness thwarted (cf. Isa. 17:4). Why Isaiah used a site in Judah, not Israel, is uncertain. "Rephaim" is the name used for a group of tall Canaanites.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS

entries.title: Isaiah 17:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:6 The initial harvest of olive trees was by shaking or striking the tree (cf. Isa. 24:13; Deut. 24:20). There were always a few olives left that would not fall. These were usually left for the poor (i.e. gleaners). Isaiah uses them as a symbol for a remnant of survivors.

▣ "Two or three. . .Four or five" This is an example of a Hebrew idiom for an indefinite amount.

entries.title: Isaiah 17:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:7 The parallelism of the verse links "Maker" (i.e. the Creator of heaven and earth or the creator of Israel, cf. Isa. 51:13) with "the Holy One of Israel" (a title used almost exclusively by Isaiah). This is an allusion to monotheism!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

entries.title: Isaiah 17:7-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:7-8 These verses form a contrast. Isaiah 17:7 denotes repentance, Isa. 17:8 what they turn from (i.e. idolatry). The question is to whom are these two verses directed.

  1. Israel
  2. Israel and Syria
  3. Israel, Syria, and Assyria
  4. all ANE cultures (i.e. "men," האדם)

Is this meant to be parallel to Isa. 7, 9, and 11? Also notice the promised victory of God's people in Isa. 17:12-14 (esp. 14d)!

entries.title: Isaiah 17:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:8 Instead of YHWH being the "maker" they have made their own gods (i.e. Ba'als and Asherim, line 3; 2:8,20; 30:22; 31:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "incense stands" The term (BDB 329 calls it a "sun-pillar," but KB 329 calls it a transportable "incense-altar"). It is always used in a negative sense in the context of idol worship (cf. Lev. 26:30; 2 Chr. 14:5; 34:4,7; Isa. 17:8; 27:9; Ezek. 6:4,6).

The NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 903, suggests that it may refer to the sanctuary of a foreign god.

entries.title: Isaiah 17:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:9 This seems to begin a new thought unit. It describes the coming judgment in hyperbolic agricultural imagery (MT)

  1. like the forsaken places of the forest
  2. like branches which they abandoned
  3. the land will be a desolation

This verse is translated very differently by the Septuagint and its translation is followed by JB, NRSV, and REB (and the JPSOA seems to acknowledge its validity in its footnote). The phrase denotes

  1. a rapid exodus where useless things are abandoned
  2. people groups conquered by the Israelites in the Conquest (i.e. the Amorites and Hivites)
NASB  "or like branches"
NKJV  "And an uppermost branch"
NRSV, TEV, REB  "of the Hivites and the Amorites"
NJB  "as were the woods and heaths"
JPSOA  "the Horesh and the Amir"
LXX  "the Amorites and Hivites"
Peshitta  "like an emirate"
NET  "summits of the Amorite"
MT  "places of the wood and the highest bough"

This phrase can be viewed as

  1. relating to Israel's past victories during the Conquest (i.e. Joshua)
    (NRSV, LXX, NET)
  2. relating to Assyria's invasion and destruction

entries.title: Isaiah 17:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:10 This verse is uniquely addressed to Israel and the reason for their judgment by their covenant Deity.

  1. forgotten the God (Eloah, BDB 43) of your salvation (i.e. Ps. 78:11,42; see note below)
  2. not remembered the rock of your refuge (i.e. Ps. 18:1-3; 78:35)
  3. planted delightful plants in honor of a strange god (cf. Isa. 1:29-30; 65:3; 66:17, i.e. sacred gardens or trees. It may refer to Adonis/Tammuz, a vegetation god to whom flowers were planted early in the spring, cf. AB, vol. 6, p. 318)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

▣ "the God of your salvation" This is a recurrent description of Israel's God (cf. Isa. 12:2; 17:10; 33:2; 45:17; 61:16; 62:10; Ps. 65:5; 68:19; 85:4). Salvation denotes deliverance from any force or pressure that denies or cancels YHWH's covenant desire for His people. Only Israel's sin can thwart His desires for them and yet, He remains "the God of your salvation" (cf. Micah 7:7; Hab. 3:13,18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT term)

entries.title: Isaiah 17:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:11 This refers to the sacred gardens #3 in Isa. 17:10 above.

  1. they plant it carefully
  2. they fence it
  3. they fertilize it

It will grow and reproduce amazingly fast, but will result in

  1. harvest a heap
  2. sickliness
  3. incurable pain (cf. Job 34:6; Jer. 15:18; 17:9; 30:12,15; Micah 1:9)

entries.title: Isaiah 17:12-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:12-14 The strophe of invasion and destruction could refer to

  1. the Assyrian army defeating and destroying much of Syria and Israel
  2. the Syrian and Israelite armies approaching Jerusalem to force Judah into joining their rebellion against Assyria

This is the final strophe of chapter 17. It is characterized by parallelism and the repeated use of two roots.

  1. BDB 242, KB 250, "murmur," "grown," "roar," or "be boisterous"
    1. NOUN, Isa. 17:12
    2. Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, Isa. 17:12
    3. Qal IMPERFECT VERB, Isa. 17:12
  2. BDB 980, KB 1367, "roar," "uproar," "din," or "crash"
    1. NOUN (BDB 981), Isa. 17:12
    2. NOUN (BDB 981), Isa. 17:12
    3. Niphal IMPERFECT VERB, Isa. 17:12
    4. NOUN (BDB 981), Isa. 17:13
    5. Niphal IMPERFECT VERB, Isa. 17:13
  3. parallel imagery, Isa. 17:13
    1. like chaff, Isa. 17:13
    2. like dust, Isa. 17:13
    YHWH's roar is louder than the tumult of the nations and they will retreat as a result! He overcomes the chaotic waters again as in creation (cf. Psalm 29. see SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS).
  4. contrast, Isa. 17:14
    1. at evening, behold there is terror
    2. before morning they are no more
  5. synonyms, Isa. 17:14
    1. plunder, BDB 1042, KB 1367, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
    2. pillage, BDB 102, KB 117, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE

entries.title: Isaiah 17:14 "Before morning they are no more"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
17:14 "Before morning they are no more" This phrase has no VERBAL, which in Hebrew, would denote emphasis. This line gives a restorative context to Isa. 17:12-14. This strophe is parallel to the thoughts of Psalm 2. YHWH sends the nations (i.e. to punish His people for their covenant disobedience and lack of faithfulness), but He judges the very same nations. His people are safe in Him! This reversal is similar to Isa. 10:33-34.

Often in Isaiah God's deliverance is connected to the coming of light (cf. Isa. 8:22-9:2; 17:14; 29:18; 30:26; 33:2; 42:16; 49:9-10; 58:8,10; 60:1-3,19-20).

▣ "the portion" This term (BDB 324) denotes God's will in the imagery of a divine lot cast. It does not mean an arbitrary destiny or fate, but events are in the hand of God (cf. Jer. 13:25).

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

(1-6)
18:3
(3)		 18:3-6
(3-6)		 18:3-6
18:4-6
(4-6)
18:7 18:7 18:7 18:7

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

18:1
NASB  "Alas"
NKJV, Peshitta  "woe"
NRSV, JPSOA, LXX  "Ah"

This INTERJECTION (BDB 222) is used often in the prophets (i.e. Isa. 1:4,24; 5:8,11,18,20,21,22; 10:1,5; 17:12; 18:1; 28:1; 29:1,15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1; 45:9; 55:1). Mostly it expresses a negative reaction to the coming pain of divine judgment. However, in some contexts it denotes sympathy or pity, as in Isa. 18:1; 55:1; Jer. 47:6.

NASB, NKJV  "land of whirring wings"
NKJV  "the land shadowed with buzzing wings"
TEV  "a land where the sound of wings is hears"
NJB  "Land of the whirring locust"
LXX  "wings of a land of ships"
Peshitta  "the land of shadowing wings"
REB  "a land of sailing ships"
 (from Arabic and Aramaic cognates, Targums, and LXX)
JPSOA  "land of the deep shadow of wings"

This root (צלצל, BDB 852) has several possible meanings.

  1. BDB 852 I, whirring, buzzing as of the wings of insects
  2. BDB 852 II, spear whizzing in flight (cf. Job 40:7)
  3. same CONSONANTS, but different VOWELS, whirring locust (cf. Deut. 28:42)
  4. PLURAL, musical percussion instrument (cf. 2 Sam. 6:5; 1 Chr. 13:8; Ps. 150:5)
  5. related VERB (צלל, BDB 852), tingle (cf. 1 Sam. 3:11; 2 Kgs. 21:12; Jer. 19:3) or quiver (cf. Hab. 3:16)
  6. BDB 853 II, sink (cf. Exod. 15:10)
  7. BDB 853 III, grow dark (cf. Neh. 13:19; Ezek. 31:3)
  8. related NOUN, צל, shadow (BDB 853, cf. Isa. 4:6; 16:3; 25:4,5; 30:2,3; 32:2; 34:15; 38:8; 49:2; 51:16 (this is how JPSOA translates the phrase)
NASB, MT, NJB, REB  "Cush"
NKJV, LXX, Peshitta  "Ethiopia"
NRSV footnote, JPSOA  "Nubia"

This refers to the land area south of the first cataract of the Nile. It was known in Genesis as "Cush" (BDB 468, cf. Gen. 2:13; 10:6,7,8). In the Greek period it was called "Ethiopia." Today it would include the Sudan and parts of modern Ethiopia (TEV footnote, p. 625).

In this context (i.e. Isaiah 19), it may refer to the 25th Dynasty of Nubian rulers of Egypt (i.e. Pianchia, Shabaka).

However, notice that the people addressed are "beyond the rivers of Cush." Maybe Egypt herself is looking for mercenaries!

entries.title: Isaiah 18:2 "papyrus vessels"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:2 "papyrus vessels" At first one would think this must refer to sailing vessels on the Nile, but these same kinds of boats also were used on the Tigris and Euphrates (cf. James M. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible, p. 2560

▣ "Go" This is a Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 229, KB 246). To whom is this addressed?

  1. envoys from Cush
  2. envoys from Egypt
  3. envoys from mercenary groups south of Cush
  4. envoys from Assyria
  5. all human armies opposing YHWH and His covenant people

Isaiah regularly switches from a historical setting or event to an eschatological setting. The events and crises of his day foreshadow the events of the climatic conclusion of history. This fluidity is difficult to lock down into one historical referent (time, place, people). Cosmic consequences and purposes are at work behind existential events (i.e. Daniel 10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

▣ This verse characterizes the nation.

  1. seafaring people (i.e. reed boats of the Nile or even possibly the Euphrates, BDB 479 CONSTRUCT BDB 167)
  2. tall people (BDB 604, KB 645, Pual PARTICIPLE, lit. "to extend"; Herodotus says they were the tallest people in Africa)
  3. smooth people, BDB 598, KB 634, Pual PARTICIPLE (used of bald heads, but also polished swords and people's skin:
    1. no blemishes, REB, TEV, "smooth-skinned'
    2. consistent color, "bronzed", NJB
    3. clean shaven, no facial hair)
  4. feared far and wide
  5. a powerful nation (Hebrew uncertain, but possibly an idiom for "strange language"; see JPSOA and NET Bible, p. 1216, #4)
  6. an oppressive nation (Hebrew uncertain)
  7. land divided by rivers (Hebrew uncertain, this VERB, BDB 102, KB 107, Qal PERFECT, occurs only in this chapter, twice. The translation "divide" is based on an Aramaic root. REB has "scourged," referring to an annual flood, however, it could refer to the Tigris and Euphrates or the White and Blue Nile)

Numbers 2-6 are repeated in Isa. 18:7. This description fits the people south of the first cataract of the Nile, a tall, dark, warlike people group, but it does not fit Assyrians.

However, this context could be understood as Egypt seeking military alliances against Assyria. The term translated "tall" is never translated this way anywhere else. The universal ring of Isa. 18:3 could turn this poem into a message from YHWH that there is no one who can save a nation from His judgment. Egypt herself, nor any other notorious warlike people, can help Judah (cf. Isaiah 7), only YHWH.

Contextually the question

  1. is Isaiah 18 an independent poem?
  2. is Isaiah 18 related to Isaiah 17?
  3. is Isaiah 18 related to Isaiah 19?
NASB  "a powerful and oppressive nation"
NKJV  "a nation powerful and treading down"
NRSV  "a nation mighty and conquering"
TEV  "a strong and powerful nation"
JPSOA  "a nation of gibber and chatter"
LXX  "a foreign and fierce people"

The LXX and Peshitta translate this text as addressing a defeated nation, but this is not followed by modern translations.

There are two descriptive NOUNS used of these people.

  1. The term "mighty" (BDB 876) is doubled. This could intensify the term (i.e. sound of their marching armies, IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 608) or, like JPSOA, change it into a description of their language.
  2. The second term (BDB 101) is literally "to tread down" (NKJV) as imagery of conquest.

entries.title: Isaiah 18:3 "All you inhabitants of the world and dwellers on earth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:3 "All you inhabitants of the world and dwellers on earth" Isaiah has addressed this larger group several times (cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 9:7; 11:10,11-12; 12:4-6; 17:7-8; 26:9). What happens to YHWH's covenant people affects all nations. The term can refer to worldwide redemption or judgment (cf. Isa. 13:11; 24:4; 34:1). In a sense, the use of this term "world" (BDB 385) shows YHWH's universal significance, power, and presence, as does the literary unit of judgment on the surrounding ANE nations. YHWH's acts affect all the earth. He is the Lord of creation! See SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD, I. E.

Who sends the message of Isa. 18:3 and to whom is it addressed?

  1. Cush to Assyria
  2. Anti-Assyrian coalition to Cush (NRSV footnote)
  3. Anti-Assyrian message of possible cooperation to Syria and Israel (REB footnote). This makes Isaiah 18 related to Isaiah 17.
  4. Cush responding to a message for help from Judah (Jewish Study Bible footnote)
  5. JB footnote says that this whole passage refers to Egypt because at this period the Pharaohs were Nubian. So it would be a literary unit related to Isaiah 19, not 17!
  6. Assyria to the world (i.e. inhabited, known world)
  7. YHWH to all human enemies who oppose His purpose and people (cf. Psalm 2)

Thus we see again the ambiguous, yet powerful, imagery of Hebrew poetry.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ These were means of communicating in battle (i.e. raised standard and trumpet). These symbols could be for

  1. judgment (cf. Isa. 18:5-6)
  2. salvation (cf. Isa. 18:7)

How wonderfully this little poem depicts the chaos of earth vs. the tranquility of heaven, as well as what looked like a judgment becomes an invitation (i.e. Isa. 2:2-4; 11:10; 49:6; 51:4-8).

entries.title: Isaiah 18:4 "For thus the Lord has told me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:4 "For thus the Lord has told me" This is another specific reference to Isaiah's claim of inspiration. His message was not his own, but YHWH's! This is the issue of biblical authority! Has God spoken? Can we understand it? Can we trust it? These are foundational questions that must be answered by everyone and anyone who comes in contact with the Bible. See my sermons: "The Trustworthiness of the Old Testament" and "The Trustworthiness of the New Testament" online at www.freebiblecommentary.org. The video links are in the opening paragraph on the home page.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

▣ Lines 2 describes God's message to Cush or to Assyria. He speaks securely (two COHORTATIVES) from

  1. Mt. Moriah, the temple where He dwells between the wings of the Cherubim over the Ark of the Covenant
  2. a reference to heaven (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:39,43,49). His presence is radiant!

In the book of Isaiah Jerusalem will never be taken. This verse may reflect that theology. The world may be at war (Isa. 18:3), but Judah is secure in YHWH's security (i.e. Isa. 7:4; 8:8). Judah need not form an alliance with Syria/Israel or Egypt. Assyria will be totally defeated.

YHWH's security, tranquility, and peace in heaven are contrasted with the chaos on earth. This is very similar to the literary structure of the NT book of Revelation, where chaos on earth is described in chapters 2-3, but the heavenly throne room is quiet and peaceful in Isaiah 4-5! History is not a flux, but a means to a teleological climax designed and orchestrated by God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ARK OF THE COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

entries.title: Isaiah 18:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:5 YHWH's message of judgment is given in agricultural imagery, which is so common in Isaiah. A lost harvest would devastate those who depended on annual food crops.

This is imagery of rapid judgment (cf. Isa. 17:14).

entries.title: Isaiah 18:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 18:6 The death of the human population will become a banquet for the birds of prey and wild beasts (cf. Isa. 56:9; Jer. 7:33; Ezek. 32:4-6; 39:17-20).

entries.title: Isaiah 18:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:7 A time is coming when the remnant of these people (or possibly the whole Gentile world) will send another message, but this time not a threat (cf. Isa. 18:3), but an offering to YHWH in Jerusalem (cf. Isa. 18:7, line 6). The gift would be a cultural/religious symbol acknowledging YHWH's lordship and reign. The enemies of Isa. 18:1-2 are now worshipers! This is the fulfillment of Gen. 3:15. The redemptive purpose is wider than Abraham's physical seed. It encompasses his spiritual seed (cf. Isa. 12:4-5; 25:6-9; 42:6-12; 45:22-23; 49:5-6; 51:4-5; 60:1-3; 66:23; Rom. 2:28-29)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, REB, LXX  "from"
NJB  "on behalf of"

The MT has the NOUN "people" (BDB 766 I), but no PREPOSITION. Possibly the people themselves are the offering.

The DSS and Septuagint and Vulgate have the preposition "from."

▣ "a people" The NASB gives several descriptive terms to characterize this nation.

  1. tall (BDB 604, KB 645, Pual PARTICIPLE)
  2. smooth (BDB 598, KB 634, Pual PARTICIPLE)
  3. feared far and wide (BDB 431, KB 432, Niphal PARTICIPLE)
  4. powerful (BDB 876)
  5. oppressive (BDB 876)
  6. conquering (BDB 101)
  7. whose land the river divides (BDB 102, KB 117, Qal PERFECT, found only here, possibly Aramaic root, "to cleave")

▣ "the name of the Lord of hosts" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE NAME OF YHWH

SPECIAL TOPIC: The Lord of Hosts

▣ "Mount Zion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ZION

entries.title: Isaiah 19:1 "the Lord is riding on a swift cloud"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:1 "the Lord is riding on a swift cloud" This is imagery describing YHWH as

  1. controller of nature
  2. director of nature's power
  3. swift in His coming

See Ps. 18:10; 104:3. The phrase has Messianic connections in Dan. 7:13 and Matt. 26:64; Mark 14:62.

As with many OT phrases that describe YHWH we find that similar ones are used of pagan deities or rulers of the ANE. Riding on clouds is used of Ba'al in Ugaritic poems. As God's people encountered the hyperbolic statements/claims of the surrounding nations, she attributed them to her God, the only God (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM). The one in whom they may truly find peace and fulfillment. This is true of phrases such as "King of kings and Lord of lords" and so many other popular titles of YHWH.

It is verses like this that have caused me to rethink my eschatological understanding of several passages in the NT. The "coming on the clouds" imagery is misunderstood by modern, western literalitsts. YHWH used a foreign army to judge Egypt. This is what He did to apostate Judaism in the Jewish War with Rome (A.D. 66-70). I hope you will look at my Partial Preterist commentary of

  1. the Olivet Discourse (Matt. 24-25; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21; also note Matt. 23)
  2. 2 Thessalonians 2 (i.e. Nero)
  3. the book of Revelation (2024)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COMING ON THE CLOUDS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.

▣ "and is about to come to Egypt" YHWH's presence again is both a judgment (Isa. 19:1-15) and a salvation (Isa. 19:16-23). It is this double meaning that runs through much of Hebrew prophecy. The literary technique known as "reversal" dominates this genre. It is like antithetical parallelism taken to a larger piece of writing (as is paradox).

Egypt will be judged to be cleansed and prepared to worship YHWH. He will come to her in deliverance as He has to Judah. YHWH's heart is directed at humans made in His image (cf. Gen. 1:26-27), not just a select group of humans (i.e. Israel). He uses Abraham's seed to accomplish a larger purpose (cf. Gen. 3:15)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

▣ "The idols of Egypt" Egypt had many gods (Exod. 12:12; Num. 33:4). Her idolatry and spiritism are delineated in Isa. 19:3.

  1. idols (BDB 47)
  2. ghosts of the dead (BDB 31, found only here)
  3. mediums (BDB 15, "necromancers," cf. Deut. 18:11)
  4. spiritists (BDB 396, "wizards," "familiar spirits," cf. Deut. 18:11)

See note at Isa. 8:19.

The plagues of the Exodus purposefully depreciated many of the Egyptian gods for the purposes of producing faith in both Israelites and Egyptians (i.e. "mixed multitude," cf. Exod. 12:38).

In this text the people claimed to have the power or spiritual connection (i.e. familiar spirit) to communicate with the dead (cf. Lev. 19:31; 20:6,27; Deut. 18:11; 1 Sam. 28:8; 2 Kgs. 21:6; 2 Chr. 33:6; Isa. 8:19; 19:3). They were seeking information about and control of the future, but apart from YHWH. This is caused by

  1. the fallen nature of humanity (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND)
  2. self-deceived priests/prophets
  3. demon activity (see SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONIC IN THE OT)
  4. search for spiritual power over our lives and the lives of others (see SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY [OT])

▣ The last two lines of Isa. 19:1 are parallel (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY).

  1. the idols of Egypt will tremble, BDB 631, KB 681, Qal PERFECT with waw, cf. Isa. 6:4; 7:2 (twice); 19:1; 24:20 (twice); 29:9; 37:22 (i.e. personification of lifeless idols)
  2. the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them, BDB 587, KB 606, Niphal IMPERFECT, cf. Isa. 13:7; Josh. 2:11; 5:1; 7:5 (i.e. "holy war" terminology)
