READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 19:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:2 One wonders if this relates to

  1. the military advance of the Nubian rulers against the native Egyptians of the Delta region of the Nile (8th century B.C.; 25th Dynasty)
  2. the conflicts between the different cities of Egypt, each with their special gods (i.e. vv. 11-13)

This internal conflict between the same people and their armies is another example of "holy war" (i.e. Jdg. 7:22; 1 Sam. 14:20; 2 Chr. 20:23).

▣ "I will. . ." Isaiah is speaking directly for YHWH (Isa. 19:2,3,4). YHWH causes

  1. civil war, Isa. 19:2
  2. demoralization, Isa. 19:3a
  3. confused counsel/strategy, Isa. 19:3b
  4. reliance on false gods, Isa. 19:3,c,d
  5. the coming of a cruel master, a mighty king, Isa. 19:4

He is in control of the nations and their destinies (i.e. Dan. 2:21; Job 14:5; Ps. 31:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

▣
NASB, REB, JPSOA  "I will incite"
NKJV  "I will set"
NRSV, TEV, NJB, LXX, Peshitta  "I will stir up"

This uncertain VERB (possibly BDB 696 I or BDB 1127) is used twice in the Pilpel stem (Isa. 9:11 and here). In context it seems to mean

  1. stir up
  2. provoke
  3. incite (Ethiopian root)
  4. cause to stink (an Arabic root, cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 233)

entries.title: Isaiah 19:3 "confound"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:3 "confound" This Hebrew root (BDB 118 I, KB 134, Piel IMPERFECT) normally means "to swallow." Many scholars assume a second meaning for the same root, "confound" or "confuse" (BDB 118, Piel, #2a, cf. Isa. 3:12; 9:15; 28:7).

▣  "they will resort to idols and ghosts of the dead,

And to mediums and spiritists"

  1. idols (BDB 47, cf. Isa. 2:18,20; 10:10; 31:7)
  2. ghosts (i.e. sorcerers, BDB 31, cf. Isa. 8:19; 29:4; 47:12-13)
  3. mediums (BDB 3, linked to the word "father," i.e. necromancers)
  4. spiritists (i.e. wizards, BDB 396, cf. Lev. 19:31; 20:6,27; Deut. 18:11; 2 Kgs. 21:6; Isa. 8:19)

Initially, Egypt will seek help from its wise men, but they cannot help. In this wonderful chapter, they will eventually seek YHWH (see SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord). For more information:

  1. see my exegetical commentary on Deut. 18:9-14 online, free
  2. see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 196-302
  3. see SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

entries.title: Isaiah 19:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:4 In context (cf. Isa. 20:4) this could refer to

  1. Assyria (cf. chap. 20)
  2. Nubian invaders (cf. chap. 18)
  3. The same terminology is used for Babylon in Jer. 46:26; Ezek. 29:19.

YHWH directs world empires for His purposes.

You must decide if this is typical ANE royal hyperbole, so common in the ancient world (see D Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks), or reality (i.e. a biblical world view). Inspired authors take the terminology of the ANE and apply it to YHWH. Its validity is a faith issue! Is the Bible a unique, inspired, self-revelation of the one true God? This is the issue! See my sermons on "Why I Trust the OT" and "Why I Trust the NT" online at www.freebiblecommentary.org in the first paragraph).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

▣ "I will deliver" This VERB (BDB 698, KB 755, Piel PERFECT with waw) means "hand over to" (cf. Targums, LXX, Peshitta). The Piel appears only here. The VERB does appear in the Niphal in Gen. 8:2 and Ps. 63:11, where it means "be stopped." The Piel connotation comes from an old Aramaic root. Therefore, there may be two separate Hebrew roots.

entries.title: Isaiah 19:5-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:5-10 This strophe describes YHWH's judgment on Egypt.

  1. their abundant water from the Nile dries up
  2. with its loss the river vegetation dies (i.e. reeds [BDB 889] and rushes [BDB 693])
  3. with its loss irrigated crops die
  4. with its loss the fishing industry will lament and languish
  5. with the loss the clothing industry stops (i.e. linen from flax)
  6. Egyptian society comes to a crushing, grinding stop.
  7. all hired laborers will grieve.

There are three related VERBS which denote the loss of water.

  1. "dry up," BDB 677, KB 732, Niphal PERFECT with waw, Isa. 19:5; 41:17;
  2. "be parched," BDB 351, KB 349, Qal IMPERFECT, Isa. 19:5,6; 11:15; 37:25; 44:27; 50:2; 51:10
  3. "be dry," BDB 386, KB 384, Qal PERFECT with waw, Isa. 19:5,7; 15:6; 27:11; 40:7,8,24; 42:15 (twice); 44:27

God's ability to control water is recurrent in the OT.

  1. separated water above and water below, Gen. 1:7
  2. gathered the waters so dry land could appear, Gen. 1:9-10
  3. sent the flood, Gen. 7:4,7
  4. dried up the flood, Gen. 8:2-3
  5. provided a well of water for Hagar, Gen. 21:19
  6. split and restored the Sea of Reeds, Exod. 14:16,27
  7. purified the water at Marah, Exod. 15:22-25
  8. provided water that came from rocks in the wilderness, Num. 20:8,11
  9. promised agricultural abundance if covenant was obeyed, Deuteronomy 27-28
  10. split the Jordan River, Josh. 3:14-17; 4:23-24
  11. dried up the Nile and its tributaries, Isa. 19:5
  12. will dry up the Euphrates, Rev. 16:12
  13. water flows from the new temple (Ezek. 47:1) from Jerusalem (Zech. 14:8) and the new heavenly city, Rev. 22:1

For desert people these were truly mighty miracles and proof of God's power because water was a symbol of life itself. Remember, the Nile was viewed as one of the main deities of Egypt (as was Re, the sun god, cf. Isa. 19:18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS/SEA

entries.title: Isaiah 19:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:11 Line 4 is idiomatic for a group of wise men, similar to which Daniel was a part in Babylon. The JPSOA has "A scion of Kedomite king."

The word "son" functions as "member of a group."

SPECIAL TOPIC: "SONS OF. . ."

entries.title: Isaiah 19:11-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:11-15 This strophe is an elaboration of Isa. 19:3.

  1. v. 11, "the princes of Zoan" (Tanis, capital of the Delta region) are mere fools (BDB 17, used of Judah in Jer. 4:22)
  2. v. 11, "the advice of Pharaoh's wisest advisers has become stupid" (lit. "brutish," BDB 129 II, KB 146, Niphal PARTICIPLE, cf. Jer. 10:14,21; 51:17)
  3. v. 13, "the princes of Zoan have acted foolishly" (BDB 383, KB 381, Niphal PARTICIPLE, cf. Jer. 5:4; 50:36)
  4. v. 13, "the princes of Memphis (Noph, another Egyptian capital) are deluded" (BDB 674, KB 728, Niphal PERFECT; Hiphil PERFECT used in Gen. 3:13)
  5. v. 13, "have led Egypt astray" (BDB 1073, KB 1766, Hiphil PERFECT, cf. Isa. 19:14; 3:12; 9:16; Jer. 23:13,32; Hosea 4:12; Micah 3:5)
  6. v. 14, "led astray. . .staggers" (same VERB as #5, here denoting drunkenness)

entries.title: Isaiah 19:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:12 YHWH asks a sarcastic rhetorical question. It is structured as two IMPERFECTS (BDB 616, KB 615, and BDB 393, KB 390) used in a JUSSIVE sense (i.e. "let them. . .").

They claimed to be wise (Isa. 19:11d; 1 Kgs. 4:30; Acts 7:22). They claimed to have plans (Isa. 19:3b), but their wisdom and plans are negated in YHWH's purposes (Isa. 19:12a).

entries.title: Isaiah 19:13 "Those who are the cornerstone of her tribes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:13 "Those who are the cornerstone of her tribes" Here, "cornerstone" (BDB 819) denotes city leaders (cf. Jdg. 20:2; 1 Sam. 14:38).

19:14
NASB, LXX, JPSOA  "mixed"
NKJV, Peshitta  "mingled"
NRSV, JB  "poured"
REB, NJB  "infused"

The MT has the VERB "mixed" (מסך, BDB 587, KB 605, Qal PERFECT), which denotes a strong drink (cf. Isa. 5:22). However, because of Isa. 29:10 it is possible the VERB should be נסך ("poured out," BDB 650, KB 703, Qal PERFECT), which is found in the DSS. In either case the point is drunkenness as imagery for confusion and instability.

▣ "a spirit of distortion" The term "spirit" (ruah, BDB 924) could denote

  1. mental confusion caused by YHWH
  2. these cities being influenced by the demonic
  3. simply parallel to drunkenness
    SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE, I.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEMONIC IN THE OT

The term "distortion" (DB 730) is found only here in the OT. It is from the VERB "to warp," BDB says it implies "warped judgment." City leaders unable to think clearly or in a way not affected by their idolatrous worldview.

This "confusion" is often a characteristic of YHWH's actions involved in "holy war."

entries.title: Isaiah 19:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:15 The second line has two contrasting idioms which denote all levels of society (cf. Isa. 9:14-15).

  1. head ‒ tail
  2. palm ‒ bulrush

There will be a God-sent (cf. Isa. 19:14a) total inability! Those who claimed to be wise (cf. Isa. 19:11d, 12a, 13c) have proven to be unwise because they trusted in

  1. false gods
  2. false religionists
  3. poor plans (cf. Isa. 19:3)

All of Egypt's leadership (cf. Isa. 19:11-12), civil and religious, are out of a job, as are all her laborers (cf. Isa. 19:8-10).

entries.title: Isaiah 19:16 "the Lord of hosts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:16 "the Lord of hosts" As the phrase "in that day" links these last five strophes (cf. Isa. 19:16, 18, 19, 23, 24), so does this recurrent title for YHWH (cf. Isa. 19:16, 17, 18, 20, 25 and Lord alone in Isa. 19:19, 20, 21, 22). The covenant God is very active in these wonderfully redemptive strophes for the nations!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

entries.title: Isaiah 19:16-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:16-17 This describes what YHWH's actions (i.e. "the waving of the hand of the Lord of hosts"; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND, I. C.) will do. His purpose (Isa. 19:17b, BDB 420) is that

  1. Egyptians will become like women, Isa. 19:16
  2. they will tremble, Isa. 19:16 (BDB 353, KB 350, Qal PERFECT with waw; as did their gods in v. 1)
  3. they will be in dread, Isa. 19:16 (BDB 808, KB 922, Qal PERFECT with waw)
  4. Judah will become a terror to Egypt, Isa. 19:17 (NOUN, "terror" or "reeling," BDB 291, found only here)
  5. they will be in dread, Isa. 19:17 (BDB 808, KB 922, Qal IMPERFECT, same as #3)

entries.title: Isaiah 19:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:18 This is a separate paragraph. It denotes the conversion from idol worship to the worship of YWHH. The "language of Canaan" would denote Hebrew (BDB 488 I). This may be an allusion to Isa. 6:5 or even Gen. 11:1.

The phrase "swearing allegiance" (BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal PARTICIPLE) denotes a new relationship with Judah's God (cf. Isa. 19:19-22, 23, 24-25). This has always been the purpose of divine judgment!

▣ "In that day" Notice the recurrent phrase, "in that day," Isa. 19:16, 18, 19, 23, 24. This points toward specific future days.

  1. one of judgment and dread, Isa. 19:16-17
  2. one of conversion (Isa. 19:18, 19-22) and worldwide worship (Isa. 19:23, 24-25)

Again, a current crisis (cf. Isa. 19:20) in the ANE reflects an eschatological event. Judgment has a redemptive purpose (cf. Isa. 19:22). Evil, rebellion, and ignorance will not be the last word! YHWH has an eternal redemptive plan and purpose for the whole world (cf. Isa. 19:24b).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "five cities" The reason for this specific number is uncertain. It denotes a conversion, but not a complete (i.e. half of ten, see SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #5) conversion. The question remains, "To whom does it refer?"

  1. cities of Jewish settlers
  2. cities of Egyptian deities

Because of Isa. 19:19-22, 23, 24-25 I choose option #2. This context is not addressing Jews, but Egyptians.

▣
NASB, NKJV  "the City of Destruction"
NRSV, TEV, NJB, DSS, Targums, Vulgate, REB  "the City of the Sun"
JPSOA  "Town of Heres"
LXX  "the city of Asedec"

The MT's "destruction" (BDB 249) appears only here. The VERB of the same root (BDB 248) means "to throw down," "break," or "tear down." It may be a play on the Egyptian city that worshiped the "Sun" god (On-Heliopolis, i.e. sun city) or the Jewish temple founded on an island in the Nile River by priests in 162 B.C.

  1. חרס, city of the Sun (BDB 357, cf. DSS, Targums, Vulgate)
  2. הרס, city of destruction (BDB 249)

The implication is that the temples to Ra (sun god) have been torn down.

The Hebrew word sun has the same consonants as "ban" (i.e. devoted to destruction). There may be a double wordplay.

entries.title: Isaiah 19:19 "an altar (BDB 258). . .a pillar (BDB 663)"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:19 "an altar (BDB 258). . .a pillar (BDB 663)" This raised stone represented the place where deity appeared or was worshiped. It could be positive (represent YHWH) or negative (represent the fertility gods of Canaan).

  1. positive
    1. Jacob at Bethel ‒ Gen. 28:18; 35:14
    2. Jacob at Mizpah, a covenant sign with his father-in-law ‒ Gen. 31:45,51-52
    3. Moses at Sinai ‒ Exod. 24:4
    4. Transjordan tribes ‒ Josh. 22:10,26-27
  2. negative
    1. Moses' warning about sacred pillars, stone figures ‒ Lev. 26:1; Deut. 7:5; 12:3
    2. symbol of Ba'al, the male fertility god of Canaan ‒ 2 Kgs. 3:2; 10:26-27; 17:10; Isa. 27:9
    3. Micah ‒ Micah 5:10-15

For the Israelites these stone pillars must be uncut, no human or animal features. YHWH, therefore, could be represented in some ways by a natural, physical object.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE DEITY, I. E.

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "in the midst of the land of Egypt"
NRSV, NJB  "in the center of the land of Egypt"
REB  "in the heart of Egypt"
LXX  "at its border"
JPSOA  "inside the land of Egypt"

Because of the use of this term (BDB 1063) in Josh. 3:17; 4:3,9,10,18, it should be understood as "brink," not "middle." This is the origin of "at its border" in the LXX.

When does this event occur?

  1. the small Jewish temple built by Jewish mercenaries on an island in the Nile (Elephantine, modern Aswan, at the first cataract of the Nile), sometime before 525 B.C.
  2. the Jewish temple (modeled after the temple in Jerusalem) built at Leontopolis by Onias IV, an outcast Jewish high priest from Jerusalem, about 160 B.C. (cf. Josephus, Antiq. 12.9.7; 13.3.3)
  3. an eschatological event

For more historical information on these two Jewish temples in Egypt, see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 340-342.

entries.title: Isaiah 19:19-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:19-20 What a wonderful, but surprising event that a physical presence of YHWH will be established in Egypt. YHWH loves the people of the nations! They are made in His image. He seeks them. He wants to know them!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "a sign" See SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN (OT)

entries.title: Isaiah 19:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:20 This process is comparable to how YHWH dealt with Israel in the book of Judges. The cruel judgment of invasion and occupation (cf. Isa. 19:4) brings repentance and faith in God and His ability and willingness to act in deliverance. Egypt has come to that spiritual moment and YHWH responds.

What a great witness this context is about the character of Israel's God. He is willing to forgive and fully accept His covenant people's enemies. He is truly the God of the nations, the Savior of the world (cf. John 3:16; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: OUR SAVIOR (title)

▣ "a Savior and a Champion" In context this refers to one who will defeat the cruel master and mighty king of Isa. 19:4, but ultimately it has Messianic implications. In Isaiah this "Savior" is YHWH Himself and no other (cf. Isa. 43:3,11; 45:15,21), but from the NT we know it was the Messiah acting as YHWH's representative (i.e. Isa. 28:16; Rom. 9:30-33; 10:9-13; 1 Pet. 2:6-10).

  1. a Savior, BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil PARTICIPLE
  2. a defender, BDB 936, KB 1224, Qal PARTICIPLE
  3. a deliverer, BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil PERFECT with waw

entries.title: Isaiah 19:21 "the Lord will make Himself known to Egypt, and the Egyptians will know the Lord
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:21 "the Lord will make Himself known to Egypt, and the Egyptians will know the Lord" This is a play on the Hebrew word "know" (BDB 393, KB 390), which denotes both knowledge of and personal relationship with.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW (using mostly Deuteronomy as a paradigm)

▣ "worship" Notice the elements of worship (BDB 712, KB 773, Qal PERFECT with waw) mentioned.

  1. sacrifice, BDB 257
  2. offering, BDB 585
  3. vow, BDB 623, KB 674, Qal PERFECT

They will not only do the rituals of worship, but will live out (BDB 1022, KB 1532, Piel PERFECT with waw, lit. "perform") those rituals (i.e. vows).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

SPECIAL TOPIC: CALL ON HIS NAME

entries.title: Isaiah 19:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:22 YHWH's actions toward Egypt mimic His actions toward the covenant people.

  1. He strikes them (twice, BDB 619, KB 669)
  2. they cry out to Him, Isa. 19:20
  3. He heals them (twice, BDB 950, KB 1272)
  4. they return to Him (BDB 996, KB 1427, this is the Hebrew term for repentance; see SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE)
  5. He responds to them (BDB 801 I, KB 905, Niphal PERFECT with waw, see IMPERFECT in Gen. 25:21; 2 Chr. 33:13; Ezra 8:23. YHWH hears and responds to faithful repentance).

Be sure to note that judgment (i.e. striking) was for the purpose of establishing (or for Israel, restoring) a relationship with YHWH.

entries.title: Isaiah 19:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:23 There will be a free-flowing movement between nations for the purpose of worshiping YHWH. The nations have come!

It is interesting how many times Isaiah uses the imagery of a highway.

  1. a highway for the exiled Jews to return, Isa. 11:16; 57:14
  2. a highway for Gentile worshipers to come, Isa. 19:23
  3. a highway of holiness, Isa. 26:7; 35:8; 43:19; 49:11; 51:10
  4. a Messianic highway, Isa. 40:3; 42:16

entries.title: Isaiah 19:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:25 These are covenant phrases now used for the hated Egyptians and Assyrians.

Compare this with Isa. 45:14-17. What a contrast. It is so hard to hold these together (i.e. the nations loved, the nations judged). I choose Isa. 19:22! I choose Isa. 19:20!

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 20:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:1 This verse gives modern readers the exact historical setting of YHWH's judgment of the Philistines by the description of the fall of Ashdod (one of the five main city-states of Philistia [Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gaza, Gath, Ekron]). The fall of one denoted the fall of all (see earlier oracle in Isa. 14:28-32).

They were destroyed twice (1) by Sargon II (named specifically in the OT only here, he reigned from 722-705 B.C.), King of Assyria. In 713 B.C. the King of Ashdod, Azuri, revolted and in 711 B.C. Sargon II's army came and stopped the rebellion and (2) by Sennacherib in 705-701 B.C.

However, this chapter does not form a new oracle about the destruction of Philisita (or "coast lands," cf. Isa. 20:6), but a continuation of the judgment on Cush/Egypt, started in chapter 18. The humiliation of Ashdod was a foreshadowing of the shameful, humiliating exile of Egyptians by Assyrian armies on several different historical occasions. Segments of the Egyptian army were captured in battle and exiled.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF EGYPT

▣ "the commander" The term (BDB 1077) denotes a field general (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:17 and also note Isa. 36:2, where the name of the general in 2 Kings 18 appears, but not his title).

entries.title: Isaiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
ISAIAH 20

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
Prophecy About Egypt and Ethiopia The Sign Against Egypt and Ethiopia Against Egypt The Sign of the Naked Prophet Relating to the Capture of Ashdod
20:1-6 20:1-6 20:1-6 20:1-6 20:1-6

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 20:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:2 Isaiah is told to dress (or better, undress) a certain way to denote current cultural mourning rites, but also to denote shame, at Assyria's defeat and exile of several nations.

  1. Ashdod (Philistia)
  2. Egypt
  3. Cush or synonym of Egypt of the 25 Dynasties who were Nubian.

What happened to Ashdod would in three years (cf. Isa. 20:3) happen to Egypt.

▣ "spoke through Isaiah" The word (BDB 388) translated "through" is literally "with the hand." Therefore, it might denote a physical gesture. This is simply an idiom for a way to communicate.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣
NASB, NRSV, Peshitta  "loosen the sackcloth"
NKJV, NET  "remove the sackcloth"
TEV, LXX  "take off. . .the sackcloth"
REB  "strip the sackcloth"
JPSOA  "untie the sackcloth"

The common VERB (BDB 834, KB 986, Piel PERFECT with waw) basically means "to open." So the question is, "Does it mean 'loosen' (mourning) or 'take off' (shame)?"

  1. "remove," NIV, Ps. 30:11; NASB has "loose," but means "remove" in Isa. 52:2; Jer. 40:4
  2. "loosen," Isa. 5:27

Normally wearing "sackcloth" (BDB 974) would denote mourning, as would being barefoot (cf. Micah 1:8), but it is possible that Isaiah removed the symbol of his prophetic office ("hairy robe," BDB 12 CONSTRUCT, BDB 972, cf. Matt. 3:4). If this is correct then the text is not talking about nudity (but "naked," BDB 736 in Isa. 20:2,3,4 may, cf. Gen. 2:25). However, most uses of the term "naked" mean partially clothed (cf. Isa. 47:1-3; 1 Sam. 19:24; 2 Sam. 6:14,20; Amos 2:16; Micah 1:8; John 19:23; 21:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

entries.title: Isaiah 20:3 "as a sign"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:3 "as a sign" The NOUN ,"sign" (BDB 16), is used

  1. as a marker of time, Gen. 1:14
  2. as a marker of person, Gen. 4:15
  3. as a marker of covenant, Gen. 9:12,13,17; 17:11
  4. as a marker of a faith promise, Exod. 3:12
  5. as a miracle to affirm God's representative (i.e. Moses), Exod. 4:8 (twice),9,17,28,30; 7:3; 8:23, etc.
  6. tribal standard, Num. 2:2; Ps. 74:4
  7. as a warning, Num. 16:38; 17:10

It is used often in Isaiah.

  1. special birth, Isa. 7:14
  2. Isaiah's children, Isa. 8:18
  3. altar and pillar in Egypt, Isa. 19:20
  4. Isaiah's dress, Isa. 20:3
  5. harvest, Isa. 37:30
  6. sparing Jerusalem from Assyria, Isa. 38:7
  7. Hezekiah's healing, Isa. 38:22
  8. false signs, Isa. 44:25
  9. agricultural blessings, Isa. 55:13
  10. missionaries to the nations, Isa. 66:19

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN (OT)

▣
NASB  "a token"
NKJV, Peshitta  "a wonder"
NRSV, REB, NJB, JPSOA, LXX  "portent"

The term "wonder," "sign," "portent" (BDB 68) is synonymous with "sign," "mark" (BDB 16). It is used often in Exodus and Deuteronomy, but only twice in Isaiah (i.e. Isa. 8:18 and 20:3).

BDB has two main usages.

  1. a special demonstration of God's power
  2. a token of future events or symbolic acts denoting future events (cf. Zech. 3:8).

entries.title: Isaiah 20:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:4 This verse describes exile.

  1. young and old taken (idiom for the entire population)
  2. naked (BDB 736, idiom for shame, still had a tight-fitting undergarment)
  3. barefoot (BDB 405, idiom for mourning)
  4. buttocks uncovered (BDB 1059, only here and 2 Sam. 10:4, idiom of shame)
  5. shame/nakedness (BDB 788, see Assyrian wall pictures)

This verse makes it very clear that Isaiah shocked his culture by going partially nude/naked for three years to illustrate a theological truth/prophecy. Nakedness was part of the cursing of Deuteronomy (cf. Isa. 28:48), which reflected exile.

entries.title: Isaiah 20:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:5 Because of Cush/Egypt's trust in themselves (i.e. army, wisdom, wealth, religion) they will be

  1. dismayed, BDB 369, KB 365, Qal PERFECT with waw, cf. Isa. 7:8; 8:9 (thrice); 9:4; 20:5; 30:31; 31:4,9; 37:27; 51:6,7
  2. ashamed, BDB 101, KB 116, Qal PERFECT with waw, cf. Isa. 1:29; 19:9; 20:5; 24:23; 26:11; 29:22; 30:5; 37:27; 41:11; 44:9,11 (twice); Isa. 45:16,17,24; 49:23; 50:7; 54:4; 65:13; 66:5

Obviously these two terms are a major part of Isaiah's message, both negatively and positively! Judah will suffer in the same way because she hoped in allies, not in YHWH.

entries.title: Isaiah 20:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:6 This verse links Ashdod (Isa. 20:1) with all the inhabitants of the coastal plain of Palestine. Apparently the Egyptians had promised military aid if Assyria invaded, but they could/did not (cf. Isa. 30:7; 31:3). There was no one to deliver (cf. Isa. 10:3).

Surely, this chapter bolstered Isaiah's message to Hezekiah not to make an alliance with Egypt (cf. Isa. 30:1-5; 31:1-3).

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 21:1 "oracle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:1 "oracle" This NOUN (BDB 672) is litrally "burden" (cf. Exod. 23:5). See full note at isa. 13:1.

▣ "the wilderness of the sea" This may be an attempt to translate

  1. the Assyrian name for Babylon (Mat + Amil, cf. JB footnote)
  2. the Akkadian title "Land of the Sea" (Mat tam-tim, i.e. southern Babylon), but it was now destroyed, so "land" changed to "wilderness"
  3. The Peshitta and JPSOA translate it as "the desert of the sea," probably referring to the marshy area near the mouths of the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers.
  4. TEV just has "Babylon."

The term "wilderness" (BDB 184) denotes large pieces of uninhabited land.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter lists several nations addressed by YHWH through His prophet, all introduced by the literary marker, "the oracle about."

  2. I have mentioned earlier that I think the oracle addressed to the "king of Babylon" really deals with Assyria (i.e. Isa. 13:1-14:27). This chapter (i.e. Isa. 21:1-10) is about Babylon.
     This is not Neo-Babylon of Nabonidus and Nebuchadnezzar (see SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON), but the Chaldean people close to the mouth of the Tigris and Euphrates. Their capital would be the city of Babylon and their king Merodach-baladan, who rebelled in 720 B.C., but was defeated by Sargon II (see SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA) and escaped into the marshes and fled to Elam in 710 B.C. (IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 611). The city of Babylon was destroyed by Assyria in 703 B.C. and the King of Assyria took the title "King of Babylon."
    SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

  3. This chapter also addresses
    1. Edom, Isa. 21:11-12
    2. Arabia, Isa. 21:13-17

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 21:1-2a
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:1-2a Isaiah tries to express his deep emotion when he receives this oracle.

  1. like a windstorm in the Negev, Isa. 21:1
  2. from a wilderness, Isa. 21:1
  3. from a terrifying (BDB 431, KB 432, Niphal PARTICIPLE) land, Isa. 21:1
  4. harsh (BDB 904) vision, Isa. 21:2a

entries.title: Isaiah 21:2b
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:2b This describes the invasion of old Babylon by Assyria in 703 B.C. (cf. Isa. 21:9; see IVP Bible Background Commentary, OT, p. 611).

  1. the treacherous one still deals treacherously, play on BDB 93, KB 108, two Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLES, 24:16; 33:1; Jer. 3:20; 5:11 (it is possible that the NIV and REB translations "traitor," or NRSV, "betrayer" historically fits Merodach-baladan, the king of old Babylon, better)
  2. the destroyer still destroys, play on BDB 994, KB 1418, two Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLES, 16:4; 33:1; Jer. 6:26

entries.title: Isaiah 21:2c
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:2c God commands two northern Mesopotamian powers to attack old Babylon.

  1. "Go up" (BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERATIVE) Elam (BDB 743). This is surprising since initially Elam helped old Babylon to hold off Assyrian domination.
  2. "Lay siege" (BDB 848, KB 1015, Qal IMPERATIVE) Media (BDB 552). This was another ethnic group in the northern Euphrates area.

It is possible that these are war cries of those in the anti-Assyrian coalition (i.e. Elam, Media, so says the Jewish commentator Ibn Ezra). This would make more sense if Babylon of Isaiah's day is being addressed.

entries.title: Isaiah 21:2d "I have made an end of all the groaning she has caused"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:2d "I have made an end of all the groaning she has caused" The MT has "all the sighing I bring to an end" (BDB 991, KB 1407, Hiphil PERFECT). The JPSOA footnote suggests an emendation, "Put an end to all her merrymaking."

The phrase, "she has caused," NASB, is not in the MT. If it is to be assumed, it must be stated that this line of poetry fits Neo-Babylon better. This later empire had a much larger area of influence (i.e. Nebuchadnezzar II, cf. Daniel 4).

Again, some (including me) see this last line as a statement from the old Babylonian king (Merodach-baladan) or his deities (Marduk) directed to a "to-be-defeated" Assyria/Nineveh. There are so many speakers in this chapter it is hard to know the intended speaker (the prophet, YHWH, Babylonian king, several watchmen, unknown voices).

entries.title: Isaiah 21:3-4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:3-4 The prophet describes the effect the message had on him personally. Daniel also experienced physical distress at YHWH's revelations (cf. Dan. 7:15,28; 8:27; 10:16-17).

  1. loins are full of anguish
  2. pains have seized me like the pains of a woman in labor, cf. Isa. 13:8; 26:17
  3. I am so bewildered (i.e. bent over) I cannot hear, cf. Isa. 19:14 (i.e. an idiom of drunkenness)
  4. so terrified I cannot see
  5. my mind reels
  6. horror overwhelms me
  7. the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling ("twilight" possibly Babylon's defeat meant a stronger, more expansionistic Assyria)

All of these VERBS are PERFECTS, which denote a complete situation. Why was he so distressed? There is no one to stop Assyria now! She is coming!

21:3
NASB  "bewildered"
NKJV, NJB  "distressed"
NRSV  "bowed down"
REB  "distraught"
JPSOA  "to anguished"
Peshitta  "dismayed"

The VERB (BDB 730, KB 796, Niphal PERFECT) basically means "to bend" or "to twist." It is regularly used of human sin as a perversion of God's truth/law (Isa. 21:3; Prov. 12:8; Lam. 3:9).

For a brief word study, see Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, 2nd ed., pp. 592-593.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIN IN THE OT, A. #2

entries.title: Isaiah 21:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:4 This verse expands on Isa. 21:2a ("a harsh vision"). It describes Isaiah's reaction to this oracle.

  1. my mind reels, BDB 1073, KB 1766, Qal PERFECT
  2. horror overwhelms me, BDB 129, KB 147, Piel PERFECT
  3. the twilight I long for has been turned for me into trembling, BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal PERFECT

The question is, "Why was Isaiah so upset at the fall of old Babylon?" Possibly because of

  1. the terrible violence involved
  2. Babylon kept Assyria in balance. Now Assyria was free to expand region-wide (see Exposition Bible Commentary, vol. 6, p. 134).

entries.title: Isaiah 21:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:5 This verse has a series of four Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTES (functioning as IMPERATIVES) and then two Qal IMPERATIVE.

  1. set the table
  2. spread the rugs (see note following)
  3. eat
  4. drink

This would denote a lavish meal. Some commentators see this as referring to Daniel 5. If so, then this chapter refers to Neo-Babylon of a later period (i.e. Nebuchadnezzar II).

In the midst of the party a messenger arrives and calls them to military preparations ("captains," BDB 978).

  1. rise up, BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. oil the shields, BDB 602, KB 643, Qal IMPERATIVE. The ancient warriors covered their shields with leather so that flaming arrows would penetrate the soft leather and be extinguished, cf. 2 Sam. 1:21.
▣
NASB, NJB  "spread out the cloth"
NKJV, Peshitta  "set a watchman in the tower"
NRSV, TEV, REB  "spread the rugs"
JB  "cover it with cloth"
LXX  "prepare the table"
JPSOA  "set the table"

This phrase is made up of a NOUN and a very similar VERBAL root.

  1. NOUN, צפית (BDB 860 II) found only here, some scholars see it as "carpet," others as "watchman" (BDB 859, מצפה)
  2. VERBAL, צפה (BDB 860 II, INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE), meaning "lay out" or "lay over"

Since people of the ANE ate sitting on the floor with pillows, this could refer to this type of sitting/eating arrangement (i.e. "arrange the pillows," cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 832).

entries.title: Isaiah 21:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:6 Notice the prophet is relaying YHWH's words.

  1. go, BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. station the lookout, BDB 763, KB 840, Hiphil IMPERATIVE ("sentry," lit. "one who watches," BDB 859, KB 1044, Piel PARTICIPLE)
  3. let him report, BDB 616, KB 665, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

entries.title: Isaiah 21:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:7 He is instructed to watch for a very specific kind of military formation.

  1. riders on horses in pairs
  2. a train of donkeys
  3. a train of camels

The term "riders" (BDB 935) could be understood as chariots pulled by two horses (NKJV, Peshitta; see SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS). For #2 and #3, this could also designate riders (cf. NRSV, LXX). Cavalry were used in places that chariots could not go.

At the sight of this type of military equipment and formation, he is to report immediately (double use of "attention," BDB 904). Assyria is coming!

entries.title: Isaiah 21:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:8 This is a way of announcing a loud military-type (i.e. like a lion) report by the watchman on the wall. He has so far seen nothing.

The MT is difficult but the Hebrew manuscripts from DSS make the watchman call out like a lion, which is the best option for understanding this cryptic Hebrew text.

However, it is possible to see "lion," אריה (BDB 71) as a copyist's error for "saw," ראה (BDB 906, DSS text has "lookout"), thereby resulting in the translation, "then the one who sees the sentry" (i.e. watchman) cries out.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

entries.title: Isaiah 21:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:9 Suddenly the military formation and equipment come into view! Its presence in Palestine shows the previous fall of the city of Babylon. This fall is expressed by doubling the VERB (BDB 656, KB 709, Qal PERFECTS), which is so common in Isaiah. The city of Babylon fell several times to different Assyrian kings.

Her demise is complete as illustrated by the shattering (BDB 990, KB 1402, Piel PERFECT) of her idols (cf. Isaiah 46-47). With Babylon defeated and Elam and Media inactive, Assyria can resume her expansionistic intentions!

entries.title: Isaiah 21:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:10 The prophet tells the oppressed covenant people that their God (i.e. "Lord of hosts," "God of Israel") has acted, but how?

  1. The fall of Babylon was not a victory for them, but a sure promise that Assyria will come.
  2. The question remains which Babylon is the prophet referring to?
    1. old Babylon of Merodach-baladan of Isaiah's day (8th century B.C.)
    2. Neo-Babylon of Nebuchadnezzar II of Ezekiel's and Jeremiah's day (7th century B.C.)

The issue is not one of the reality of the predictive prophecy, but of historical setting!

Just a note about an alternate way of interpreting this verse. It is possible that the ones who are addressed are the Babylonians who Assyria will destroy. YHWH has earlier heard the fall of Moab (cf. Isa. 15:5; 16:11) and the prayers of the oppressed Egyptians (cf. Isa. 19:20).

Timeline (Old Testament)

▣ "my afflicted of the threshing floor" This is a Hebrew idiom "son of my threshing floor." The Hebrew term "son" has many semantic usages in Isaiah.

  1. son of fatness, Isa. 5:1 (see note at Isa. 5:1)
  2. son of dawn, Isa. 14:12
  3. son of the wise, Isa. 19:11
  4. son of man, Isa. 56:2
  5. son of a foreign land (lit. "foreigners"), Isa. 56:6

SPECIAL TOPIC: "SONS OF. . ." (OT)

entries.title: Isaiah 21:11 "The oracle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:11 "The oracle" This (BDB 672) is literally "burden." see full note at Isa. 13:1.

▣
NASB, TEV  "Edom"
NKJV, NRSV, NJB, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "Dumah"
LXX  "Idumea"
Rotherham footnote  "silence"

A new message starts (i.e. use of the literary marker, "oracle"; see full note at Isa. 13:1). The MT has "Dumah" (BDB 189, cf. Gen. 25:14). It is a play on the Hebrew term for "silence" (BDB 189). Edom will be silenced. Edom was part of the anti-Assyrian coalition, as was Philistia. All were crushed in 711 B.C. by Sargon II's army.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA

▣ "Seir" This (BDB 973) can refer to the land of Edom (cf. Gen. 32:3; 36:30; Num. 24:18; Deut. 2:4,8, 12,22,29; Jdg. 5:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

entries.title: Isaiah 21:11c-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:11c-12 This is a very cryptic strophe with several IMPERATIVES. A watchman on the wall, as in Isa. 21:6 and 8, is addressed by an unknown voice which asks about the time of the night (twice). The answer is also strange.

  1. morning comes
  2. but also night
  3. ask again
  4. ask again

It possibly means, "when will all this take place?"

These last two brief oracles of Assyrian attack seem to reflect two groups allied with old Babylon.

entries.title: Isaiah 21:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:13 A new message (use of the literary transition marker, "oracle"; see full note at Isa. 13:1) is addressed to Arabia. It is unsure who the antagonist is.

  1. Assyria (invasion)
  2. Kedar (civil war)

It is interesting that "Dumah" (Isa. 21:11) and Seir (Isa. 21:11) are also place names in, or close to, Arabia.

▣ "the thickets" Isaiah uses "forestry" imagery often. This term (BDB 420) can mean

  1. forest
  2. thicket

Since Arabia is desert, the second fits best. It would refer to ravines with thick brushy vegetation, where animals hide. Now fugitives, refugees, and caravan traders (i.e. Dedanites were a Bedouin people associated with Sheba) hide there to escape military invasion (cf. Isa. 21:15). They could not use the usual roads or resting places.

entries.title: Isaiah 21:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:14 The Arabians are commanded (BDB 87, KB 102, Hiphil IMPERATIVE) to bring water and food for them.

▣ "Tema" This was a major northern city, home to the worship of the moon goddess.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOON WORSHIP

entries.title: Isaiah 21:16 "In a year, as a hired man would count it"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:16 "In a year, as a hired man would count it" This same idiom of precise timing is found earlier in Isa. 16:14.

▣ "Kedar" This is another large city of Arabia. It, and by implication all of Arabia's army, will be defeated. Sargon II attacked this area in 715 B.C.

Again the theological phrase "for the Lord God of Israel has spoken." It was not the power of ancient armies that directed ANE events, but the God of Israel! This is a claim to monotheism.

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 22:1 "oracle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:1 "oracle" This is a textual marker of a new message from YHWH directed at a national/ethnic group (see full lexical note at Isa. 13:1). Surprisingly, in the midst of YHWH's judgment on the surrounding pagan nations He addresses Judah, who because of her covenant disobedience was just another among the goim (nations).

It is surely possible that these messages are related to specific historical invasions. In differing years, different armies and nations were affected. But Hebrew poetry is so vague that a specific historical situation is difficult to ascertain. Possibly there has been a later editing of Isaiah's messages based on certain word plays or key words, not historical events (i.e. the poems of Isaiah are out of chronological order).

Remember the main point of the whole oracle and the main truth of each strophe is the way to approach the prophet's (i.e. YHWH) meaning, not attention to all the historical details and rare words.

22:1
NASB, NRSV, Peshitta  "the valley of vision"
NKJV, TEV, NJB, REB, NET  "the Valley of Vision"
LXX  "the ravine of Sion"
JB  "valley of Hinnom"

Because of the use of this phrase in Isa. 22:5b, it must be imagery to refer to the "day of panic" sent by the Lord of hosts (note Joel 3:14) against Jerusalem (cf. vv. 9-10).

entries.title: Isaiah 22:1b-2b
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:1b-2b These are a description of a time

  1. of mourning (JPSOA, cf. Isa. 15:3; Jer. 19:13; 48:38; Zeph. 1:5)
  2. of rejoicing (cf. v. 13) in Jerusalem. The JB (footnote) assumes it relates to Hezekiah's initial victories over Assyria in 705 B.C. or 713 B.C. (Jewish Study Bible, p. 825).
  3. of idolatry of astral worship

Their activities are described.

  1. up to the housetops
  2. you who were full of noise
  3. you boisterous town
  4. you exultant city

entries.content:

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 22:2c-3d
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:2c-3d Apparently some of the city (i.e. leaders and soldiers) fled before the invaders.

  1. they were captured and put to death, but not in battle
  2. their leaders fled too, but were also captured and killed
  3. all of them who fled were taken into exile (c. 3 c-d)

Because of these lines of poetry many believe this chapter refers to the siege of Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 B.C., when Zedekiah fled the city and was captured (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:4-6), but I think it refers to Assyria's invasion (possibly 701 B.C.) by one of the following:

  1. Tiglath-pileser III (Isaiah 7-12)
  2. Shalmaneser V (cf. 2 Kings 17)
  3. Sargon II (fall of Samaria in 722 B.C., cf. Isa. 28:1-6)
  4. Sennacherib (705 and 701 B.C., Isaiah 36-39; 2 Kings 18-19)

This chapter seems to relate specifically to Hezekiah's reign (715-687 B.C.). But as often happens in Isaiah, these invasions are presented as mingled. Isaiah was primarily concerned with theology; history was a servant to present these truths about God, mankind, sin, and salvation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA

entries.title: Isaiah 22:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:4 The prophet speaks of himself, as he did in Isa. 21:3-4

  1. turn your eyes away from me, BDB 1043, KB 1609, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. let me weep bitterly, BDB 600, KB 638, Piel IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense
  3. do not try to comfort me, BDB 21, KB 23, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense ("to comfort," BDB 636, KB 688, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

The prophet wanted to be left alone so as to work through his grief privately.

▣ "the daughter of my people" This is an idiomatic phrase for a people or ethnic group (cf. Isa. 1:8; 10:30, 32; 16:1; 23:10-12; 37:22; 47:1,5; 52:5; 62:11). Here it refers to the covenant people of Judah (i.e. "daughter of Zion").

entries.title: Isaiah 22:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:5 This verse describes YHWH's "day of panic." It is just the opposite of Isa. 22:1-2.

  1. panic, BDB 223, cf. Deut. 28:20
  2. subjugation, BDB 101, used only thrice, cf. Isa. 18:2,7
  3. confusion, BDB 100, used only twice, cf. Micah 7:4
  4. breaking down of walls, קרר, BDB 903 II, KB 1148, Pilpel PARTICIPLE (only here; some scholars think the root is an Arabic or Ugaritic root meaning, "shout," "crackle," or "make noise" (KB 1128 I, קר)
  5. crying to the mountain (no VERBAL)

▣ The JPSOA sees the last two lines of v. 5 as place names.

  1. Kir, cf. Isa. 22:6; 2 Kgs. 16:9; Amos 1:5; 9:7 ("wall," BDB 885 I; "Kir," BDB 885 II)
  2. Shoa, cf. Ezek. 23:23 ("crying," BDB 1002; "Shoa, BDB 1003 III)

No other English translation follows this understanding.

▣ "to the mountain" The NOUN (BDB 249) is SINGULAR and may refer to the temple mount (i.e. cry out to YHWH).

entries.title: Isaiah 22:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:6-7 These verses describe the military aspects of the invasion. Elam and Kir (possibly Media, cf. Isa. 21:2; 2 Kgs. 16:9) were northern areas of Mesopotamia. Soldiers from this area became mercenaries in the Assyrian army to keep their own lands from being invaded.

22:6
NASB  "infantry"
NKJV, Peshitta  "men"
NRSV  "cavalry"
REB  "Aram"
JPSOA, LXX  "mounted men"

The MT has "men" (אדם, BDB 9, see Isa. 31:8, where "adam" is also used in a military sense), but for parallelism some change it to "Aram," ארם. This ד (d) vs. ר (r) is a common confusion in Hebrew.

The UBS Text Project gives "with manned chariots" an "A" rating, meaning, "a very high probability."

entries.title: Isaiah 22:8 "He removed the defense of Judah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:8 "He removed the defense of Judah" "Defense" in this verse means "covering" (BDB 697). They did not trust in YHWH (cf. Isa. 22:11c,d) so He removed His protective presence (i.e. a cloud, cf. Isa. 4:5; Ps. 105:39). This has been the problem through all of Israel's history. God's people do not trust and obey Him and there are consequences (i.e. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28)!

"The defense" may have literally referred to the fortress Azekah at the head of the valley of Elath (Jewish Study Bible, footnote, p. 825). The way to Jerusalem was open and undefended.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

▣ "In that day" This is a common idiom in the Prophets for the day of God's visitation (i.e. Isa. 19:16,18, 19,21,23,24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

NASB  "you depended on"
NKJV, NRSV  "you looked to"
NJB  "you lturned your gaze to"
REB  "you checked"
JPSOA  "you gave thought to"

The VERB (BDB 613, KB 661, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw) denotes that they trusted in their weaponry, not YHWH.

▣ "of the house of the forest" This was the name of the king's armory in Jerusalem (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:2; 10:17).

entries.title: Isaiah 22:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:9 The historical setting appears to be the time of Hezekiah. He built (2 Kgs. 20:20) pools for the collection of water during sieges (cf. Isa. 22:11; 7:3; Neh. 3:16). Apparently Hezekiah did a lot of physical preparation to the defenses of Jerusalem (cf. 2 Chr. 32:5) just before Sennacherib came in 701 B.C., but they are not what saved the city of Jerusalem; it was YHWH and His greater purpose (Isa. 22:11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

entries.title: Isaiah 22:10-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:10-11 This verse seems to describe the walls of Jerusalem as double walls (which has no archaeological confirmation). Many people moving into the city for refuge had built temporary houses in the space between the two walls. But these houses had to be removed (see IVP Bible Background Commentary, OT, p. 614).

Another possible way to understand the text was that some houses were destroyed to fill up the space between walls. This made it more difficult for siege machines to knock a hole in the city's wall.

This same area may have been filled with water at certain low places (cf. Isa. 22:11). This served as

  1. a barrier to those who breached the outer wall
  2. a surplus water supply for the city which was full of refugees

entries.title: Isaiah 22:11 "For the waters of the old pool"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:11 "For the waters of the old pool" This apparently refers to a water project started by Hezekiah to secretly supply water from outside Jerusalem's walls to come into the city (cf. 2 Kgs. 20:20). This water project is today called "Siloam Tunnel." It was discovered in A.D. 1625 but not fully explored until the 19th century.

▣ "But you did not depend on Him who made it" This is the theological key to the context. The same VERB of Isa. 22:8b is repeated (here a Hiphil PERFECT, lit. "look," BDSB 613, KB 661). They were trusting in their own fortifications and provisions for war, not in their covenant God (i.e. Isa. 30:15; Jer. 2:13)!

▣ "Nor did you take into consideration Him" The VERB (BDB 906, KB 1157) is a Qal PERFECT. God's people had forsaken the promises of preservation that He made to them. Isaiah emphasizes these promises and asserts regularly that Jerusalem will not fall.

The reason God will not let her fall is His overarching purpose (i.e. "plan," lit. "formed," BDB 427, KB 428, Qal PARTICIPLE, cf. Isa. 37:26; 46:11; Jer. 18:11) for His people.

  1. inform the world about YHWH
  2. model a godly society
  3. be the channel for the coming Messiah

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Isaiah 22:12-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:12-14 This is another strophe which starts with "in that day."

Verse 12 lists the mourning rites (see SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES) that would characterize Jerusalem.

  1. weeping, BDB 113 (no VERB)
  2. wailing, BDB 704 (no VERB)
  3. shaving the head, BDB 901 (no VERB, the baldness could be by shaving or plucking, cf. Ezra 9:3; Job 1:20; Jer. 7:29; 16:6; 41:5; 48:37; Mic. 1:16)
  4. wearing sackcloth, BDB 291, KB 291, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

Isaiah 22:13 describes what Jerusalem was doing instead. They should have been seeking YHWH (SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord) in repentance and prayer, but no, they were caught up in

  1. gaiety, BDB 965
  2. gladness, BDB 970
  3. sacrificing as normal, two Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTES (BDB 246, BDB 133)
  4. eating fellowship sacrifices, BDB 37, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
  5. drinking, BDB 1059 I, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE

entries.title: Isaiah 22:13d
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:13d Their attitude toward life is expressed in this line of poetry. It is similar to Belshazzar's party in Daniel 5.

This attitude reflects their lack of understanding about the plans (BDB 427, KB 428, Qal PARTICIPLE, cf. Isa. 22:11d) of YHWH for Jerusalem and His people (cf. Isa. 5:11-12). Instead of a sense of corporate purpose and hope, they sought immediate individual gratification!

entries.title: Isaiah 22:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:14 Judah's lack of faith will result in their deaths. Judgment has come to Judah. Jerusalem itself will be spared, but Judah will be devastated.

Judah has missed the time of YHWH's visitation (for deliverance), so now they will experience His visitation for destruction!

▣ "shall not be forgiven" This is a major theological term, literally, "cover" (BDB 497, KB 493). See SPECIAL TOPIC: FORGIVENESS IN THE OT, #3 and SPECIAL TOPIC: ATONEMENT (OT)

▣ "Surely this iniquity shall not be forgiven you" What sin? I think the sin of lack of trust and reliance on God mentioned in Isa. 22:11c,d.

entries.title: Isaiah 22:15-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:15-19 This describes YHWH's judgment on Shebna, King Hezekiah's steward. The exact reason for Shebna's replacement with Eliakim (cf. Isa. 22:20-25) is uncertain, but it must have been serious and in context, may be a "self-reliant spirit."

Shebna is probably "Shebnah" of 2 Kgs. 18:18, who was Eliakim's scribe.

entries.title: Isaiah 22:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:16 This is a series of questions challenging Shebna's right to serve. Isaiah uses the imagery of an expensive tomb in a prominent place to show Shebna's usurption of power and prestige.

entries.title: Isaiah 22:17-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:17-19 Sin has consequences. Leaders are especially responsible (they trusted in their armaments, cf. vv. 8,18). YHWH is described as the personal agent of judgment.

  1. to hurl you, Isa. 22:17, BDB 376, KB 373, Pipel PARTICIPLE; and related NOUN (BDB 376), "hurl you violently"
  2. to grasp you firmly, Isa. 22:17, Qal PERFECT and Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of BDB 742 II, KB 814 II
  3. "roll you tightly like a ball to be cast," Isa. 22:18, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal IMPERFECT VERB, as well as the NOUN, of the same root (BDB 857, KB 1039)
  4. die an outcast in a foreign land, Isa. 22:18c,d
  5. "I will depose you," Isa. 22:19, BDB 213, KB 239, Qal PERFECT with waw
  6. "I will pull you down," Isa. 22:19, BDB 248, KB 256, Qal IMPERFECT

There is an interesting lexical theory connected to #2. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 380-381, suggests that the root means "delouse," as imagery for a complete destruction (cf. Jer. 43:12).

entries.title: Isaiah 22:18 "splendid chariots"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:18 "splendid chariots" See SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS

entries.title: Isaiah 22:20-25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:20-25 These verses describe what YHWH will do to Shebna's successor, Eliakim (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:18, 26,37; 19:2; Isa. 22:20; 36:3,11,22; 37:2).

  1. YHWH will summon him, lit. "call," Isa. 22:20, BDB 894, KB 1128, Qal PERFECT with waw
  2. YHWH will clothe him with your tunic, Isa. 22:21, BDB 527, KB 519, Hiphil PERFECT with waw (i.e. transfer of authority)
  3. YHWH will tie a sash securely about him, Isa. 22:21, VERB from #2 implied
  4. YHWH will entrust him with your authority (lit. "rule," BDB 606), Isa. 22:21, BDB 304, KB 302, Piel IMPERFECT
  5. YHWH will set the key of the house of David on his shoulders, Isa. 22:22, BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT with waw
  6. YHWH will drive him like a peg into a firm place, Isa. 22:23, BDB 1075, KB 1787, Qal PERFECT with waw

entries.title: Isaiah 22:21-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:21-23 These verses describe what Eliakim will do.

  1. he will become a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and of the house of Judah, Isa. 22:21
  2. he opens and no one will shut, he shuts and no will open ("key" is imagery for authority), Isa. 22:22; Rev. 3:7
  3. he will be one who will not be moved, Isa. 22:23
  4. he will become a throne of glory to his father's house, Isa. 22:23 (cf. Isa. 22:24)

In some sense these verses see Eliakim as a type or foreshadowing of the Messiah. This same foreshadowing is seen in Zechariah with Zerubbabel and Joshua (cf. Zech. 3-4).

entries.title: Isaiah 22:23 "firm"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:23 "firm" See SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT (אמן), especially II., A., 1., b., (2).

22:24
NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "offspring and issue"
TEV  "his relatives and dependants"
NJB  "the descendants and offspring"
REB  "even to the meanest members"
JPSOA  "the sprouts and the leaves"
LXX  "from small to great"
Peshitta  "both the honorable men and
 the glorious men"
NET  "the offspring and the offshoots"

The MT has

  1. the offspring ‒ BDB 425, KB 993
    1. plants ‒ Isa 34:1; 42:5
    2. animals ‒ Job 31:8
    3. humans ‒ Job 5:25; 21:8; 27:14; Isa. 2:3; 22:24; 44:3; 48:19; 61:9; 65:23
  2. the issue ‒ BDB 861, KB 1048; this unknown root is found only here; parallelism implies some kind of offshoot or leaf

entries.title: Isaiah 22:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:25 Even Eliakim (i.e. the peg driven in a firm place), with all of YHWH's help, cannot stop the judgment that is coming.

  1. peg will give way (BDB 559 I, KB 561, Qal IMPERFECT)
  2. peg will break off (BDB 154, KB 180, Niphal PERFECT with waw)
  3. peg will fall (BDB 656, KB 709, Qal PERFECT with waw)
  4. load will be cut off (BDB 503, KB 500, Niphal PERFECT with waw)

Judgment is coming, YHWH said (BDB 180, KB 210, Piel PERFECT).

▣ "the peg" It (BDB 450) may refer to

  1. Shebna
  2. Eliakim
  3. Judah
  4. Jerusalem
  5. Messiah

In context #1 or #2 is best (I think #2 is a better historical and contextual fit), but the others address YHWH's future plans (cf. Isa. 22:11).

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 23:1 "oracle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:1 "oracle" See full lexical note at Isa. 13:1.

▣ "Tyre" See Contextual Insights, A. and B.

▣ "Wail, O ships of Tarshish" "Wail" (ילל, BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE) denotes loud shrieking. It is used often in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 13:6; 14:31; 15:2,3; 16:7 [twice]; 23:1,6,14; 52:5; 65:14 and a related term [יללה] in Isa. 15:8 [twice]). See SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES.

Note this same phrase appears in Isa. 23:14. Often a repeated phrase marks a literary unit, but here that does not fit well.

The ships of Tarshish were large commercial grain carriers, usually from Egypt. They became an idiom (as did "Phoenicia" and "Canaanite") for merchants. Here they are personified for literary effect.

▣ "Tarshish" This place name (BDB 1077) could refer to

  1. a city in southern Spain on the Atlantic side, which was a Phoenician colony (i.e. Tartessus, possibly modern Sevilla)
  2. the island of Sardinia (cf. Gen. 10:4)
  3. a city on the north African coast (Carthage was a colony of Phoenicia)
  4. a metaphor for a far distant port
  5. a type of large sea-going commercial ship
  6. a rival maritime nation (cf. 1 Kgs. 10:22)

SPECIAL TOPIC: TARSHISH (place)

▣ "without house or harbor" The city of Tyre had two inhabited areas.

  1. most of the houses and shops were located on the mainland coast (cf. Josh. 19:29; 2 Sam. 24:7)
  2. the palace, temple, and fortress were on an island (originally two small islands) just off the coast (cf. Ezek. 27:32)

This made it almost invulnerable until Alexander the Great in 332 B.C. destroyed the coastal part and used the debris to build a causeway to the island fortress (cf. Ezek. 26:3-5).

The ships from Tarshish had no where to offload their cargo, nor receive different cargo to transport.

There is a textual issue with both "house" and "harbor."

  1. The word "house" in the MT (BDB 108) could also be "harbor" with only a revocalization.
    1. "without house" (REV) ‒ מבית
    2. "harbor" (NEB) ‒ מבית
  2. The word "harbor" is literally a Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT (BDB 97, KB 112) meaning "to come in," which in this context, denotes coming into a place of anchorage or dock.

Both #1 and #2 seem to refer to the Port of Tyre.

▣ "Cyprus" The MT has "Kittim" (BDB 508), possibly taken from the name of a Roman city on the island of Cyprus called "Citium," which was originally a Phoenician colony (cf. Isa. 23:7).

Some identify the inhabitants with one of the sons of Javan, Elishah (cf. Gen. 10:4; Ezek. 27:7).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This condemnation of Phoenicia is paralleled in Ezekiel 26-28 and Amos 1:9-10. Tyre (capital of Phoenicia) was a powerful and wealthy maritime nation, which caused them to be prideful and self-reliant.

  2. Because it was such a widespread empire several nations and geographical areas mourned for the loss of trade.
    1. ship of Tarshish (i.e. western Mediterranean area), Isa. 23:1,6,14
    2. coastlands, Isa. 23:2,6
    3. merchants of Sidon (i.e. second largest Phoenician city), Isa. 23:2
    4. Egypt, Isa. 23:3,5
    5. Canaan, Isa. 23:11
    6. Cyprus, Isa. 23:12

  3. Notice the number of IMPERATIVES directed at Tyre/Phoenicia.
    1. wail, Isa. 23:1, BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Isa. 13:6; 14:31; 15:2,3; 16:7 (twice); 65:14
    2. be silent (lit. "be still"), Isa. 23:2, BDB 198, KB 226, Qal IMPERATIVE
    3. be ashamed, Isa. 23:4, BDB 101, KB 116, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Isa. 1:29; 19:9; 20:5; 24:23; 26:11; 29:22; 30:5; 37:27; 41:11; 42:17; 44:9,11; 45:16,17,24; 49:23; 50:7; 54:4; 65:13; 66:5; Micah 3:7; 7:16
    4. pass over, Isa. 23:6, BDB 716, KB 778, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Isa. 23:2
    5. wail, Isa. 23:6, same as #1
    6. overflow (lit. "pass over"), Isa. 23:10, same as #4
    7. arise, Isa. 23:12, BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE
    8. pass over, Isa. 23:12, same as #4,6
    9. wail, Isa. 23:14, same as #1,5
    10. take your harp, Isa. 23:16, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE
    11. walk about the city, Isa. 23:16, BDB 685, KB 738, Qal IMPERATIVE
    12. pluck the strings (lit. "play skillfully"), Isa. 23:16, BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. 1 Sam. 16:17; Ps. 33:3; Ezek. 33:32
    13. sing many songs, v 16, BDB 915, KB 1176, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

  4. As always in trying to interpret the poems of Isaiah the historical setting would be very helpful in understanding the details and allusions, but these poems could fit several different invasions. The book of Isaiah is a collection of messages from throughout his life combined at some future date (an anthology by Isaiah's disciples). They are structured in non-chronological ways based on
    1. related words
    2. related geographical areas
    3. word plays
    4. themes
    5. and more

      Moderns do not know how, when, or by whom the OT books were finally compiled/edited.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 23:2 "Be silent"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:2 "Be silent" This Qal IMPERATIVE is parallel to "wail" in Isa. 23:1 (BDB 198 I). There is speculation based on a Ugaritic root that it reflects a separate root (BDB 199 II) "lament" ("wail," TEV; "lament," REB).

▣ "Sidon" This was a coastal city (cf. Gen. 10:19) of Phoenicia about twenty-five miles north of Tyre. It was originally the main city (cf. Josh. 13:4,6). The name seems to have come from the eldest son of Canaan, son of Ham (cf. Gen. 10:15). Tyre and Sidon are often linked together in the NT in reference to the nation of Phoenicia (cf. Matt. 11:21,22; 15:21; Acts 12:20).

NASB, NRSV, NJB "Your messengers crossed the sea"
NKJV "Whom those who cross the sea have filled"
TEV "You sent agents across the sea"
JB "whose goods traveled over the sea"
JPSOA "traders of Sidon"
Peshitta "the merchants of Zidon that passed over the sea"
LXX "the merchants of Phoenicia crossing the sea"

The NASB follows the Isaiah scroll from the DSS. The MT has "passed over (BDB 716, KB 778, Qal PARTICIPLE) the sea (BDB 410) they replenish you."

The term "your messengers," in its inflected form, is very similar in Hebrew to the VERB "fill."

  1. VERB, מלאוך ("fill," BDB 569, KB 583; Piel PERFECT, NKJV)
  2. NOUN, מלאכוך ("messenger," BDB 521, NASB)

The UBS Text Project, p.51, gives option #2 a C rating (considerable doubt).

23:3
NASB, JB  "the grain of the Nile"
NKJV, NRSV, REB, JPSOA  "the grain of Shihor"
NJB  "the grain of the Canal "
Peshitta  "the harvest of the river"
JPSOA  "the harvest of the Nile"

The MT has "grain of Shihor, harvest of the Nile." Shihor (BDB 1009) means "the pond of Horus" (KB 1477). It referred to

  1. an eastern branch of the Nile (BDB 1009)
  2. a canal of black (BDB 1007 I) water
  3. a lake in the eastern delta region

It is spelled differently in

  1. Josh. 13:13; 1 Chr. 13:5, שׁיחור
  2. Jer. 2:18, שׁחור
  3. Isa. 23:3, שׁחר

but all refer to the same area in Egypt.

▣ "she was the market of nations" See Ezek. 27:3-23.

entries.title: Isaiah 23:4 "Be ashamed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:4 "Be ashamed" The VERB (BDB 101, KB 116, Qal IMPERATIVE) is used of God's judgment on idols (cf. Jer. 50:2). Here it denotes the shame of a defeated nation (cf. Isa. 1:29; 19:9; 37:27; 41:11). These nations can experience forgiveness and restoration if they will turn to YHWH (cf. Isa. 49:23); this is also true of His own people (cf. Isa. 29:23; 45:17; 54:4).

▣ "Sidon" Sidon is personified. The NRSV footnote says "Ruined Sidon is barren like the sea without sailors (i.e. young men)."

It is possible that the speaker is not personified Sidon but the Canaannite god, Yam ("sea"). If so, then the next phrase is a characterization of the Canaanite sea god, "Mighty One of the Sea" (J. Oswalt, Isaiah, pp. 430-431).

entries.title: Isaiah 23:6 "Tarshish"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 23:6 "Tarshish" See SPECIAL TOPIC: TARSHISH

entries.title: Isaiah 23:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:7 This describes Tyre (cf. Isa. 23:5)

  1. jubilant city (i.e. prideful and self-satisfied, cf. Isa. 22:2; 24:8; 32:13)
  2. very old city (i.e. pride in their antiquity)
  3. colonizing nation (pride in their international influence)

entries.title: Isaiah 23:8-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:8-12 This strophe is united by the use of the VERB "planned" (lit. "advised" or "purposed," BDB 419, KB 421, Qal PERFECT, cf. Isa. 23:8,9; 14:24, 26, 27; 19:12,17). There is an intentionality behind history-YHWH! The kingdoms of this world make their plans (Isa. 23:8), but the God of creation also makes His (Isa. 23:9).

23:8
NASB, NRSv  "the bestower of crowns"
NKJV, Peshitta  "the crowning city"
TEV  "the imperial city"
NJB  "who used to hand out crowns"
REB  "the city with crowns in its gifts"
JPSOA  "crown-wearing"

The VERB (BDB 742, KB 815, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) means "to crown." It could refer to

  1. crown bestower (NASB, NRSV, NJB, REB, JPSOA)
  2. crown wearer (TEV, NKJV, Peshitta)

entries.title: Isaiah 23:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:10 The rival maritime empire of Tarshish (possibly Spain or Sardinia) is invited to expand and overflow because of the destruction of Phoenicia.

An alternate understanding of the phrase is in the Septuagint, "Till your land; for no more ships come out of Carthage." This is followed by the REB, "Take to the tillage of your fields, you people of Tarshish; for your market is lost." Your trading days are over, just settle down and farm your own land.

▣
NASB  "no more restraint"
NKJV  "no more strength"
TEV  "no one to protect you"
Peshitta  "no one to drive you away"
REB  "your market is lost"
JPSOA  "harbor no more"
NET  "no longer any marketplace"

The MT is difficult. The question of line two is—should it read

  1. belt, waistband, BDB 561, מזח
  2. haven, JPSOA
  3. market, מחז, NEB, NET

The UBS Text Project, p. 54, gives the MT, option #1, a B rating (some doubt).

entries.title: Isaiah 23:11 "He has stretched His hand out over the sea"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:11 "He has stretched His hand out over the sea" See note at Isa. 14:26.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "He has made the kingdoms tremble" The VERB (BDB 919, KB 1182, Hiphil PERFECT) is used of YHWH "shaking" several things.

  1. mountains, Isa. 5:25
  2. heavens, Isa. 13:13
  3. Sheol, Isa. 14:9
  4. sea, Isa. 23:11
  5. YHWH Himself, Isa. 28:21
  6. those who feel secure, Isa. 32:10,11
  7. nations, Isa. 64:2

and once of Judah as she opposes YHWH in Isa. Isa. 37:29.

▣ "Canaan" This could refer to Tyre as the only good fortress/harbor on the Canaanite coast or Canaan as a way of referring to the merchant kingdom of Phoenicia.

▣ "its strongholds" This PLURAL NOUN (BDB 731) is understood this way by most English translations. The Peshitta has "destroy its mighty men." The most creative translation is the NEB, REB, "its marts."

  1. her strongholds ‒ מעזניה
  2. her marts ‒ מעזניה

The only difference is vocalization. The UBS Text Project, P55 cannot decide on the original Hebrew text, but rejects the conjecture of the NEB, REB.

The TEV tries to combine both options with "centers of commerce."

entries.title: Isaiah 23:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:12 In this chapter Phoenicia (NIV) is called by the name of its old capital, "Sidon," and also its new current capital, "Tyre."

▣ "Arise, pass over to Cyprus; even there you will find no rest" Some see this as referring specifically to the king of Sidon, "Lulli," fleeing from the Assyrian army to Cyprus in 701 B.C., where he was killed (JB footnote, p. 1177). This is surely possible, but not certain. Hebrew poetry is ambiguous.

entries.title: Isaiah 23:13 "the land of the Chaldeans"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:13 "the land of the Chaldeans" This seems to refer to the destruction of old Babylon (not Neo-Babylon) by Assyria (cf. chapters 13-14). There are two "Babylons" mentioned in the Prophets.

  1. small semi-autonomous region close to the mouth of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers that rebelled against Assyria and was invaded and their capital "Babylon" destroyed by Sargon II (722-705 B.C.), who took the Babylonian throne name "King of Babylon." Then it would refer to the Babylonian kings
    1. Merodach-baladan, reigned 721-710 and again 703-702 B.C. (He sent messengers to Hezekiah in 712 B.C., cf. 2 Kgs. 20:12-21; Isaiah 39)
    2. Shamash-shum-ukim, son of Esarhaddon, 681-669 B.C. and rival brother to Ashurbanipal [669-633 B.C.] who was made king of Assyria
  2. a Neo (i.e. "new") Babylon appeared on the scene in 626 B.C. with the rise of Nabopolassor (626-605 B.C.), the father of Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 B.C.). Nabopolassor was instrumental in the fall of Asshur (one Assyrian capital) in 614 B.C. and Nineveh (the main Assyrian capital) in 612 B.C.. (see of "Brief Historical Survey of the Powers of Mesopotamia" in Appendix Three).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF BABYLON

▣ "it" Does this refer to the Chaldean capital Babylon or Sidon/Tyre? In context it refers to the city of Babylon destroyed by Sargon II in 710 or Sennacherib in 689 B.C. Tyre would look like Babylon. Assyria, Neo-Babylon, and Alexander the Great are coming!!!

▣ "for desert creatures" This term (BDB 850 II) denotes wild desert animals of some kind. It has the added connotation of being inhabited by the demonic (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 79, and NEB, REB translations).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEMONIC IN THE OT

entries.title: Isaiah 23:15 "for seventy years"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:15 "for seventy years" The time designation appears here and in Isa. 23:17. It seems to allude to a complete time (from 7 x 10, see SPECIAL TOPIC: SEVENTY YEARS). Notice some of its usages in Scripture.

  1. revenge, Gen. 4:24
  2. age of Terah when Abram was born, Gen. 11:26
  3. seventy in Jacob's family moved to Egypt, Exod. 1:5
  4. seventy elders during the Wilderness Wandering Period, Exod. 24:1,9; Num. 11:16,24,25 (also Ezek. 8:11)
  5. number of Abimelech's brothers who were killed, Jdg. 9:56
  6. expected life span, Ps. 90:10 (double is a special blessing from God, Job 42:16)
  7. the plague of YHWH killed 70,000, 2 Sam. 24:15; 1 Chr. 21:14
  8. Ahab's seventy sons, 2 Kgs. 10:1,6,7
  9. seventy year judgment
    1. Judah in Babylon, Jer. 25:11; Dan. 9:2; Zech. 7:5
    2. Tyre, Isa. 23:15
  10. Jesus sent out seventy, Luke 10:1,17
  11. forgiveness 70 times 7, Matt. 18:22

▣ "like the days of one king" This phrase designates the expected reign of a monarch. Seventy years was the time span for a normal life, but here it refers to a very long reign, which probably shows the symbolic nature of the round number.

entries.title: Isaiah 23:17-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:17-18 The riches of Phoenicia will flow to God's restored people (note also Isa. 18:7 and 45:14, which denote similar actions). Phoenicia will not respond to the witness of Israel, but will remain pagan (i.e. Ba'al worship).

The Jewish Study Bible, p. 828, thinks vv. 15-18 are theologically parallel to Isa. 19:18-25, which describes Egypt and Assyria coming to YHWH. However, the use of "harlot" in vv. 15,17,18 surely points in a different direction.

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 24:1 "the Lord lays the earth waste"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
24:1 "the Lord lays the earth waste" Verses 1 and 3 use a series of strong VERBS to describe YHWH's judgment on the earth (not "land" here because of parallel to "world" [BDB 385, cf. Isa. 14:16-17; 34:1; Jer. 10:12; 51:15], see Special Topic following).

  1. lays. . .waste, Isa. 24:1, BDB 132, KB 150, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, cf. Isa. 24:3; Nah. 2:2
  2. devastates, Isa. 24:1, BDB 118, KB 135, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, cf. Nah. 2:10
  3. distorts (lit. "twists," cf. NRSV), BDB 730, KB 796, Piel PERFECT with waw
  4. scatters, Isa. 24:1, BDB 806, KB 918, Hiphil PERFECT with waw
  5. completely laid waste, Isa. 24:3, BDB 132, KB 150, Niphal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root denote intensity
  6. completely despoiled, Isa. 24:3, BDB 102, KB 117, Niphal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root denotes intensity. YHWH takes back His gifts, given in creation (cf. Isa. 24:5-6). This is a reversal of the purpose of original creation, but a faithful remnant will survive (cf. Isa. 24:6)!

Verses 1 and 3 are very similar to God's judgment of the earth (ץרא, BDB 75) in Noah's day (cf. Genesis 6-9; also note the attempts to avoid God's judgment in Isa. 2:10,19,21). Worldwide emptying is exactly the opposite of creation's purpose!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH

▣ "distorts its surface" This could either be imagery of God's judgment on the earth in physical terms (lit. "twist," BDB 730, KB 796, Piel PERFECT with waw) or it may be imagery of God emptying earth's inhabitants as someone would clean dirty kitchen pans.

▣ "and scatters its inhabitants" This is very similar to the terminology used in Genesis 10 for the tower of Babel. Here it denotes exile.
