READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This context refers to the many revolts against Assyria after the death of Sargon II in 705 B.C. These revolts by numerous vassal states were put down by the new King Sennacherib.

  2. The Egyptian dynasty from which Hezekiah sought a political/military alliance was the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. It was led by the Cushite/Nubian king, Shabaka, who aggressively tried to rally all the small nations, from the head waters of the Euphrates to Egypt's borders, against Assyria.

  3. There are six woe oracles in this literary unit (i.e. Isa. 28-33).
    1. woe to the northern and southern tribes of Israel, Isa. 28
    2. woe to Jerusalem, Isa. 29:1-14
    3. woe to those who seek help in political alliances and not in YHWH, Isa. 29:15-24
    4. woe to those seeking help from Egypt, Isa. 30
    5. woe to those seeking help from Egypt, Isa. 31-32
    6. woe to Assyria, Isa. 33

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 30:2 "Without consulting Me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:2 "Without consulting Me" These Judeans apparently consulted the occult (cf. Isa. 8:19), but not YHWH's prophet (lit. "without asking my mouth," cf. Exod. 4:16; Jos. 9:14).

▣ "refuge. . .shelter in the shadow of" These reflect two terms (BDB 731, KB 797 and BDB 340, KB 337, both Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS) usually used of YHWH's protection, but here they are used to describe Egypt.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW AS METAPHOR FOR PROTECTION AND CARE

SPECIAL TOPIC: REFUGE (OT)

entries.title: Isaiah 30:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 30:3 There is no hope in Egypt (cf. Isa. 30:3,5,7; 20:5-6; 36:6). Amazingly Judah left her covenant God for the protection of a previous task master! Judah will do it again in Jeremiah's day (cf. Jer. 2:13; 42:18-22)!

entries.title: Isaiah 30:4 "their princes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:4 "their princes" The MT has "his," which is followed by most English translations. These "princes" may refer to Pharaoh's leaders (cf. Isa. 19:11), but in context they refer to Hezekiah's representatives seeking a political/military alliance with Egypt.

▣ "Zoan. . .Hanes" These were two cities that were recently freed by the Twenty-fifth Nubian Dynasty. They were used to show the power of the Egyptian army.

The two cities mentioned are connected to the delta region of the Nile.

  1. Zoan is also known as Tanis or Avaris (cf. Num. 13:22; Ps. 78:12,43; Isa. 19:11).
  2. Hanes is unknown (LXX omits), but possibly connected to Tahpanhes (ABD, vol. 6, p. 308, cf. Jer. 2:16; 43:7,8,9; 44:1; 46:14), a nearby fortress. Some scholars relate this name to Heracleopolis Magna because it was a regional capital during the Nubian Dynasty.
30:5
NASB, NKJV  "ashamed"
NRSV, JPSOA, NET  "shame"
TEV  "regret"
NJB  "disappointed"
LXX, Peshitta  "cannot profit"
REB  "unprofitable"

All of these English translations chose the Qere option (i.e. marginal reading) of the Masoretic scholars (הבושׁ, BDB 101, KB 116, Hiphil PERFECT, the NOUN [BDB 102] is used later in this verse). The MT text (Kethib) has "cause to stink" (הבאיש, BDB 92, KB 107, Hiphil PERFECT; the VERB is used in Isa. 50:2 and the NOUN in Isa. 34:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

entries.title: Isaiah 30:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:6 Notice the "beasts" (BDB 96) of the Negev (BDB 616) listed.

  1. lioness, BDB 522
  2. lion, BDB 539 I
  3. viper, BDB 821
  4. flying serpent, BDB 977 I with the Polel PARTICIPLE "flying" (BDB 733, KB 800), see notes at Isa. 14:29; 27:1 and SPECIAL TOPIC: SERAPHIM
  5. donkeys, BDB 747, SPECIAL TOPIC: MULES/DONKEYS
  6. camels, BDB 168

Numbers 1-4 speak of the danger of the trip, while 5-6 speak of the beasts of burden that carried the financial incentive.

30:7
NASB  "Rahab who has been exterminated"
NKJV  "Rahab-Hem-Shebeth" ("Rahab sits idle," footnote)
NRSV  "Rahab who sits still"
TEV  "So I have nicknamed Egypt, 'The Harmless Dragon'"
NJB  "and so I call her 'Rahab-the-collapsed"
REB  "Rahab subdued"

The point is that Egypt (i.e. Rahab, cf. Ps. 87:4; see full note at Isa. 51:9) cannot stop or even help against the Assyrian invasion of Palestine. The serpent (Rahab, BDB 923, KB 1193) is toothless!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LEVIATHAN

entries.title: Isaiah 30:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:6-7 This describes the Judean caravans that were sent through the dangerous Judean and Egyptian deserts (i.e. Isa. 30:6b,c), bearing gifts (Isa. 30:6d,e) in an attempt to try to form a political alliance with Egypt (i.e. Rahab, BDB 923, see note at Isa. 27:1).

The NASB Study Bible makes the comment that the caravan might have had to take the back roads to Egypt because of the Assyrian army's control of the main caravan routes (p. 997, also IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 621).

The NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 87, makes the comment that this might represent a reverse Exodus. But I think in context a political alliance fits best. I listed some of the interpretive options to illustrate.

  1. how ambiguous Hebrew poetry can be
  2. how different allusions or connotations can be seen behind different words and phrases
  3. to emphasize again the importance of finding the main point of the strophe and its relationship to the larger context and not basing one's main theological points on the details of Hebrew poetry

entries.title: Isaiah 30:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:8 There are two reasons for having a written record.

  1. God wants a written evidence of His people's rebellion so when He brings them to court, the evidence is obvious (cf. Isa. 8:1; Hab. 2:2)
  2. to show His control of history, thereby confirming Himself and His prophet so that future generations may trust in His word.

There are several commands in this verse.

  1. go, BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. write, BDB 507, KB 503, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. inscribe, BDB 349, KB 347, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. let it be a witness forever, BDB 224, KB 243, Qal JUSSIVE

The MT has "a witness" (BDB 723 I), "forever" (BDB 761, cf. NKJV, NJB, LXX, Peshitta), but the root, דע (last poetic line), normally means "perpetuity" (i.e. "a segment of time," similar to 'olam). Often English translations do not fully reflect the possible semantic range of Hebrew terms. That is why comparing English translations is helpful.

The first two poetic lines of v. 8 are parallel.

  1. write ‒ inscribe
  2. tablet ‒ scroll

This is not referring to two different kinds of writing material, but emphasizing that the revelation be saved and later consulted. Predictive prophecy is a powerful evidence of the uniqueness and inspiration of the Bible.
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)
SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

This passage may demonstrate that most of the prophets' messages were oral presentations. Someone listening, possibly a prophetic helper, recorded what was spoken (i.e. Baruch for Jeremiah, cf. Jer. 36:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

entries.title: Isaiah 30:9 "For this is a rebellious people, false sons,
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:9 "For this is a rebellious people, false sons,

 Sons who refuse to listen

 To the instruction of the Lord" See Isa. 30:1; 1:2-3; 6:9-10; 29:9-12. The VERBAL "to listen" (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) denotes "hearing so as to do" (i.e. Deut. 4:1; 6:4). This concept of a lifestyle response to divine revelation is the heart of OT faith (cf. Deut. 29:4). As this verse clearly shows, obedience is a recurrent problem for fallen humanity. The weakness of the OT is not its revelation, but the human covenant partners (cf. Galatians 3). Herein is the need for a "new covenant" (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36). The new one, like the first one, is designed to promote fellowship between God and mankind and to reveal God's characteristics to a fallen world. Obedience is crucial in both (cf. Matt. 11:29; Luke 6:46).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

entries.title: Isaiah 30:10 "seers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:10 "seers" This term (BDB 909) is obviously related to the common VERB "to see" (BDB 906).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHET (the different Hebrew terms)

entries.title: Isaiah 30:10-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:10-11 The godless Judeans not only do not want to follow YHWH, they do not want to hear from His messengers (i.e. Jer. 7:25-26; Amos 2:12)!

  1. to the seers, see not
    1. seers, BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
    2. see not, BDB 906, KB 1157, negated Qal IMPERFECT
  2. to the prophets, prophesy not
    1. prophets, BDB 302
    2. prophesy not, BDB 302, KB 301, negated Qal IMPERFECT
  3. speak to us pleasant words, BDB 180, KB 210, Piel IMPERATIVE
  4. prophesy illusions, BDB 302, KB 301, Qal IMPERATIVE. "Illusions" (BDB 1122) is found only here. They wanted any message but YHWH's message!
  5. get out of the way (lit. "turn aside from the way"), BDB 693, KB 747, Qal IMPERATIVE
  6. turn aside from the path, BDB 639, KB 692, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Deut. 5:32; 17:20; 28:14; Josh. 1:7; 23:6 for "do not turn"
  7. let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel (lit. "remove from before us"), BDB 991, KB 1407, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

These are shocking statements. Isaiah is using the literary technique known as "diatribe" (cf. Habakkuk) to forcibly make his point. These people are YHWHists in name only!

entries.title: Isaiah 30:11 "path"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:11 "path" The imagery of YHWH's revelation as a "path" or "way" is common. Faithful followers are to stay on the clear, smooth, straight path of divine revelation (cf. Ps. 119:105). These covenant people did not want to hear (v. 10) or follow YHWH's law (v. 12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

▣ "the Holy One of Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

entries.title: Isaiah 30:12 "And have put your trust in"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:12 "And have put your trust in" This VERB (BDB 105, KB 120, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) is used often in Isaiah.

  1. trust in God, cf. Isa. 12:2; 26:3,4; 36:7,15; 37:10; 50:10 (in the name of the Lord; see SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" of YHWH)
  2. trust in things
    1. Isa. 30:12, oppression and guile
    2. Isa. 31:1, Egyptian military
    3. Isa. 36:6,9, Egypt
    4. Isa. 42:17, idols
    5. Isa. 47:10, wickedness
    6. Isa. 59:4, confusion
  3. trust in persons, Isa. 36:5,6,9

▣ "relied" This VERB (BDB 1043, KB 1612, Niphal IMPERFECT with waw) is parallel to "trust" (cf. 2 Chr. 13:18; 14:11; 16:7,8). It is found only in the Niphal stem and is used several times in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 10:20 [twice]; 31:1; 50:10). It literally means "to lean on" or "support oneself" (cf. Gen. 18:4).

entries.title: Isaiah 30:13-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:13-14 These are two images used for the destruction to come:

  1. the imminent collapse of a wall
  2. the complete shattering of a clay pot

entries.title: Isaiah 30:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:15 Notice the names for Judah's God.

  1. Adon YHWH (Lord God)
  2. the Holy One of Israel, cf. Isa. 1:4; 30:11,12

These are covenant titles! These should have been covenant people!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣ "In repentance and rest you will be saved" Isaiah 30:15-17 describes two reactions to God's promises. Isa. 30:15 describes true faith (cf. Ps. 118:6-9), while Isa. 30:16-17 describe false faith.

Salvation (BDB 446, KB 448, Niphal IMPERFECT) is described with two NOUNS.

  1. repentance (lit. "turning back"), BDB 1000, KB 1435; this is a rare term found only here. Some scholars suggest a connection with Micah 2:8, but this is not certain. The basic root, שׁוב, means "to turn back" and fits the context.
  2. rest, BDB 629 I, KB 692 II, means "calm," "patience," "peace"
    1. Job 17:16; Eccl. 6:5, rest in death
    2. Prov. 29:9, no rest for the fool
    3. Isa. 30:15, possibly rest from war, based on the parallel with Micah 2:8, #1 above

The evangelical in me wants to turn these key words, "saved," "repentance," and "rest," into a gospel message, but this is not the NT! This is a strophe about Judea seeking a military alliance with Egypt. She has turned away from her God and is not resting in Him (cf. Isa. 15d).

▣ "In quietness and trust is your strength" This line is parallel to the above line, so there are four terms used in YHWH's address to them.

  1. repentance, see above
  2. rest, see above
  3. quietness, BDB 1052, KB 1641, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE, cf. Isa. 7:4; 32:17
  4. trust, BDB 105, cf. Isa. 32:17

Remember this is a theological parallel to Isaiah's call for Ahaz to "take care, and be calm, have no fear and do not be fainthearted" in Isa. 7:4. Now YHWH is addressing Hezekiah with the same message! Trust Me!

entries.title: Isaiah 30:16 "those who pursue you shall be swift"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 30:16 "those who pursue you shall be swift" Judah was trusting in military might which she planned on getting from Egypt (cf. Isa. 2:6-7; 31:1). However, as she trusted in the swiftness of her mercenary cavalry, God asserts the swiftness of His surrogate Assyrian army.

entries.title: Isaiah 30:17 "One thousand will flee at the threat of one man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:17 "One thousand will flee at the threat of one man" This is Holy War terminology (cf. Lev. 26:8; Deut. 32:30; Jos. 23:10). It is taken from the Exodus and Conquest of Palestine. However, the tables are now turned as God is on Assyria's side.

The term "threat" or "rebuke" (BDB 172) may, in this context, refer to a battle cry. In Ps. 76:6; 80:11, this same term is used of YHWH. "Lips" and "tongue" in v. 27.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

entries.title: Isaiah 30:18 "the Lord longs to be gracious to you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:18 "the Lord longs to be gracious to you" What a wonderful verse (and a shocking reversal) that reveals the character of YHWH.

  1. longs to be gracious
    1. longs (lit. "waits"), BDB 314, KB 313, Piel IMPERFECT
    2. gracious, BDB 335, KB 334, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  2. waits on high to have compassion
    1. waits (lit. "is on high"), BDB 926, KB 1202, Qal IMPERFECT
    2. compassion, BDB 933, KB 1216, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

Humans must trust in the character of God. He wants to bless (BDB 80) all those who long (lit. "wait," same VERB as #1 above, but here a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, cf. Isa. 25:9; 26:8; 33:2; Ps. 33:20) for Him. This "waiting" expresses a trusting, patient world-view of YHWH's presence, promises, and purposes (cf. Isa. 48:9-11; Hosea 11:8-11), even in times of crises and uncertainty.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "He waits on high to have compassion" This implies the conditional nature of the Mosaic Covenant. The "if. . .then" pattern of OT texts is common. See SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

"On high" implies YHWH's abode as the Third Heaven. See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

▣ "the Lord is a God of justice" This is an important title. YHWH is not only a merciful God (v. 18a), but also a just God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGE, JUDGMENT AND JUSTICE IN ISAIAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUSTICE

▣ "all those who long for Him" The VERBAL (BDB 314, KB 313, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, cf. Isa. 8:17; 25:9; 26:8; 33:2) is literally "wait" and is repeated from line 2. YHWH "waits" for humans to respond (i.e. James 4:8). In this verse, "wait for Him" is imagery for trusting Him through life (cf. Isa. 40:31; 64:4; Ps. 33:18-22).

The divine covenant is unconditional on God's promises to redeem fallen mankind, but conditional on individuals responding in faith, repentance, obedience, service, worship, and perseverance.

Salvation is absolutely free in the mercy of God, but costs everything on the part of His faithful followers (i.e. Eph. 2:8-9 and v. 10; Phil. 2:12-13),

entries.title: Isaiah 30:19-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:19-22 Notice the radical transition from judgment to mercy. YHWH will have mercy on a future repentant, faithful Judah.

  1. they will weep no longer ‒ this is emphatic. The Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the Qal IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 113, KB 129). This new day is also alluded to in Isa. 25:8; 60:20; 61:1-3.
  2. He will surely be gracious ‒ this is made emphatic by using the Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 335, KB 334; see note at Isa. 30:18).
  3. He hears the sound of their cry ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT.
  4. He will answer ‒ BDB 772, KB 851, Qal PERFECT, cf. Isa. 58:9; 65:24 (i.e. the covenant is active and strong)
  5. He will no longer hide Himself ‒ BDB 489, KB 486, Niphal IMPERFECT. This is a rare term found only here. It literally means "to thrust into a corner" (NKJV). The NASB gets "hide" from an Arabic root, "to enclose" or "to guard."
  6. your eyes will behold your Teacher ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE.
  7. your ears will hear a word behind you ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERFECT. This is the reversal of Isa. 6:9-10 and the reinstatement of Deut. 29:4. The "word" (BDB 182) which they will hear is the rest of the verse, which is imagery for lifestyle faith.
    1. the way, BDB 202 (i.e. covenant living, cf. Isa. 35:8-9; 42:16; Ps. 25:8-9)
    2. walk in it, BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERFECT (cf. Lev. 26:3; Deut. 8:6; 10:12; 11:22; 28:9; 1 Kgs. 6:12; 8:36,61; 2 Chr. 6:16,27; Neh. 10:29; Isa. 2:3; Jer. 6:16; 44:10,23; Ezek. 5:6-7; 11:20; 18:17; 20:13,16,19,21; 33:15; 37:24; Dan. 9:10; Micah 4:2)
    3. turn to the right or to the left (another idiom related to staying in the way)
  8. you will turn from your idols (notice the conditional aspect of YHWH's promises)
    1. defile them, BDB 379, KB 375, Piel PERFECT with waw
    2. scatter them, BDB 279, KB 280, Qal IMPERFECT
    3. say to them "Be gone," BDB 422, KB 425, Qal IMPERATIVE

Isaiah is unique in its assertion that Jerusalem will never fall (if Judah repents and trusts YHWH), but Jeremiah asserts that it will because they refuse to trust and obey. Both assert it will be restored if and when it turns back to YHWH!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Isaiah 30:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:20 In this verse there are several persons mentioned.

  1. "the Lord" ‒ Adon
  2. "your Teacher" (twice)
  3. "you" (i.e. Judeans, PLURAL)

The "teacher" could refer to

  1. YHWH (PLURAL OF MAJESTY, TEV, this is in direct contrast to Isa. 45:15, "You are a God who hides Himself," but different VERB)
  2. Messiah (YHWH's representative; this may reflect the New Covenant, cf. Jer. 31:31-34)
  3. prophets/priests (i.e. restoration of true revelation, which is the opposite of vv. 10-11, also note Ps. 74:9)

The term "teacher" (מוריך, BDB 435) can be understood as

  1. SINGULAR, John J. Owens, Analytical Key to the OT, vol. 4, p. 90, see NASB, JPSOA, NRSV, ASV
  2. PLURAL, Benjamin Davidson, Analytical Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon, p. 475, see NKJV, REB

The Hebrew form could reflect either one (NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 538).

For me, I think "teachers" refers to prophets and priests who were told not to speak in vv. 10-11. The problem was not that God was not revealing Himself, but His covenant people did not want to hear!

30:22
NASB, NRSV, NJB, LXX  "scatter them"
NKJV, TEV  "will throw them away"
REB  "will loathe them"
Peshitta, JPSOA  "shall cast them away"

The MT has the VERB "scatter" (BDB 279, KB 280, Qal IMPERFECT) but a revocalization results in "loathe." The UBS Text Project, p. 70, gives the MT an "A" rating (almost certain).

NASB  "an impure thing"
NKJV  "an unclean thing"
NRSV  "like filthy rags"
NJB  "like the polluted things"
Peshitta  "like unclean water of a menstrous woman"

This is the term (BDB 188) which denotes the rags used during a woman's menstrual period (cf. Lev. 15:33; 20:18). This would have been a strong cultural idiom of a ceremonially unclean thing which must be set apart (cf. Isa. 64:6).

The LXX (REB) takes the next word "be gone" (BDB 422, KB 425) as a similar term, "feces," which would be another cultural idiom of ceremonial defilement.

entries.title: Isaiah 30:23-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:23-26 This describes the agricultural and pastoral blessing promised to Abraham's seed if they walk in YHWH's covenant (cf. Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28).

  1. rain at the proper time, Isa. 30:23,25, cf. Isa. 35:6,7; 41:18; 43:19,20
  2. good crops, Isa. 30:23
    1. rich (BDB 206)
    2. plenteous (BDB 1032)
  3. green pastures for the livestock, Isa. 30:23, cf. Isa. 32:20
  4. a special food for the working livestock, Isa. 30:24 (term BDB 330 is found only here)
  5. enemies defeated, Isa. 30:25 ("on every high hill." This same idiom was used for Ba'al worship in Hosea)
  6. plenty of light for health and growth, Isa. 30:26, cf. Isa. 60:20-21 (seven being symbolic of the perfect amount and light being symbolic of God's presence, i.e. His name, Isa. 30:27)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

30:25
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta  "the Towers"
TEV  "forts"
NJB  "strongholds"
REB  "fortresses"
NEB  "the highest"

The MT has "Towers" (BDB 153), but the same consonants revocalized can mean "the great ones" (BDB 152, i.e. wealthy, powerful people). The UBS Text Project, p. 71, gives "towers"a "B" rating (some doubt).

entries.title: Isaiah 30:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:26 These blessings of restoration (cf. Isa. 11:6-9; Rom. 8:18-22; see full note at 30:20) are after

  1. the day of great slaughter when the towers fall, Isa. 30:25
  2. the day of the Lord binds up the fracture of His people, Isa. 30:26
  3. the day the Lord heals the bruise He has inflicted, Isa. 30:26

Notice #2 and #3 are imagery of YHWH as the great physician!

▣ "heals the bruise He has inflicted" This phrase and others like it (i.e. Deut. 32:39; 1 Sam. 2:6; 2 Kgs. 5:7; Job 5:18; Isa. 45:7; Jer. 1:10; 24:6; 31:28; Hosea 6:1; Amos 3:6) have caused moderns to question the merciful character of God. These are all idiomatic ways of asserting monotheism (i.e. one and only one causality; see full note at Isa. 14:24-27). Modern western people assume that there are many causalities in their experiences and their histories. The Bible asserts the sovereignty of God in all areas of reality. He is present and active!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

entries.title: Isaiah 30:27 "the name of the Lord comes. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:27 "the name of the Lord comes. . ." The name represents the personal presence of YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "Burning in His anger. . .lips. . .tongue" The only vocabulary humans have to descirbe God is

  1. analogy ‒ what He is like
  2. negation ‒ what He is not
  3. personification

YHWH is an eternal, spiritual Being present throughout the entire universe and not limited by time/space. Humans must speak of Him in practical, but not exhaustive, terms.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE DEITY

▣
NASB  "dense is His smoke"
NKJV  "His burden is heavy"
NRSV  "in thick rising smoke"
NJB  "heavy his threat"
NET  "awesome splendor"
REB  "doom heavy"
JPSOA  "with a heavy burden"
Peshitta  "his train is glorious"

The MT has כבד, BDB 457, KB 451, CONSTRUCT BDB 673, "rising smoke." The first word can mean

  1. be heavy
  2. weighty
  3. burdensome
  4. honored

The second term (משאה, BDB 673, KB 640) is found only here in the OT. BDB says it means "the uplifted" (cloud). KB says it means "lifting up, exaltation," but it also lists Jdg. 20:38-40 as a parallel where משאת, Isa. 30:38, denotes rising smoke from a burning city. The context of Isa. 30:27 is one of theophany and judgment, so both fit.

  1. exaltation, denoting a cloud (i.e. Shekinah)
  2. heavy smoke

▣ "lips. . .tongue" This is imagery about the power of YHWH's revelation (cf. vv. 30a, 31a; Isa. 11:4; 49:2; 55:11). This is parallel to "breath" (vv. 28, 33). YHWH's word equals YHWH's personal presence. To ignore either is disastrous!

In the NT this same imagery is seen in Jesus with a two-edged sword coming out of His mouth (cf. Rev. 1:16; 2:12; 19:21).

entries.title: Isaiah 30:27-33
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:27-33 This strophe reflects God's judgment on Assyria in the imagery of a theophany as an approaching storm (cf. Exod. 19:16ff; Jdg. 5:4-5; Ps. 18:7ff; 50:3-5; Hab. 3:3-4).

  1. elements of theophany ‒ Isa. 30:27, 30a-c, 33e
  2. elements of storm ‒ Isa. 30:28, 30d
  3. elements of restoration ‒ Isa. 30:29
  4. elements of judgment ‒ Assyria, Isa. 30:31-33

entries.title: Isaiah 30:28 "Which reaches to the neck"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:28 "Which reaches to the neck" This same idiom was used of the Assyrian invasion in Isa. 8:8. Here, the idiom is reversed and YHWH fights on Judah's side against Assyria.

▣
NASB  "To shake the nations back and forth in a sieve"
NKJV  "to sift the nations with a sieve of futility"
NRSV, NJB  "to sift nations with a sieve of destruction"
REB  "He sieves the nations for destruction"
Peshitta  "to confuse the nations because of their
 erring vanity"
LXX  "to confound the nations for their vain error"
JPSOA  "to set misguiding yoke upon the nations"

The MT has "to sift (lit. "swing" or "to move to and fro") nations with the sieve (BDB 632) of worthlessness (BDB 996)." The interpretive question is, "Do we seek the imagery from

  1. the VERB ‒ a sieve swinging back and forth to separate grain from the husk
  2. the NOUN ‒ nothingness, emptiness, vanity possibly denoting idol worship

In context, it is the mercenary army of the Assyrian Empire with its King that will be judged, cf. vv. 30-33. Verses 23-26 and 29 refer to Judah being blessed.

entries.title: Isaiah 30:29 "the mountain of the Lord, to the Rock of Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 30:29 "the mountain of the Lord, to the Rock of Israel" These are idioms for the temple in Jerusalem because of parallelism. Often "the rock" refers to YHWH Himself (cf. Isa. 17:10; Deut. 32:4,18,30; 1 Sam. 2:2; Ps. 18:2,31,46; 28:1; 31:3; 42:9).

entries.title: Isaiah 30:30 "His voice"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:30 "His voice" Literally, "the majesty (BDB 217) of His voice." God's will is accomplished through speaking (i.e. creation, Genesis 1). His voice is effective (cf. Isa. 45:23; 55:11; Matt. 24:35). The imagery of Jesus with a two-edged sword (cf. Heb. 4:12) coming out of His mouth (cf. Isa. 49:2; Rev. 1:16; 2:12,16; 19:15) is theologically parallel, as is "the rod of His mouth" in Isa. 11:4.

▣ "hailstones" God used them in Jos. 10:11 as a way to defeat the Canaanites and give victory to Israel (cf. Jos. 10:14,42; 23:3,10).

30:31
NASB, TEV, NJB  "will be terrified"
NKJV  "will be beaten down"
NRSV  "will be terror-stricken"
JB  "will be battered"
LXX. Peshitta  "will be defeated"
JPSOA  "shall be cowed"
NET  "shatter"

The VERB (BDB 369, KB 365, Qal IMPERFECT) literally means "be shattered," denoting a complete defeat in battle which is preceded by a numbing, paralyzing fear of the upcoming defeat (cf. Isa. 7:8; 8:9 [thrice]; 9:4; 20:5; 30:31; 31:4,9; 37:27; 51:6,7). YHWH is fighting on His people's side against Assyria. The fear and panic and loss experienced by Israel and Judah is now being felt by Assyria, which in the past, was the rod of YHWH's anger (cf. Isa. 10:5).

▣ "He strikes with a rod" In Isaiah 10:5, Assyria is called the "rod of God's anger," but here the roles are reversed and God is back on His people's side. The rod (BDB 986) now feels the rod!

entries.title: Isaiah 30:32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:32 The judgment of the Lord is expressed by the imagery of a beating with a rod. It is possible that the next two lines (Isa. 30:32c,d) depict

  1. strokes being given at the musical beat of rejoicing
  2. that Judah's rejoicing follows Assyria's defeat by YHWH (cf. Isa. 30:32d).

entries.title: Isaiah 30:33 "Topheth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
30:33 "Topheth" This Hebrew word, found only here, apparently means a "place of burning" (BDB 1075). It is often identified with "Topheth" (BDB 1075 II), which was a valley outside the southern walls of Jerusalem and is often used in connection with the worship of the god, Molech (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH). Here, the context could imply

  1. a place of sacrifice to YHWH prepared by the king of His restored people
  2. the funeral pyre for Assyria's king prepared by YHWH Himself (cf. Isa. 31:9)
  3. "the King" which refers to Molech, the Phoenician fire god (cf. Lev. 18:21)

In context #2 fits best.

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 31:1 "Woe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:1 "Woe" This is the fifth in a series of "woes" that began in Isa. 28:1; 29:1,15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1. The term introduces the poetic meter of a funeral lament. See note at Isa. 5:8.

▣ "who go down to Egypt for help" The people of God were attempting to trust (BDB 105, KB 120) in political alliances instead of the power, presence, and promises of YHWH for their help (cf. chapters 28-34).

▣ "horses. . .chariots. . .horsemen" The Assyrians were known for their very large cavalry. Egypt was known for her very large contingent of chariots. Judah was afraid of the Assyrians and was trusting in Egypt instead of the Holy One of Israel. Humans of all periods of history must be careful of trusting in the current level of technology or numerical superiority instead of the biblical God of creation and mercy.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "chariots" Egypt exported chariots to all the surrounding countries (cf. 1 Kgs. 10:29), but they could be effective only on flat land, not the hill country of Judah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS

▣ "the Holy One of Israel. . .the Lord" These two terms apply to the Covenant God (cf. Isa. 1:4). The first refers to His nature as righteous, yet the God that calls sinful humans to be His children.

The second term is the Covenant name for God, "YHWH" (cf. Exod. 3:14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

▣ "look. . .seek" Both of these VERBS are negated Qal PERFECTS, which denotes a settled condition.

  1. look (lit. "to gaze at intently"), BDB 1043, KB 1609, cf. Isa. 17:7,8
  2. seek, BDB 205, KB 233, cf. Isa. 9:13; 55:6; 58:2; 65:10

These VERBS denote an intense personal element (cf. Dan. 9:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
ISAIAH 31

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Isaiah 31-32 is a literary unit that deals with the same historical event as Isa. 29:15-30:33. Hezekiah attempted to seek an alliance with Egypt to protect themselves from Assyrian aggression, but in 701 B.C. Senacherib invaded Judah and destroyed forty-six walled cities, though Jerusalem itself was spared.

  2. The Anchor Bible Commentary has an interesting chart that shows the characteristic prophetic swings between judgment and hope (p. 426).

    Isa. 28:14-15

    Isa. 29:17-21
    Isa. 30:29-33
    Isa. 31:4-5, 8-9

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 31:2 "He also is wise and will bring disaster"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:2 "He also is wise and will bring disaster" The NET Bible sees this as a sarcastic comment about Judah's advisors who are seeking help from Egypt (p. 1237). However, the whole verse, not just the last two lines, speaks of YHWH.

▣ "And does not retract His words" When God speaks, His words can be depended on (cf. Isa. 45:23; 55:11; Jer. 44:29).

▣ "will arise" This VERB (BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal PERFECT with waw) is used anthropomorphically of YHWH rising from His throne to do battle on behalf of His people (cf. Isa. 14:22) or against His people (cf. Amos 7:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

▣ "the house of evil-doers. . .the workers of iniquity" These two phrases refer to Judah (i.e., "he who is helped," Isa. 31:3e) and her political alliances (i.e., Egypt, "he who helps," Isa. 31:3d).

entries.title: Isaiah 31:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:3 This is a comparison between the frailty of human beings and the eternality of God (El). Specifically here it may refer to Exod. 14:26-31a.

This verse also clearly contrasts God (El) with flesh. God is "spirit" (cf. John 4:24). He can take a human form (theophany), but He is spirit and dwells simultaneously throughout his creation (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:27; Jer. 23:24). He chooses to fellowship with humble, repentant believers (i.e., Isa. 66:1-2).

▣ "the Lord will stretch out His hand" This is an anthropomorphic idiom of God's actions.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE DEITY

▣ "all of them will come to an end together" This VERB (BDB 477, KB 476, Qal IMPERFECT) denotes a complete destruction and end (cf. Isa. 1:28; 16:4; 29:20). What looks powerful and long lasting is not! This is similar to the common proverb about the transitoriness of humans as grass (cf. Isa. 40:6-8; Ps. 90:5-6; 103:15; 104:14; James 1:10-11; 1 Pet. 1:24).

entries.title: Isaiah 31:4 "the lion"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:4 "the lion" This imagery seems to describe God as powerful and tenacious over His own special place (i.e., temple). If so, it is a reversal of the first strophe (Isa. 31:1-3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

▣ "the Lord of hosts come down" This VERB (BDB 432, KB 434, Qal IMPERFECT) means "to come down," "to go down," "to descend." It is used several times of YHWH leaving His abode in the heavens and coming to earth

  1. to see and respond to the actions of humans, Gen. 11:5,7; 18:21
  2. to reveal Himself to humans, Exod. 3:8; 19:11,18,20; Num. 11:17,25; 12:5 (two special places where His attributes are listed are Exod. 34:5,6-7; Neh. 9:13,17)
  3. to characterize YWWH, 2 Sam. 22:10; Ps. 18:9; 144:5
  4. for judgment, Micah 1:3 (like #1)

This VERB is spacial (i.e., down), but it is imagery when referring to the relationship between heaven and earth (cf. Acts 1:2,9).

Judah went down to Egypt (Isa. 31:1, same VERB), YHWH comes down to defend Jerusalem even amidst their unbelief. Isaiah uniquely asserts the inviolability of Jerusalem! However, later prophets do not share his optimism of Judah's ability to repent and trust in YHWH (cf. Jer. 26:18; Micah 3:11-12; 5:5b-6,7-8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

entries.title: Isaiah 31:5 "Like flying birds"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:5 "Like flying birds" This is a reference to God as tender and loyal like a mother bird ("will protect," BDB 170, KB 199, both Hiphil IMPERFECT and Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root to denote intensity; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW). Often times in the Bible, God is described by feminine imagery (cf. Gen. 1:2; Deut. 32:11; Isa. 40:31; Hosea 11:4; Matt. 23:37; Luke 13:24).

Notice the things YHWH will do for His people in Isa. 31:5.

  1. will protect, BDB 170, KB 199 Hiphil IMPERFECT
  2. will protect, BDB 170, KB 199, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
  3. will deliver, BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil PERFECT with waw
  4. will pass over, BDB 820, KB 947, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
  5. will rescue, BDB 572, KB 589, Hiphil PERFECT with waw

▣ "He will pass over" This VERB (BDB 820, KB 947, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE, cf. Exod. 12:11-27) refers to God's protection against human forces. There seems to be an allusion to the Passover event of the book of Exodus where God, against all human odds, protected and delivered His people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PASSOVER

entries.title: Isaiah 31:6 "Return to Him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:6 "Return to Him" The VERB is shub (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERATIVE), which basically means "to turn back" or "return." It can be used of

  1. turning from God, Num. 14:43; Josh. 22:16,18,23,29; Jdg. 2:19; 8:33; 1 Sam. 15:11; 1 Kgs. 9:6; Jer. 3:19; 8:4
  2. turning to God, 1 Kgs. 8:33,48; 2 Chr. 15:4; 30:9; Ps. 51:13; 116:7; Isa. 6:10; 10:21,22; 31:6; Jer. 3:7,12,14,22; 4:1; 5:3; Hosea 3:5; 5:4; 6:1; 7:10,16; 11:5; 14:1,2; Amos 4:6,8,9,10,11 (notice esp. Jeremiah 7 and Amos 4)
  3. YHWH initially telling Isaiah that Judah would not/could not repent (cf. Isa. 6:10), but not for the first time in the book He calls on them to return to Him.

Repentance is not so much an emotion as it is an attitude toward God. It is a reorientation of life from self to Him. It denotes a willingness to change and be changed. It is not the complete cessation of sin, but a daily cessation of known rebellion! It is a reversal of the self-centered results of the Fall of Genesis 3. It denotes that the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1:26-27), though damaged, has been restored! Fellowship with God by fallen humans is possible again.

Repentance in the OT primarily means "change of action," while "repentance" in the NT primarily means "change of mind." Both of these are necessary for true biblical repentance. It is also necessary to realize that repentance is both an initial act and an ongoing process. The initial act can be seen in Mark 1:15; Acts 3:16 and 19; 20:21, while the ongoing process can be seen in 1 John 1:9; Revelation 2 and 3. Repentance is not an option (cf. Luke 13:3)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE IN THE OT

▣ "deeply defected" This speaks of Judah's rebellion against YHWH.

  1. "deeply," BDB 770, KB 847, Hiphil PERFECT, this word was used in Isa. 30:33 to describe the funeral pyre of the King of Assyria. It can also describe sin, as it does here and in Hosea 5:2; 9:9. It may specifically refer to Judah's "secret" plan to seek help from Egypt (cf. Isa. 29:15).
  2. "defected," BDB 694, here refers to apostasy, cf. Deut. 13:5; Isa. 1:5; 31:6; Jer. 28:16; 29:32

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOSTASY

▣ "O sons of Israel" In the Bible the term "Israel" can refer to several things:

  1. it can refer to the Patriarch Jacob and his children
  2. it can refer to the Northern Ten Tribes-also called Samaria and Ephraim
  3. it can refer to Judah. In this context it is #3

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (THE NAME)

entries.title: Isaiah 31:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:7 Israel had become eclectic in her faith and tried to incorporate the Canaanite fertility rites along with her worship of YHWH (i.e. the golden calves at Dan and Bethel). This is always a disaster. YHWH will be the only God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY (OT)

▣ "which your hands have made" The idols (BDB 47, cf. Isa. 2:8,18,20; 10:10-11; 19:1,3) are worthless, empty, vain human productions that cannot see, hear, or act. They are superstitious non-existent things which are used by the demonic forces to enslave people and keep them from a knowledge of the One True God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS (fallen angesl)

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS IN THE OT

entries.title: Isaiah 31:8 "the Assyrian will fall"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:8 "the Assyrian will fall" Assyria was the tool which God used to judge the Northern Ten Tribes (cf. Isa. 10:5), but God would deal justly with the godless nation of Assyria also (cf. Isa. 10:12; 14:15; 30:31-33; 37:7). Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, fell to Neo-Babylon in 612 B.C.

▣ "a sword not of man will devour him" Read chapters 36 and 37 of Isaiah, which describe the invasion and siege of Jerusalem under Sennacherib. Notice God's miraculous deliverance (not by human sword) in Isa. 37:36.

This verse demonstrates the hermeneutical issue involved in lexical study. Obviously, the first two lines are in a synonymous parallel relationship (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY, II., III.) These words for "man,"

  1. ish (BDB 35), line 1
  2. adam (BDB 9), line 2

have distinct connotations, but here they seem to be synonymous (cf. Isa. 2:9; 5:15). For a good brief discussion of the Hebrew words for humanity, mankind, see Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, pp. 45-54.

▣ "forced laborers" Defeated armies who survived the battle could be

  1. conscripted as mercenaries into the victorious army
  2. sold as slaves
  3. turned into forced laborers to serve the military

All other inhabitants were forced into slavery (cf. Lam. 1:1). Slavery was common in the ancient world for debtors or those who were defeated.

entries.title: Isaiah 31:9 "His rock. . .his princes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
31:9 "His rock. . .his princes" These are in a Hebrew parallel relationship, therefore, the term "rock" refers to the king of Assyria (or one of his gods, cf. Deut. 32:31,37) and his military commanders (i.e., "princes") who were terrified at YHWH's "standard" (BDB 651, cf. Isa. 13:2; Jer. 50:2; 51:12,27) over Jerusalem.

▣ "whose fire. . .furnace" This refers, not to the fire of judgment (although an allusion to Isa. 30:33 is possible), nor the fire of illumination, but to God's home fireplace, hearth (cf. "Ariel," Isa. 29:1,2,7, which referred to the altar in the temple in Jerusalem).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. How does Isaiah 31 relate to our modern situation of the arms race?
  2. Does superior technology and superior force assure the protection of a nation?
  3. Why would YHWH be described in feminine terms?
  4. Describe repentance. Is it a once-and-for-all act or ongoing experience? Is it basically an attitude or is it a change of actions?
  5. Describe how Assyria was defeated by non-human means.

entries.title: Isaiah 32:1 "a king. . .princes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:1 "a king. . .princes" Isaiah 32:1-8 reflects the reign of a godly king and his/His government (cf. Isa. 9:6-7; 11:1-5; 16:5; Jer. 23:5; 33:15; Micah 5:2-5a). There seems to be a purposeful ambiguity so that Hezekiah (possibly the immediate fulfillment of Isa. 7:14-15) and the coming Messiah (the ultimate fulfillment, cf. Isa. 7:14, cf. Matt. 1:23) are both reflected in this passage.

The leadership of Israel goes by several titles. For a good brief discussion, see Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, p. 249-251.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Isaiah 31-32 are the fifth of the six woes (Isa. 28:1; 29:1,15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1) which deal with Hezekiah's attempt to form a political military alliance with the Nubian Pharaoh of the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty of Egypt against Assyria.

  2. Judah trusted in Egypt, but not YHWH, for protection. Isaiah saw this as a violation of trust/faith in His covenant promises and presence.

  3. This chapter focuses on the future government of a Righteous King in Jerusalem (cf. Isa. 32:1; 9:6-7; 11:1-5; Micah 5:2-5a). This was what Hezekiah should have been. He came close in his faith, seen in Isa. 37:14-20,30.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 32:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:2 This verse describes in "desert" imagery the reign of this godly leader and his associates.

  1. a refuge (BDB 285, lit. "hiding place," this form is found only here) from the wind
  2. shelter (BDB 712) from the storm (parallel to #1)
  3. streams of water in a dry country
  4. the shade (BDB 853) of a huge rock in a parched land

Similar imagery is used of YHWH in Isa. 25:4. Now they describe all of God's people or at least the leadership (i.e., "rulers will rule," VERB, BDB 979, KB 1362, Qal IMPERFECT).

The VERB "each will be" (BDB 224, KB 243 Qal PERFECT with waw) could refer to "the princes" of Isa. 32:1 or to the people of the "new covenant" described in Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36.

entries.title: Isaiah 32:3-4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:3-4 This reflects the spiritual condition of the restored covenant people as contrasted with Isa. 6:9-10 (cf. Deut. 29:4).

  1. they will see
  2. they will hear
  3. they will discern truth
  4. they will speak truth ("the stammerers," BDB 748, occurs only here)

entries.title: Isaiah 32:5-8 "fool. . .rogue"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:5-8 "fool. . .rogue" These two groups will still be present in society, but they will be seen for what they are (Isa. 32:6-7). Isaiah 32:6-7 seems to describe the two wicked persons, while Isa. 32:8 describes the "true" noble person.

  1. the "fool" (BDB 614) described in Isa. 32:6
    1. speaks nonsense
    2. inclines the heart toward wickedness
      (1)  practices ungodliness (or "plots evil")
      (2)  speaks error against the Lord
    3. does not feed the hungry
    4. does not give drink to the thirsty
  2. the "rogue" (BDB 647, found only here, twice) described in Isa. 32:7
    1. has evil weapons
    2. devises wicked schemes
    3. destroys the afflicted with slander
    4. disregards the true testimony of the needy
  3. the noble man (BDB 622), Isa. 32:8
    1. devises noble (or "generous") plans in contrast to those mentioned in Isa. 32:6 and 7
    2. his plans stand, remain

entries.title: Isaiah 32:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:6 One wonders if this is alluded to in Matt. 25:31-46.

▣ "inclines toward. . .to practice" The VERB (BDB 793, KB 889) is used twice in this verse, once as a Qal IMPERFECT and again as a Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT. This was a grammatical way to show intensity. The "fool" tries to convey a false message about Israel's God and His will for an obedient covenant people.

entries.title: Isaiah 32:9-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:9-12 This strophe speaks of the rich, wealthy society women of Jerusalem (cf Isa. 3:16-4:1; see SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH). The Jewish Study Bible, p. 847, notes that this is a counterpoint to the condemnation of male leaders in Isa. 30:1-7; 31:1-3. Notice how they are addressed.

  1. rise up you women who are at ease, Isa. 32:9, BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE. The same VERB was used in the previous verse in the sense of "stand" or "remain," but here it means "stand up" when I the Lord (or His prophet) address you.
  2. hear my voice, Isa. 32:9, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. give an ear to my word, Isa. 32:9, BDB 24, KB 27, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (cf. Isa. 28:23). Notice how the second and third VERBS are parallel, as are the descriptive phrases "women who are at ease," (cf. Isa. 32:11) and "you complacent daughters," and again in Isa. 32:10,11.
  4. you will be troubled, Isa. 32:10, BDB 919, KB 1182, Qal IMPERFECT. This term denotes "agitation," "shaking," "being perturbed." Note the "time" elements in Isa. 32:10.
    1. within a year and a few days
    2. time of the vintage is ended
    3. the fruit gathering will not come
  5. tremble, Isa. 32:11, BDB 353, KB 350, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Isa. 10:29; 19:16; 41:5. This is parallel to "troubled" in Isa. 32:10 (surprisingly all the IMPERATIVES of Isa. 32:11 are MASCULINE, but addressed to women).
  6. be troubled, Isa. 32:11, BDB 919, KB 1182, Qal IMPERATIVE, same VERB as Isa. 32:10
  7. strip, Isa. 32:11, BDB 832 II, KB 980, Qal IMPERATIVE. This could be a sign of
    1. mourning (cf. Ezek. 26:16)
    2. humiliation (cf. Hosea 2:5)
  8. undress, Isa. 32:11, BDB 792, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE
  9. put sackcloth on your waist, Isa. 32:11, BDB 291, KB 291, Qal IMPERATIVE, also a sign of mourning. See SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES.
  10. beat your breasts, Isa. 32:12, BDB 704, KB 763, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, another sign of mourning, Luke 18:13; 23:48.

All of these relate to the period of the siege of Jerusalem by Sennacherib in 701 B.C. Sieges were horrible experiences of deprivation and disease.

32:9,10,11
NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "complacent daughters"
NJB  "over-confident daughters"
REB  "daughters without a care"
LXX  "daughters of hope"
JPSOA  "confident ladies"
Peshitta  "you daughters who publish glad tidings"
NET  "carefree daughters"

The Hebrew term (BDB 105, KB 120) normally means "security" or "confidence," though some scholars see another root (BDB 105 II, KB 121) meaning "fall to the ground" (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 649).

This term also occurs in Isa. 32:17 and is translated "confidence" or "security" (NASB margin). These wealthy, elite women were over-confident (NJB).

entries.title: Isaiah 32:10 "Within a year and a few days"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:10 "Within a year and a few days" This is a very specific time reference (possibly connected to the harvest season) and seems to relate to the invasion of Sennacherib in 701 B.C.

entries.title: Isaiah 32:12 "Beat your breasts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:12 "Beat your breasts" There are three ways to deal with this phrase.

  1. relate it to the stripped and bare-breasted women of Isa. 32:11
  2. change the Hebrew "breast" (rare poetic term, BDB 994, שׁד) to "fields" (BDB 961, שדי, cf. Isa. 56:9), as JPSOA lists in a footnote. If option #2 is followed, then "fields," "the pleasant fields," and "the fruitful vine" become parallel for the loss of agricultural abundance.
  3. see it as an idiom for mourning whether male or female (Peshitta, cf. Luke 18:13; 23:48)

entries.title: Isaiah 32:13 "the joyful houses"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:13 "the joyful houses" This same term "joyful" (BDB 965) is used in Isa. 32:14 for "a delight for wild donkeys." Isaiah uses

  1. doubling
  2. word plays
  3. repeated metaphors

to communicate his messages. The Hebrew text of Isaiah is far more dynamic and artistic than can be captured in translation. He was a master poet. One wonders if YHWH communicated the messages in poetry or Isaiah crafted them. Since all of YHWH's revelations are not in artistic poetry, it seems this was Isaiah's skill. Many of the word choices in Isaiah have far more to do with sound plays than lexical meaning. Rare words are used, as are unique meanings to common words. This is where the purposeful ambiguity is confusing for modern interpreters!

▣ "the jubilant city" See note at Isa. 24:10 and SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO "CITIES" IN ISAIAH. God wanted to uniquely bless the people of the Abrahamic covenant to attract the attention of "the nations," but because of Israel and Judah's rebellion, instead of abundance and peace came thorns and briars (cf. Isa. 5:6; 7:23-25; 9:18; 10:17; 27:4; Gen. 3:18).

entries.title: Isaiah 32:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:14 This verse describes the destruction of Jerusalem (cf. Isa. 6:11; 64:10), which is unusual for Isaiah who usually sees its deliverance (cf. Isa. 1:8-9; 28:16; 29:1-8; 37:36-37). Isaiah asserts Jerusalem's sanctity because of YHWH's presence there (i.e., the temple), but later Jeremiah clearly adds to this theological issue by focusing on the conditional nature of YHWH's promises to His covenant people (i.e., Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28). Isaiah trusts God's word, but His promises must be matched by appropriate human faith, repentance, obedience, service, worship. Covenant is a two-way street!

Notice how the destruction is characterized.

  1. the palace has been abandoned (i.e., the Davidic seed forsaken)
  2. the populated city has been forsaken (i.e., the Abrahamic seed forsaken)
  3. NASB ‒ "hill"
    NJB ‒ "Ophel" (BDB 779), a section of the southeastern ridge of ancient Jerusalem (or a metaphor for the whole city, similar to "Zion"). It is mentioned in 2 Chr. 27:3; 33:14; Neh. 3:26-27; 11:21
  4. #3 is parallel to "watch-tower"; both would denote the fortifications of Jerusalem being destroyed
  5. a delight for wild donkeys
  6. a pasture for flocks, both #5 and #6 denote a deserted, destroyed city, inhabited only by animals (cf. Isa. 13:21; 34:13)

There are two parallel VERBS.

  1. has been abandoned, BDB 643, KB 695, Pual PERFECT, the Pual occurs only here
  2. forsaken, BDB 736, KB 806, Qal PASSIVE (or Pual) PERFECT, cf. Jer. 49:25

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

NASB, LXX  "caves"
NKJV  "lairs"
NRSV, Peshitta  "dens"
TEV  "the Keep"
REB  "open hearth"
JPSOA  "bare places"
JPSOA (footnote)  "brushland, deserts"

The term (BDB 792) means "cave," but in this context, "an animal's den." It is possible that Isaiah chose this term because of its sound similarity to

  1. "sepulcher" (Arabic root), ערר (context of death and destruction)
  2. "strip oneself," ערר, rare VERB used in Isa. 32:11
  3. "bare field," מערה from Arabic root (NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 1034)

▣ "forever" This is the relative use of the Hebrew term 'olam. This term has a large semantical usage and must be interpreted in a specific context.

For a good example of the relative nature of 'olam (forever), notice the seeming counteraction between v. 14, Jerusalem destroyed "forever," and v. 15, Jerusalem restored. Often "forever" is used

  1. for intensity
  2. as hyperbole
  3. denoting a period of time
    1. this age (i.e. this covenant)
    2. eternity

Be careful of western literalism! Hebrew poetry and Eastern literature are far more figurative than western thinking.

entries.title: Isaiah 32:15-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:15-20 This strophe describes a new day, a righteous day for Jerusalem.

  1. The Spirit is poured out from God. The exact relationship between YHWH and "the Spirit" in the OT is difficult to relate to the full personal revelation of the NT. The Spirit is often associated with creation (cf. Gen. 1:2; Job 26:13; Ps. 104:29-30). Now the Spirit is active in the new creation!
  2. The wilderness becomes a fertile field. . .a forest, Isa. 32:15. This is the reversal of Isa. 32:12-13. See the same imagery of fertility in Isa. 29:17.
  3. Justice. . .righteousness abide, Isa. 32:16
  4. Peace, quietness, and confidence forever, Isa. 32:17. This means no invasions (cf. Isa. 32:18).
  5. Isa. 32:19 may refer to the destruction of Assyria.
  6. Isa. 32:20 is another blessing, but it is somewhat ambiguous.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

32:15
NASB, NKJV, NIV, Peshitta  "Until the Spirit is poured out upon us
  from on high"
NKJV, JPSOA  "until a spirit from on high is poured
  out on us"
TEV  "God will send us his spirit"
NJB  "until the spirit is poured out on us
  from above"
Net Bible  "until new life is poured out on us
  from heaven"
REB, LXX  "until a spirit from on high is lavished
  upon me"

The Hebrew text has no ARTICLE, PRONOUN, or descriptive phrase (i.e., "of the Lord," as in Isa. 11:2 or "My," Isa. 44:3; 59:21; Joel 2:28) linked to the NOUN "spirit" (BDB 924). The question is to whom does it refer.

  1. the cultural spirit of the new age
  2. the Holy Spirit
  3. a spirit of faithful followers in repentance and trust from God

Grammar suggests #1 or #3, but context suggests #2.

This is a radical break in the context. Similar passages which speak of God's Spirit are Isa. 44:3; Ezek. 39:29; Joel 2:28-29; Zech. 12:10; Acts 2:1-21. The same VERB is used in a sacrificial sense of the Messiah in Isa. 53:12. There is a series of seven blessings that will result because of the Spirit's presence: (1) fertility, (2) justice, (3) righteousness, (4) peace, (5) quietness, (6) confidence, and (7) secure dwelling.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4

▣ "from on high" This is an idiom for "heaven," the place of YHWH's abode (cf. Job 16:19; 31:2; Isa. 33:5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

entries.title: Isaiah 32:16 "justice. . .righteousness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:16 "justice. . .righteousness" These are a common pair in the OT (cf. 2 Sam. 8:15; 1 Kgs. 10:9; 1 Chr. 18:14; 2 Chr. 9:8; Ps. 99:4; Isa. 9:7; 32:16; 33:5; 59:14; Jer. 4:2; 9:24; 22:3,15; 23:5; 33:15; Ezek. 18:5,19, 21,27; 33:14,16,19; 45:9; Amos 5:7,24). They denote the kind of society (cf. Isa. 32:17-18) where all people are honored and treated fairly as covenant partners. They then characterize the unique presence of God among His people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUSTICE

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: IMMANUEL'S PERSON AND REIGN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE MESSIANIC ERA

entries.title: Isaiah 32:17 "peace"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:17 "peace" See SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (shalom, OT)

▣ "quietness and confidence" These two terms (BDB 1052 and BDB 105) also occur in Isa. 30:15, which characterizes the new age of justice, righteousness, and peace (cf. Isa. 32:1,16).

entries.title: Isaiah 32:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:19 This is a very difficult verse which seems out of place. It may refer to Assyria.

  1. The phrase "the forest" is used of Assyria in Isa. 10:18-19,33,34.
  2. The phrase "the city" is used of Assyria in Isa. 24:10; 25:2,3; 26:5.
NASB  "it will hail"
NKJV  "though hail"
NRSV  "will disappear completely"
TEV  "(but hail will fall. . .)"
NJB  "be totally destroyed"
LXX  "if hail descends"
Peshitta  "hail shall come down"
REB  "it will be cool on the slopes"
JPSOA  "shall sink and vanish"

The ancient versions see the MT's ברד, BDB 135, "hail," cf. NOUN in Isa. 28:2,17; 30:30, which is related to an Arabic root for "cool."

It is possible to see the MT as reflecting another root, ירד, which means "to descend" or "come down" (BDB 432, twice), denoting the complete destruction of faithless Jerusalem, NRSV, NJB, and JPSOA.

The UBS Text Project, p. 73, gives "hail" a "B" rating (some doubt).

entries.title: Isaiah 32:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:20 This verse is also very difficult to fit into the context. However, the consensus seems to be that in the days of God's blessings, the crops will be so abundant that the cattle could roam freely and eat without really affecting the outcome of the crop.

D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, p. 23, gives a good list of the verses in Isaiah that speak of a new day of covenant prosperity.

  1. Isa. 2:4 ‒ swords turned into plowshares
  2. Isa. 29:18 ‒ blind see, deaf hear
  3. Isa. 30:25; 43:30 ‒ rivers flow in the desert
  4. Isa. 30:26 ‒ sun and moon shine brightly to aid agriculture
  5. Jer. 31:4,13; 33:11 ‒ sounds of community joy
  6. Isa. 32:20 ‒ livestock graze freely and the harvest is not negatively affected
  7. Isa. 34:16 ‒ every person will have a life partner (in context, this may refer to animals, Isa. 34:13-15)
  8. Isa. 35:1; 41:19 ‒ plant life returns to the desert
  9. Isa. 35:1; 41:18 ‒ pools of water collect in dry places
  10. Isa. 35:8 ‒ special highway of holiness provided by YHWH for His people
  11. Isa. 40:4 ‒ natural impediments (i.e. mountains and hills) removed (i.e. leveled) for easy access to YHWH

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 33:1 "Woe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:1 "Woe" Isaiah 28-33 forms a unit often called the "Unit of Doom" because of the recurrent use of the term "woe," (cf. Isa. 28:1; 29:1,15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1). See note on "Woe" at Isa. 5:8.

▣ "O destroyer" Isaiah 33:1 speaks of Assyria, as does Isa. 33:3,4,7-9,11-12,17-19,23; even Isa. 33:21 may refer to the cities located on the Tigris and Euphrates. This chapter follows a common theme pattern of Isaiah.

  1. the current rebellious state of God's people
  2. God's judgment by foreign powers
  3. God's judgment of these foreign powers (here Assyria)
  4. the future glorious conditions of His people through the righteous king (cf. Isa. 32:1)

The Hebrew root שׁדד (BDB 994, KB 1418) is used four times in this verse.

  1. "O destroyer" ‒ Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  2. "not destroyed" ‒ Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE
  3. "destroying" ‒ Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  4. "will be destroyed" ‒ Qal PASSIVE IMPERFECT

Also, the Hebrew root בגד (BDB 93, KB 108) is also used four times.

  1. "he who is treacherous" ‒ Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  2. "others did not deal treacherously with him" ‒ Qal PERFECT
  3. "as soon as you shall cease to deal treacherously" ‒ Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  4. "others shall deal treacherously with you" ‒ Qal IMPERFECT

It is common in Isaiah to repeat NOUNS, VERBS for effect. This repetition was normal and expected! These roots are also used in Isa. 21:2 about the fall of old Babylon. In a theological sense Isaiah's ambiguity is purposeful. He intentionally makes the identity of Israel/Judah's aggressors fuzzy so that his poems can function as "multiple-fulfillment" prophecies. Enemies come and go by YHWH's hand and purpose, but YHWH Himself and His eternal redemptive purpose, using Abraham's seed, does not!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "cease"
NJB, JPSOA, NET  "finished"

In line 5 the MT has the VERBAL (BDB 649, KB 701, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT), which is found only here. Most translations, ancient and modern, follow the DSS, which has "to complete" or "to finish" (BDB 477, KB 476, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT), used often in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 1:28; 10:18,25; 15:6; 16:4; 21:16; 24:13; 27:10; 29:20; 31:3; 32:10; 49;4).

  1. BDB 649, כנלתך
  2. BDB 477, ככלתך
