READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. The paragraphing is ambiguous (because of the composite nature of these poems) in this chapter. Several different groups are addressed.
    1. Assyria, Isa. 33:1
    2. covenant people, Isa. 33:2
    3. brave men who cry in the streets, Isa. 33:7
    4. ambassadors of peace who weep, Isa. 33:7
    5. the traveler, Isa. 33:8
    6. the people, Isa. 33:12
    7. you who are far away, Isa. 33:13
    8. you who are near, Isa. 33:13
    9. sinners in Zion, Isa. 33:14
    10. he who walks righteously, Isa. 33:15
    11. He. . .His, Isa. 33:16
    12. your heart, Isa. 33:18-20
    13. your tackle, Isa. 33:23
    14. resident. . .people, Isa. 33:24
      It is difficult to identify the groups to which each of these relate.

  2. Notice how many names/titles and characterizations of Israel's God are mentioned in this chapter.
    1. YHWH, Isa. 33:2
    2. YHWH is exalted, Isa. 33:5,10
    3. He shall be the stability (lit. "faithfulness"), Isa. 33:6
    4. a wealth of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge, Isa. 33:6
    5. the fear of YHWH, Isa. 33:6
    6. King in His beauty, Isa. 33:17
    7. the majestic One, Isa. 33:21 
    8. several, "The Lord is. . .," Isa. 33:22

  3. It is possible that the first section of Isaiah ends after this chapter because the DSS scroll of Isaiah has a double space after this chapter, but no break after chapter 39.

  4. "Possible" outline of the poem's order/arrangement
    1. God judges Assyria who He used to judge Judah, Isa. 33:1
    2. Judah prays for help, Isa. 33:2
    3. God responds, Isa. 33:3-6,10-12
    4. Judah's current state, Isa. 33:7-9
    5. the godly spared, Isa. 33:13-16
    6. a recapitulation of the Assyrian period, Isa. 33:17-20
    7. the reign of the righteous king, Isa. 33:21-24

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 33:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:2 The content of Judah's prayer is delineated.

  1. be gracious to us, BDB 335, KB 334, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Isa. 30:18,19
  2. we have waited for You, BDB 875 I, KB 1082, Piel PERFECT, cf. Isa. 8:17; 25:9; 26:8; 40:31; 49:23; 51:5; 60:9
  3. be our strength (lit. "arm") every morning, BDB 224, KB 243, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. be our salvation in time of distress ("be" VERB assumed)

YHWH is Judah's only hope (cf. Isa. 59:16; 63:1,5), not Assyria (alliance) and not Egypt (alliance), only YHWH. Humans tend to panic and lose trust in times of crisis and uncertainty. They try to save themselves using their resources or the resources of other humans, to no avail!

▣ "strength" It is literally "arm" (BDB 283). This is a biblical anthropomorphic imagery to describe YHWH's presence and power on a daily basis.

▣ "salvation" This term (BDB 447) is commonly used in the OT for physical deliverance (cf. Isa. 12:2 [twice], 3; 25:9; 26:1,18; 33:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT term)

33:3
NASB, Peshitta  "the lifting up of Yourself"
NKJV  "when You lift Yourself up"
NRSV  "before your majesty"
TEV  "when you fight for us"
NJB  "when you stand up"
JPSOA  "before Your majesty"

The NOUN (BDB 928, KB 1206) occurs only here and its meaning is uncertain, but it seems to be related to "extolling praise" (BDB 928). The UBS Text Project, p. 74, gives "at the lifting up (the voice)" a "C" rating (considerable doubt). It seems there is a parallel with line one, therefore, some type of shout or noise. However, the NRSV, JPSOA, and NET think it refers to YHWH's actions, which fits the meaning of the verse better..

entries.title: Isaiah 33:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:4 In this verse "spoil"(BDB 1021) is imagery which denotes the destruction of YHWH's enemies.

The VERB "gathered" (BDB 62, KB 74, Pual PERFECT with waw) is also used in

  1. Isa. 32:10 to describe the judgment of Jerusalem
  2. Isa. 24:22 (same stem) to denote worldwide eschatological judgment

Humans "gather" for self, greed, and power, but God gathers for judgment. The NT describes the end-time gathering of

  1. the redeemed, Matt. 13:36-43,47-50; 24:31
  2. the wicked, Matt. 13:40-41

▣ "locusts" Locust invasions were common in the ANE. They are often compared to an invading army (cf. Deut. 28:38,42; Joel 1:4; 2:25; Amos 7:1-2). God directs armies as He directs all things! These locusts gather the ill-gotten spoils of Assyria.

There are many Semitic words for this insect which apparently denote (see Joel 2:25)

  1. different species
  2. different stages of growth

entries.title: Isaiah 33:5 "He dwells on high"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:5 "He dwells on high" This phrase is imagery for the place of YHWH's abode (cf. Isa. 32:15; Job 16:19; 31:2). The ANE viewed heaven as above. For the Israelites the smoke from their sacrifices rose to God, therefore, He must be up. There was also the theological contrast with "down" as imagery for death. Sheol was down, but heaven was up. In our modern era these spacial images seem inaccurate, but remember they are ancient imagery never intended to carry literalness. The language of the OT is phenomenological, which means the language of description using the five human senses. The Bible is not anti-scientific, it is pre-scientific! Taking ancient imagery literally is not a sign of biblical conservatism, but of missing the intended meaning of the original historical setting of the inspired authors.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

▣ "justice and righteousness" See note at Isa. 32:16 and SPECIAL TOPIC: IMMANUEL'S PERSON AND REIGN.

33:6
NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "He will be the stability of your times"
NJB  "You can count on this all your days"
Peshitta  "Faith shall be the stability of your times"
REB  "her strength will be in your unchanging
 stability"
NET  "He is your constant source of stability"

YHWH brings "stability," lit. "faithful," BDB 53, cf. Isa. 25:1. Judah's hope and stability is the faithful character of her God (cf. Deut. 32:4; Ps. 36:5; 89:1-2,5,24,33,49; 88:11; 92:2; 143:1). This is the answer to the prayer of Isa. 33:2. Because of His faithful character He gives to His wayward people

  1. a wealth (BDB 340) of
    1. salvation (BDB 447)
    2. wisdom (BDB 315 with change of final consonant from ת to ה, cf. Isa. 11:2)
    3. knowledge (BDB 395, cf. Isa. 11:2)
  2. the fear (BDB 432, in the sense of reverential awe, cf. Isa. 11:2; Prov. 1:7,29; 2:5) of YHWH is his treasure (BDB 69, in the sense of a full storehouse, cf. 1 Chr. 27:27-28; 2 Chr. 11:11); see SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

entries.title: Isaiah 33:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:7 These two poetic lines may not be synonymous (LXX, Peshitta). Biblical scholars have been influenced by Robert Lowth, who tried to fit all Hebrew parallelism into three or four categories. Today scholars are understanding the multiplicity of poetic parallelism. Currently it is best to say that the second line "adds something" or "goes beyond" (Adele Berlin, The Dynamics of Biblical Parallelism: Revised and Expanded, p. 64).

There may be different groups addressed.

  1. line one ‒ soldiers of Jerusalem (JPSOA, "Arielites")
  2. line two ‒ the ambassador of peace sent to Egypt by Hezekiah (cf. Isa. 33:8; JPSOA)
  3. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 848, mentions that rabbinical texts see this verse as related to angels (messengers) weeping over the fall of Zion

They do similar/parallel things

  1. "cry," BDB 858, KB 1042, Qal PERFECT
  2. "weep," BDB 113, KB 129, Qal IMPERFECT

Parallelism is one of the main keys in interpreting Hebrew poetry, but we must recognize it is used in many forms and at many literary levels.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

NASB, TEV  "brave men"
NKJV, NRSV, REB  "valiant ones"
NJB  "Ariel"
JPSOA  "Arielites"
NET  "ambassadors"

The MT has אראלם (BDB 72, KB 82), which is found only here. This root is

  1. similar to "Ariel" (KB 87 II, JPSOA, i.e. Jerusalem, cf. Isa. 29:1,2,7)
  2. similar to "warrior" (NASB, NKJV, Targums)
  3. "heroes" (KB 87 I)
  4. "priests" (KB 82)
  5. "ambassadors" (NET Bible, p. 1235, #13, which assumes a parallelism between the two lines of poetry in v. 7
33:8
NASB, NKJV, JPSOA, Peshitta  "cities"
NRSV  "oaths"
NJB, RSV  "witnesses"
REB  "treaties"
TEV  "agreements"
DSS  "a pact"

The MT has "cities" (ערים, BDB 746 and DSS), but because of the parallelism, "witnesses" (עדים, BDB 729; DSS Isaiah scrolls) fits better. This could be another "R" ‒ "D" confusion. The UBS Hebrew Text Project, p. 77 gives "witness" a C rating (i.e. considerable doubt).

entries.title: Isaiah 33:7-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:7-9 This reflects the sad state of the impending siege because negotiations have failed (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:13-16).

entries.title: Isaiah 33:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:9 This verse uses agricultural imagery for the problems involved in the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem in 701 B.C. These types of agricultural imagery are common in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 16:8; 24:4,7). YHWH controls the weather for His purposes (cf. Deuteronomy 27-28). There is no distinction between the "natural" and "supernatural" in the Bible, as in the worldview of the ANE. Deity is intimately involved in His creation. Be careful of your modern, scientific worldview placing a theological grid over Scripture!

entries.title: Isaiah 33:10-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:10-12 These possibly relate to Assyria as in Isa. 33:1.

entries.title: Isaiah 33:11-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:11-12 The imagery of "chaff" and "fire" are common in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 1:7; 5:24; 9:18-19; 10:16-19; 26:11; 29:6; 30:27-28; 33:11-14; 47:14, also Joel 2:3). See Special Topic: Fire.

Isaiah uses imagery from human reproduction.

  1. here, conception, BDB 247 I, KB 255, Qal imperfect, Isa. 8:3; 26:18; 59:4,13
  2. giving birth, Isa. 9:6; 13:8; 21:3; 23:4; 26:17,18; 39:7; 51:18; 54:1; 59:4; 66:7,9

▣ "My breath" This is the term ruah (BDB 924) used as an anthropomorphic imagery for the wind of judgment from YHWH's nostrils (see SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT). It is obviously a way of showing YHWH's personal participation (cf. Exodus 15:18; 2 Sam. 22:16; Ps. 18:15) in judgment (cf. Isa. 11:4; 30:28; 40:7).

entries.title: Isaiah 33:13 "You who are far away. . .you who are near"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:13 "You who are far away. . .you who are near" In context, this refers to God's people in exile in Assyria and to God's people still in Judah (cf. Dan. 9:7). However, seen in the wider context of the new age, it may be related to the Gentile and the Jewish people (cf. Isa. 49:1; it is imagery for all, cf. Jer. 25:26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Isaiah 33:14 "Sinners in Zion are terrified"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:14 "Sinners in Zion are terrified" Again the reality of a mixture of the faithful and unfaithful within the people of God is acknowledged. Sinners

  1. are terrified, BDB 808, KB 922, Qal PERFECT, cf. NOUN ‒ Isa. 2:10,19,21; 24:17,18; VERB ‒ 12:2; 19:16,17; 44:8,11; 51:13
  2. trembling has seized the godless, BDB 28, KB 31, Qal PERFECT, cf. Isa. 13:8; 21:3

The "godless" (BDB 338) are described in Isa. 32:6 as those who practice godlessness and speak error against the Lord (cf. Isa. 9:17; 10:6).

▣  "Who among us can live with the consuming fire?

Who among us can live with the continual burning" This refers to God's holiness as seen through the imagery of fire connected with His righteousness and His judgment (cf. Deut. 4:24; 5:24; Isa. 30:27,30).

For "continual" (lit. "forever") see Special Topic: Forever ('olam).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

entries.title: Isaiah 33:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:15 This reflects the character of YHWH as seen in His people.

  1. walks righteously
  2. speaks with sincerity
  3. rejects unjust gain
  4. does not take a bribe
  5. does not listen to evil plans (i.e. bloodshed)
  6. does not look upon evil

entries.title: Isaiah 33:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:16 The person who lives the life described in Isa. 33:15

  1. will dwell on the heights
  2. will take refuge in the impregnable rock
  3. will have an abundance of food
  4. will have a sure water supply

This describes the new age person. The ideal of Deuteronomy is actualized!

entries.title: Isaiah 33:17 "Your eyes will see"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:17 "Your eyes will see" This VERB (BDB 302, KB 301) is often used to refer to spiritual insight (cf. Isa. 26:11; 33:17,20; 48:6; Job 23:8-9; Ps. 46:8; 63:2). Humans were created to function in two realms.

  1. the physical (i.e. nephesh, this planet)
  2. the spiritual (i.e. ruah, fellowship with God)

The Fall of Genesis 3 has disrupted both!

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "the King and his beauty" This is a purposeful ambiguity, much like Isa. 32:1, where the context fits both Hezekiah in his day and the coming Messiah of Isa. 7:14.

entries.title: Isaiah 33:18 "Where is he who counts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:18 "Where is he who counts" This refers to Assyrian scouts reconnoitering Jerusalem for the coming siege.

33:19
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "a fierce people"
NRSV, NJB  "the insolent people"
TEV  "arrogant foreigners"
REB, JPSOA  "barbarous people"
NET  "a defiant people"

The PARTICIPLE describing "people" is BDB 418, KB 420, Niphal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, and is found only here. Some scholars take it from another root, "to be strong" (BDB 738), but it has never been found in the Niphal stem.

There is one more interpretive option. Take it from another root (BDB 541, KB 533, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE), "to stammer" or "speak unintelligibly," which is used in the third line of v. 19, thereby paralleling all three lines.

NASB, NJB  "unintelligible speech"
NKJV, NRSV, REB, JPSOA  "obscure speech"
LXX  "deep speech"
Peshitta  "deeper speech"

The MT has the ADJECTIVE (BDB 771, KB 849) "deep" or "unfathomable" (cf. Ezek. 3:5-6). This relates to YHWH's warning of His sending foreign invaders into Canaan if His people do not keep His law (cf. Deut. 28:49). They did not; He did (cf. Isa. 28:11; Jer. 5:15). In this context, it refers to Assyria.

Paul uses this imagery to describe speaking in tongues in the NT (cf. 1 Cor. 14:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPEAKING IN TONGUES

entries.title: Isaiah 33:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:20 This is Isaiah's recurrent theology (with a few exceptions) that Jerusalem will never fall (cf. Isaiah 36-37). For a full discussion of "city" see notes at Isa. 24:10 and the chart at the Introduction to chapter 26, D. This prophecy must be understood in context because in Jeremiah's day, God gave exactly the opposite prophecy.

The imagery of "a tent" is an anachronistic allusion back to the Exodus (cf. Job 4:21; Isa. 38:12; 54:2; Jer. 10:20). It may also denote "the tabernacle" built as a portable tent. The same allusion (i.e. tent) is used in Isa. 54:2 for a worldwide expansion.

entries.title: Isaiah 33:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:21 The imagery of "rivers and sailing ships" seems to be a play on their alliances with Egypt (cf. Isa. 33:23). Instead of Egypt, YHWH (the Majestic One) will be their provider and protector (cf. Isa. 33:22).

entries.title: Isaiah 33:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:22 Jerusalem (cf. Isa. 33:20) is again the city of the Great King (YHWH Himself) as represented in His righteous surrogate (the Davidic Messiah).

YHWH is

  1. Judge (BDB 1047)
  2. Lawgiver (BDB 349)
  3. King (BDB 572 I)
  4. Savior (BDB 446; see SPECIAL TOPIC: OUR SAVIOR)

entries.title: Isaiah 33:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:23 Poetry is ambiguous. This could refer to

  1. the destruction of Assyria
  2. the empowering of Jerusalem
  3. or both

In Isaiah 33:17, both "your eyes" and "they will behold" have uncertain antecedents. Isaiah 33:18 seems to refer to Assyria checking out Jerusalem for invasion and siege. Isaiah 33:19 seems to allude to the strange-sounding language of the Assyrian invaders. Yet at Isa. 33:20 the scene changes to an undisturbed Jerusalem. Therefore, Isa. 33:21 and 22 could refer to Jerusalem, obviously Isa. 33:24 does.

Some see the "plunder" (BDB 1021) in Isa. 33:23 as related to the items that the Assyrian army abandoned before the walls of Jerusalem in 701 B.C. (NEB) and not the sack of Nineveh itself, which occurred in 612 B.C. by the Neo-Babylonian and Median armies.

entries.title: Isaiah 33:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:24 YHWH is characterized as the healer. This is an allusion to chapter 1 where God's faithless people are characterized as ill (cf. Isa. 1:5-6). Illness is imagery for "sin" and "rebellion" (cf. Ps. 41:4; 103:3; Isa. 53:5). The NT continues the Jewish concept of sickness relating to sin (cf. John 5:14; James 5:14-15). See SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

This is such a powerful verse! Not only is physical healing an aspect of God's people's restoration, but also complete forgiveness (BDB 669, KB 724, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE, see SPECIAL TOPIC: FORGIVENESS [OT]). This VERB "will be forgiven," has the basic connotation of "to lift up and bear away" (i.e. Exod. 32:32; 34:7; Num. 14:18-19; Ps. 32:1,5; 85:2).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. How are Isaiah 32 and 33 related to Isaiah 28-31?
  2. Are these two chapters Messianic or historical?
  3. List the blessings of the Spirit described in Isa. 32:15-18.
  4. Give the historical context of Isa. 33:7-9.

entries.title: Isaiah 34:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:1 There are several commands in this verse.

  1. draw near, BDB 897 I, KB 1132, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. listen, BDB 904, KB 1151, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  3. hear, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal JUSSIVE (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR)

The Sovereign of the universe is addressing His creation and announcing its judgment.

  1. "O nations," BDB 156, cf. Isa. 34:2; 43:9
  2. O peoples, BDB 522, cf. Isa. 17:12; 43:9
  3. the earth, BDB 75, cf. Isa. 37:16,20; Gen. 18:18; 22:18; Micah 1:2 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH)
  4. all it contains, BDB 571, cf. Isa. 6:3
  5. the world, BDB 385, cf. Isa. 13:11; 24:4 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD, I. E.)
  6. all that springs from it, BDB 481 CONSTRUCT BDB 425

Obviously this refers to the known world of Isaiah's day. The language is universal but hyperbolic.

entries.title: Isaiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
ISAIAH 34

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
God's Wrath Against Nations Judgment on the Nations The Terrible End of God's Enemies God Will Punish His Enemies The Sentence on Edom

(1-4)
34:5-7

34:8-15
(8-12)		 (8-17)
34:9-15 (9-11)
(12-17)

34:16-17
(16a-17)		 34:16-17
(16-17)		 34:16-17

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Isaiah 34 and 35 are very similar to Isa. 24-27. Both of these are combinations of judgment and blessing sections which are conclusions to a much longer literary unit.
    1. Isaiah 34 speaks of universal judgment in graphic terms.
    2. Isaiah 35 speaks of universal restoration in beautiful, idealistic terms.

  2. Because there is a double space between chapter 33 and chapter 34 in the Dead Sea Scrolls copy of Isaiah, it is possible that this literary unit (chapters 34-35 and 38-39) should go with 40-66 (as far as literary setting). Chapter 35 is a discussion of the new age, the days of restoration. They describe what YHWH wanted to do with mankind before the Fall of Genesis 3 and the disobedience of Abraham's seed.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 34:2 "For the Lord's indignation is against all the nations. . .He has utterly destroyed them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:2 "For the Lord's indignation is against all the nations. . .He has utterly destroyed them" The idea of "utterly destroyed" (BDB 355 I, KB 353, Hiphil PERFECT; see SPECIAL TOPIC: UTTERLY DESTROY [herem] and CURSE [anathema]) refers to the concept of "holy war." In Joshua this concept in relation to Jericho is translated "under the ban" (i.e. dedicated to YHWH for destruction, cf. Josh. 6:17,18 [thrice]; 7:1 [twice], 12 [twice], 13 [twice], 15).

entries.title: Isaiah 34:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:3 This verse expands the thought of Isa. 34:2, with graphic imagery of warfare.

  1. their slain thrown out, BDB 1020, KB 1527, Hophal IMPERFECT
  2. their corpses will give off (lit. "go up") their stench, BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERFECT, cf. Amos 4:10
  3. the mountains will be drenched (lit. "dissolve") with their blood, BDB 587, KB 606, Niphal PERFECT with waw

This reflects a battle scene where the bodies of the dead have remained unburied for an extended period of time. In the ANE improper burial was a horror and disgrace and might affect one's afterlife. It represented a total defeat, physically and spiritually.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

entries.title: Isaiah 34:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:4 This hyperbolic language relating to the host of heaven is a recurrent theme in the Bible.

  1. Isaiah 13:10,13; 34:4; 51:6
  2. Ezekiel 32:7,8
  3. Joel 2:10,31; 3:15
  4. Matthew 24:29,35
  5. 2 Peter 3:10
  6. Revelation 6:12-14; 8:12; 20:11

The phrase "host of heaven" can refer to

  1. astral deities (sun, moon, stars, planets, comets, etc.) usually associated with Babylonian idolatry
  2. the angelic army of YHWH (cf. Isa. 24:21-22; Josh. 5:14-15, based on Deut. 32:8 in the LXX and illustrated in Daniel 10)

In this context it refers to the objects of light in the sky. These objects are affected and thrown into disarray by the approach of their creator! These physical objects, often viewed as deities, are subject to YHWH! See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks, pp. 176-177.

▣ "rolled up like a scroll" This imagery is used by John in Rev. 6:14. The sky in the ANE was thought to be

  1. tightly stretched skin over the earth like a bowl (cf. Isa. 40:22)
  2. a set up tent (cf. Ps. 104:2)

The old order will be replaced by the new (cf. Rev. 21:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH

NASB, NRSV, JPSOA  "wither away"
NKJV, TEV, LXX  "fall"
REB, NET  "fade away"
Peshitta  "fall down"

This VERB (BDB 615, KB 663) occurs three times in this verse.

  1. Qal IMPERFECT
  2. Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  3. Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE

It also occurs in the parallel literary unit of Isaiah 24-27 (cf. Isa. 24:4 [twice]). Agriculture also shakes at the coming of the creator! We could say heaven and earth both fall apart at the approach of the Creator/Judge because they, too, have been affected by mankind's sin (cf. Gen. 3:17-19; Rom. 8:19-22).

34:5
NASB  "satiated"
NKJV  "bathed"
NRSV  "drunk its fill"
TEV  "prepared"
NJB  "drunk deep"
JPSOA, LXX  "shall be drunk"
REB, DSS, Targums  "appears"
Peshitta  "sharpened"

The MT has the VERB (BDB 924, KB 1194, Piel PERFECT). The ancient versions are split between

  1. satiated ‒ רותה (BDB 924)
  2. appears ‒ תראה (BDB 906; DSS, Targums)

The UBS Text Project, p. 78, cannot decide which is original. Option #1 parallels v. 6 best.

▣ "for judgment upon Edom" Edom is singled out for judgment in this literary unit just as Moab was singled out in Isa. 25:10-12. Here Edom (like Moab earlier) is symbolic of all the arrogant nations who rebel against God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

 "devoted to destruction" See SPECIAL TOPIC: UTTERLY DESTROY (herem) and CURSE (anathema).

entries.title: Isaiah 34:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:6-7 These verses use the imagery of sacrifice (cf. BDB 830, f, cf. Jer. 50:27; 51:40; Ezek. 39:17-20) to describe YHWH's judgment

  1. the blood of lambs and goats, Isa. 34:6
  2. the fat of the kidneys of rams, Isa. 34:6
  3. young bulls, Isa. 34:7

Not only are domestic animals going to be sacrificed, but also wild oxen (BDB 910). Verse 7 could be imagery for Edom's leaders.

The imagery of YHWH's sword is also found in Deut. 32:41-42 and Ezek. 21:28-32.

34:6
NASB  "is sated with fat"
NKJV  "made overflowing with fatness"
NRSV, REB, JPSOA, LXX  "is gorged with fat"
NJB  "is greasy with fat"

This VERB (BDB 206, KB 234, Hothpael PERFECT) is found only here in this rare stem. It denotes a reflexive concept, "YHWH's sword has fattened itself." The Pual IMPERFECT of the same VERB is found in Isa. 34:7, "became greasy with fat." Both speak of a huge number of sacrificial victims slain (imagery for the dead of the enemies' army). The fat of the lower organs was that part of the animal placed on the altar.

entries.title: Isaiah 34:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:8 We as modern interpreters must remember the essence of Hebrew poetry is

  1. its abbreviated form
  2. its sound plays
  3. its parallelism

Westerners tend to be Greek-thinking, logical literalists! However, this is ancient eastern poetic literature. See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, chapter 5, "Hebrew Idiom and Hebrew Thought," pp. 107-117. This is also true of Genesis 1-2. See John L. Walton, The Lost World of Genesis 1.

This verse is a good example, "day," line 1 is parallel to "year," line 2. This is not meant to be a temporal, historical comment, but the recognition that a time of judgment and accountability to God is coming! How long it will last is not an issue.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

▣ "For the Lord has a day of vengeance" The concept of the valid and appropriate judgment of YHWH is expressed by "a day of vengeance" (BDB 668, cf. Isa. 35:4; 47:3; 61:2; 63:4; Jer. 51:6).

  1. It is parallel to YHWH being against the proud in Isa. 2:12.
  2. It is parallel to the day of the Lord as destruction in Isa. 13:6.
  3. It is mentioned in Deut. 22:35,41,43; Isa. 50:17; Micah 5:14.

YHWH is an ethical, moral Being. There are consequences to sin. Humans reap what they sow (see full list of biblical texts at my exegetical commentary on Gal. 6:7-10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGE, JUDGMENT, JUSTICE IN ISAIAH

▣ "Zion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ZION

entries.title: Isaiah 34:9 "pitch. . .brimstone. . .burning pitch"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:9 "pitch. . .brimstone. . .burning pitch" These (BDB 278, 172, 278/128) are allusions to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah in Gen. 19:24. Also, see the significant parallel of Jer. 49:17-18. Sodom and Gomorrah are in the northern area of Edom (i.e. southern end of the Dead Sea).

entries.title: Isaiah 34:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:10 This is hyperbolic language which denotes a complete destruction that lasts into the indefinite future (cf. Isa. 1:31; 13:20; 66:24).

There are two terms for "forever" used.

  1. line 2, עולם (BDB 761, see SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ['olam])
  2. line 4, נצח (BDB 664, cf. 2 Sam. 2:26; Isa. 13:20; 25:8; 28:28; 33:20; 57:16)

The phrase "its smoke shall go up forever" is used in Rev. 14:11 and 19:3. It seems probable that

  1. "Moab" in Isa. 25:10-12
  2. "Edom" in this context
  3. "Babylon" in Revelation

all stand for "human society organized and functioning apart from God or even in rebellion against God."

For a good discussion of the semantic field involving the biblical uses of the concept of "forever," see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks, pp. 98-101.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL PUNISHMENT

entries.title: Isaiah 34:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:11 The terms translated "desolation" (BDB 1062, cf. Isa. 24:10) and "emptiness" (BDB 96) are used in Gen. 1:2 to describe the initial chaos of the planet. Edom (i.e. all rebellious nations) will be reduced to original chaos (i.e. Isa. 13:9-11; Jer. 4:23-26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS AND DEMONS

34:15
NASB  "tree snake"
NKJV, JPSOA  "arrow snake"
NRSV, TEV  "owl"
NJB  "snake"
REB  "sand-partridge"
Peshitta  "great owl"
LXX  "hedgehog"

This NOUN (BDB 891, KB 1118) is found only here. It is obviously an animal of some kind that lays eggs and stays to protect the young.

entries.title: Isaiah 34:11-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:11-15 There are many animals (mostly birds) mentioned in this section. All of them are unclean according to Leviticus 11. These same unclean animals are seen in the ruins of the city of Babylon (cf. Isa. 13:19-22). There are two possible interpretations for this:

  1. these ruins are symbolic of fallen human efforts judged and destroyed by God so that nothing but the animals lived there (i.e. Gen. 10-11)
  2. these cities are now inhabited by the demonic (cf. Matt. 12:43)

Modern translations such as the NEB have shown clear archaeological evidence that these animals may refer to the demonic (cf. particularly Isa. 34:14).

  1. NASB     "hairy goat"
    NKJV     "wild goat"
    NRSV, JPSOA  "goat-demons"
    TEV       "demons"
    NJB       "satyr"
    REB       "he-goats"
  2. This term "hairy goat" (BDB 972 III) refers to
    1. idols (cf. 2 Chr. 11:15)
    2. demons (cf. Lev. 17:7)
    3. wild animals (cf. Isa. 13:21)
  3. NASB, TEV  "night monster"
    NKJV     "night creature"
    NRSV, NJB  "Lilith"
    REB     "nightjar"

This term (BDB 535) in later Judaism became the name for a female night tempter. The origin of the term and concept may be the three night demons of Akkadian mythology (KB 528). The Peshitta identifies it as a "screech owl." The night with all its "nature-sounds" was terrifying to ancient people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEMONIC IN THE OT

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS (fallen angels)

entries.title: Isaiah 34:16 "Seek from the book of the Lord, and read"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:16 "Seek from the book of the Lord, and read" Except for Isa. 34:1, there are no IMPERATIVES in this chapter before this verse. YHWH's calling them to approach and to listen in Isa. 34:1 (two IMPERATIVES) is matched by the two IMPERATIVES which close the chapter (a common Semitic literary technique).

  1. seek, BDB 205, KB 233, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. read, BDB 894, KB 1128, Qal IMPERATIVE

The nations have abrogated the dominion given to mankind in Genesis 2, so the animals are divinely allotted the land!

There have been many opinions about this book (The Book of the Lord, BDB 706). Some see it as the judgment scroll (cf. Isa. 29:11,12; 30:8). Others see it as an allusion to the two books mentioned in Dan. 7:10; 12:1 and Rev. 20:4-15, which are imagery for the memory of God.

  1. "the book of life"
    1. Exod. 32:32
    2. Ps. 69:28
    3. Isa. 4:3
    4. Dan. 7:10; 12:1
    5. Luke 10:20
    6. Phil. 4:3
    7. Heb. 12:23
    8. Rev. 3:5; 13:8; 17:8; 20:12,15; 21:27
  2. "the book of deeds/remembrances"
    1. Ps. 56:8; 139:16
    2. Isa. 65:6
    3. Dan. 7:10
    4. Mal. 3:16
    5. Rev. 20:12-13

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO BOOKS OF GOD

▣ "Not one of these will be missing;

None will lack its mate.

For His mouth has commanded" Here we have two images that refer to the power of God's word. The first is military, while the second is domestic. When God speaks, His word can be counted on (cf. Isa. 24:3; 25:8; 55:10-11).

▣ "His Spirit has gathered them" See the notes at Isa. 11:2

God gathers the animals/demons listed in Isa. 34:11-15.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT

entries.title: Isaiah 34:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:17 This is an allusion to the dividing of the land by lot (i.e. Urim and Thummim; see SPECIAL TOPIC: URIM AND THUMMIM) in Joshua 12-19. But, in this context, it is the animal kingdom that possesses the earth, not sinful mankind!

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 35:1 "wilderness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:1 "wilderness" This word refers to the uninhabited pasture land of southern Judah (BDB 184, cf. Joel 1:19-20).

▣ "the desert" This word (BDB 851) refers to the arid, sterile land (cf. Isa. 41:18; 53:2; Joel 2:20). Notice that "wilderness" is linked to "desert" and parallel with "Arabah."

▣ "Arabah" This word (BDB 787) refers to the Jordan rift valley south of the Dead Sea (cf. Isa. 33:9).

▣ "will rejoice and blossom" The first two VERBS of Isa. 35:1 are also a parallel personification of the plants.

  1. will be glad, BDB 965, KB 1314, Qal IMPERFECT (possibly JUSSIVE in meaning), this VERB is used eight times in chapters 61-66
  2. will rejoice, BDB 162, KB 189, Qal JUSSIVE, cf. Isa. 35:2; 25:9; this VERB is used four times in chapters 61-66, cf. Joel 2:21,23

The third VERB "blossom," "bud" (BDB 827, KB 965, Qal IMPERFECT with INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root, which shows intensity) shows how the plants (i.e. personified) rejoice. Isaiah often uses personification of natural items (cf. Isa. 33:9; 44:23; 55:12, cf. NASB Study Bible, p. 1004). The conditions of the Garden of Eden (Genesis 1-2) are restored; the new age has come!

Verse 10 is repeated in Isa. 51:11. This is a sign of the new age of restoration (cf. Isa. 7:21-25; 27:6; 32:15; 41:8-19; 55:12-13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

NASB, NRSV, Peshitta  "crocus"
NKJV, JPSOA  "rose"
NJB, REB  "asphodel"
JB  "jonquil"
LXX, NET  "lily"

It is almost impossible to accurately identify (note TEV general term, "flowers") the flora and fauna of the Bible. The rabbis say this (BDB 287) refers to the rose, while Luther and Calvin say it refers to the lily. Anybody's guess is still a guess! A good resource about these issues is the UBS' "Helps for Translators" series, Fauna and Flora of the Bible.

entries.content:

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter is obviously the reversal of Isaiah 34.

  2. The question is to whom it is addressed and when.
    1. Does this refer to the agricultural splendor of the Promised Land in the eschaton (i.e. believing faithful Jews and Gentiles)?
    2. Does this refer to the return of the Assyrian captives to Palestine (i.e. Israel)?
    3. Does this refer to the return of the Babylonian exiles by Cyrus' decree (i.e. Judah; Jer. 31:7-9)?
    4. Does this refer to the desert between Mesopotamia and Palestine being transformed into a lush highway for God's people to return to Palestine (i.e. the fastest way for returnees to come back to Palestine)?

  3. Remember, Isaiah is an anthology of his sermons, but
    1. the historical setting is not specified
    2. the sermons are not in chronological order
    3. the method of arrangement seems to be word sound plays as a way of linking sermons together
    4. these poems were delivered orally with someone besides the prophet himself writing them down
    5. This historical ambiguity allows Isaiah's predictions to apply to both the Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian exiles, as well as Cyrus II allowing refugees to return to Judah.

This is where the theological concept of "inspiration" must be expanded to include later editors or compilers. Moderns do not know when or how the OT as we know it was complied or arranged.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 35:2 "Lebanon. . .Carmel and Sharon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:2 "Lebanon. . .Carmel and Sharon" These three areas were famous for their lush foliage. The phrase "blossom profusely" is the Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 827, KB 965) which denotes intensity or here, lush growth.

▣ "They will see" This seems to be a continuing of the personification of the plants.

▣ "the glory. . .the majesty" Notice the parallel between

  1. glory (BDB 458, KB 455; see SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY[ OT])
  2. majesty (BDB 214) is used of YHWH as
    1. Victor ‒ Ps. 45:4-5
    2. Creator ‒ Ps. 96:6; 104:1; 111:2-3
    3. Judge ‒ Isa. 2:10

Also notice the parallel between

  1. YHWH ‒ see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.
  2. Eloah ‒ see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

entries.title: Isaiah 35:3-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:3-6 These verses mention several kinds of people.

  1. the exhausted (lit. "weak hands")
  2. the feeble (lit. "weak knees")
  3. those with anxious hearts (lit. "the hurried")
  4. the blind (BDB 734)
  5. the deaf (BDB 361)
  6. the lame (BDB 820)
  7. the dumb (BDB 48)

YHWH uniquely cares for the poor, weak, sick, lonely, and socially ostracized. Here is a list of what God will do for them in this new day of restoration.

  1. for #1 "encourage" (BDB 304, KB 302, Piel IMPERATIVE)
  2. for #2 "strengthen" (BDB 54, KB 65, Piel IMPERATIVE)
  3. for #3
    1. take courage, BDB 304, KB 302, Qal IMPERATIVE
    2. fear not, BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT but JUSSIVE in meaning
  4. for #4 "open the eyes," BDB 824, KB 959, Niphal IMPERFECT
  5. for #5 "open the ears," same VERB as #4
  6. for #6 "leap like a deer," BDB 194, KB 222, Piel IMPERFECT
  7. for #7 "tongue of dumb will shout for joy," BDB 943, KB 1247, Qal IMPERFECT

This is the message that Jesus sent to John the Baptist while he was in prison (cf. Matt. 11:4-5; Luke 7:20-22). The New Age is reflected in the ministry of Jesus!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

entries.title: Isaiah 35:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:4 Notice what YHWH promises to do for His covenant people.

  1. He comes with vengeance, BDB 668, cf. Isa. 34:8; 59:17; 61:2; 63:4; Deut. 32:25; Jer. 50:28
  2. His recompense also comes, BDB 168, cf. Isa. 59:18 (twice); 66:6, also note 65:6
  3. He will save them, BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil JUSSIVE, cf. Isa. 25:9; 33:22; 38:20; 45:17; 49:25; 59:1; 63:1,5,9; 64:5

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

entries.title: Isaiah 35:6 "For waters will break forth in the wilderness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:6 "For waters will break forth in the wilderness" The blooming of nature goes back to Isa. 35:1,2. The outward sign of God's spiritual presence and blessing is nature's wonderful display of beauty and growth (cf. Isa. 35:7). This was the blessing for covenant obedience from Lev. 26 and Deut. 28. See full note at Isa. 32:20.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

entries.title: Isaiah 35:7 "In the haunt of jackals"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:7 "In the haunt of jackals" The Peshitta and KJV translate this word (BDB 1072) "dragons." We have found from the Dead Sea Scrolls that animals listed in the OT often refer to the idols of the surrounding nations, therefore, this either refers to

  1. a deserted place
  2. the residence of the demonic (cf. Isa. 34:11-15)

The literary reason for this poetic line is that the dry dens of the jackals are now filled with water and can support swamp grass.

NASB  "its resting place"
NKJV  "where each lay"
NRSV  "a swamp"
NJB, REB  "their lairs"
Peshitta  "habitation"

The MT has רבצה, BDB 918, "her resting place." The NRSV changes it to לבצה, "swamp, BDB 130 (see NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 692-693). The DSS scroll of Isaiah has "he lies down." The UBS Text Project, p. 81, gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt). The jackal's den is now flooded.

▣ "Grass becomes reeds and rushes" The grass will grow as tall as reeds and rushes to show the luxurious growth of God's blessing symbolized in nature (i.e. plenty of water everywhere).

entries.title: Isaiah 35:8 "the Highway of Holiness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:8 "the Highway of Holiness" This is a common theme in the book of Isaiah (cf. Isa. 26:7; 40:3-4; 42:13). This same imagery of a royal visit is used to describe the coming of the Messiah. John the Baptist claims he fulfilled the prophecy of Mal. 4:5 in preparing the way for the Lord. This is imagery for preparation of a physical road, but it has spiritual implications referring to repentance.

▣ Line 3 and line 5 speak of the same person being excluded from returning. YHWH will accompany His faithful people, therefore, any "unclean" person must be excluded. In this context, "fools" equal "the unclean."

This divinely created highway of holiness is for those who have repented and believed (cf. v. 10).

▣ "fools" See SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE

entries.title: Isaiah 35:9 "No lion will be there"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:9 "No lion will be there" The fact that vicious animals will be absent or changed into tame companions is a sign of a blessing of God (cf. Isa. 11:6-9). It is also a reversal of the threat of Lev. 26:22.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

▣ "the redeemed" This term was first used in connection with the dedication of the firstborn child to God (cf. Exod. 13:13,15). The primary idea here is of deliverance from bondage at a set price. The relationship between "redeemed" (BDB 145 I, KB 169, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE) in Isa. 35:9 and "ransomed" (BDB 804, KB 911, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE) in Isa. 35:10 is repeated in Isa. 51:11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RANSON/REDEEM

entries.title: Isaiah 35:10 "the ransomed of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:10 "the ransomed of the Lord" See SPECIAL TOPIC: RANSOM/REDEEM.

▣ "will return" This VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERFECT) means "turn back" (i.e. repentance or change of direction). Many commentators see this (and Isa. 35:8) as a reference to the return from Babylonian exile (i.e. therefore is connected to chapters 40-66). This is surely possible because Isaiah's poems are not always arranged in chronological order. It could express "repentance" as a lifestyle (i.e. a Highway of Holiness, v. 8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣ "Zion" This later came to be a designation for the entire city of Jerusalem (built on seven hills), in particular the temple, although the temple is geographically located on Mt. Moriah, not on Mt. Zion.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ZION

▣ The returnees are characterized as

  1. the ransomed of the Lord
  2. coming with singing
  3. coming with everlasting joy
  4. having on their heads as a crown
    1. joy
    2. gladness
  5. having no sorrow
  6. having no sighing

▣ The NET Bible, p. 1242, #16, has an interesting comment.

"'Joy' may be likened here to a crown (cf. 2 Sam. 1:10). The statement may also be an ironic twist on the idiom 'earth/dust on the head' (cf. 2 Sam. 1:2; 13:19; 15:32; Job 2:12), referring to a mourning practice."
SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "With everlasting joy upon their heads" The term "everlasting" is 'olam (BDB 761).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣ "And sorrow and sighing will flee away" See Isaiah 25:8 and Revelation 21:4.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. This kind of joy and physical blessing seems to never have accompanied the return from Exile, if this is so, what does this chapter refer to?
  2. Explain the significance and the difference between the two terms: "redeemed" and "ransomed"
  3. Why is nature used to symbolize God's presence and blessing?

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 36:1 "in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:1 "in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah" It seems from the dating of the reigns of these Judean kings and their relationship to secular history that there is a textual error in the word "fourteenth." Because 2 Kgs. 18:1 says that Hezekiah was co-regent with his father between 729 and 715 B.C. and then became king himself from 715 to 686 B.C., it is probable that this should read the "twenty-fourth year of King Hezekiah" (cf. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp. 207,211; E. J. Young, Book of Isaiah, pp. 540-542; The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 6, p. 234; J. A. Motyer, Tyndale OT Commentaries, vol. 18, p. 222).

In the chart in SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM there is a list of three different dates for Hezekiah's reign.

  1. John Bright ‒ 715-687 B.C.
  2. E. J. Young ‒ 727-699 B.C.
  3. R. K. Harrison
    1. co-reign ‒ 729-716/15
    2. reign ‒ 716/15-687/86

These are three well-respected scholars, yet note the variety. Be careful of rigid dating of these reigns and co-reigns. Scholarship is just not in agreement at this point in time. Hopefully new information from archaeology can help clarify the date!

▣ "Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and seized them" We learn from Assyrian documents that Sennacherib (reigned from 705-681 B.C.) claims to have conquered 46 walled cities. Because of the Assyrian records of Sennacherib's reign an invasion of Judah in 701 B.C. fits this passage.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BACKGROUND STUDY (36-39)

  1. Chapters 36-39 form a historical literary transition (or appendix, Jewish Study Bible, p. 853) between the life of the prophet Isaiah in Isaiah 1-39 (the Assyrian period) and the section of Isaiah which deals with the future, chapters 40-66 (the Neo-Babylonian period and the eschaton). A similar historical addition occurs at Jeremiah 52, where 2 Kings 24:18-25:30 is repeated.

  2. This section of Isaiah is paralleled in 2 Kings 18:13-20:19, except for Isa. 38:9-20; also note 2 Chronicles 32. Much of Isaiah 36-39 is not poetry but prose. It may have been incorporated into Isaiah by later editors/compilers to finish out the historical invasion of Assyria in 701 B.C.

  3. This section seems to form a needed coherent transition from an emphasis on Assyria (Isaiah 36 and 37) to Babylon (Isaiah 38 and 39).

  4. There has been some discussion about the relationship of Hezekiah's
    1. refusal to succumb to the demands and threats of Sennacherib of Assyria
    2. Hezekiah paying tribute to him in 2 Kings 18:14-16
    3. It is in the realm of possibility that Hezekiah initially paid tribute and then later refused to do so.
      The exact relationship between these two passages is only conjecture.

  5. This chapter and the parallels have a more concentrated use of "trust" (BDB 105, KB 120) than any other context in the OT.
    1. Isaiah 36:4,5,6 (twice),7,9,15
    2. 2 Kings 18:19,20,21 (twice), 22,24,30; 19:10
    3. 2 Chronicles 32:10

"Trust" (בטח) and "belief" (אמן, see SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT) are crucial in understanding the proper functioning of the personal relationship involved in covenant. It is more than obedience!

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Isaiah 36:2 "And the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:2 "And the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh" There are several ways of understanding this title (BDB 913).

  1. a proper name (NASB, NKJV)
  2. "chief steward"
  3. "field commander" (Peshitta, NIV)
  4. "governor" or "chief of staff" (NKJV footnote)
  5. "cupbearer-in-chief" (NJB)
  6. "chief advisor" (NET)

Whichever it is he was a high-ranking official (JPSOA footnote) from the Assyrian camp (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:17).

The NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 1029, lists several of these Assyrian titles.

  1. Tartān ‒ supreme commander, cf. 2 Kgs. 18:17; Isa. 20:1
  2. Rab sāris ‒ chief officer, cf. 2 Kgs. 18:17
  3. Rab sāqēh ‒ field commander, cf. 2 Kgs. 18:17
  4. Rab Kisri ‒ commander of the army
  5. Rab hanse ‒ captain of fifty
  6. Rab saqu ‒ cupbearer of the king
  7. Akkadian
    1. tartan ‒ cf. #1 above
    2. rabu sa rēsi ‒ chief eunuch or military commander
    3. rab sāqēh ‒ cf. #3 above
    4. rab saqu ‒ #6 above
  8. Aramaic ‒ rb swq ‒ chief of the march

▣ "Lachish" This was one of the walled cities on the coastal plain which was captured by the Assyrian army. It was about thirty miles southwest of Jerusalem in the Shephelah.

▣ "And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway of the fuller's field" This is the same location where Isaiah confronted Ahaz in Isa. 7:3 with the appeal not to trust in Assyria. There may be a purposeful connecting of the geographical site to the response of Hezekiah (belief, cf. Isa. 37:14-20,30) versus the response of Ahaz (unbelief).

entries.title: Isaiah 36:3 "Eliakim. . .Shebna. . .Joah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:3 "Eliakim. . .Shebna. . .Joah" When one compares Isa. 22:15 and Isa. 22:20-24 it seems that these two men have exchanged offices.

If we can use Egyptian parallels it seems that these men represented different levels of administrative authority in the ANE.

  1. Eliakim
    1. NASB, NKJV, "over the household"
    2. NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, "in charge of the palace"
    3. REB, "the comptroller of the household"
    4. NJB, "master of the palace"
  2. Shebna
    1. NASB, NKJV, JPSOA, "the scribe"
    2. NRSV, NJB, "the secretary"
    3. REB, "the adjutant-general"
    4. TEV, "court secretary"
  3. Joah
    1. NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, "the recorder"
    2. REB, "the secretary of state"
    3. NJB, "the herald"

entries.title: Isaiah 36:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:4 The message of Sennacherib was read loudly in Hebrew (cf. Isa. 36:11) before the walls of Jerusalem so that everyone could hear and fear (cf. Isa. 36:11-12)!

This verse has three uses of the VERB "say" (BDB 55, KB 65).

  1. Qal IMPERFECT with waw
  2. Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. Qal PERFECT

▣ "What is this confidence that you have" This is a very significant statement for the rest of chapter 36 and 37 because it is a play on the Hebrew word "trust" (BDB 105, KB 120, Qal perfect, cf. Isa. 12:2; 26:3,4; 31:1; 32:9-11; 36:4,5,6 [twice],7,9,15; 37:10) or the question "what are you trusting in?" Notice that the Assyrian logic is based on their military victories over numerous other national gods. The line of psychological attack seems to impugn Hezekiah's actions on behalf of YHWH in order to impugn His power and to impugn the people's trust in Him (cf. Isa. 36:4,5,7,10,15,18; 37:4,6,10,17,20 esp., 23,29). This sets the stage, much like Daniel 3, for YHWH's confrontation with the Assyrian gods for the purpose that all of the world may know that YHWH is God (cf. Isa. 37:20; 45:6; 2 Chr. 32:7-8).

This question is the theological purpose of the literary unit!

36:5
NASB, NJB  "empty words"
NKJV  "vain words"
NRSV  "mere words"
LXX  "words of the lips"

The LXX is a literal translation of the MT (BDB 182 CONSTRUCT BDB 973). This is an idiom for someone who speaks without thinking (cf. Prov. 14:23).

▣ "rebelled against me" This (BDB 597, KB 623, Qal PERFECT) refers to the fact that Hezekiah initially stopped paying tribute to Assyria (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:7), but then apparently began it again when Sennacherib invaded (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:14-16) and then refused a second time to pay tribute.

entries.title: Isaiah 36:6 "Behold, you rely on the staff of this crushed reed, even on Egypt"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:6 "Behold, you rely on the staff of this crushed reed, even on Egypt" Apparently, the Assyrians had inside information on Hezekiah's ill-conceived design for a military alliance with Egypt. Isaiah had earlier condemned this alliance (cf. Isa. 30:1-5; 31:1-3).

entries.title: Isaiah 36:7 "whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has taken away"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:7 "whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has taken away" This is an attempt to impugn Hezekiah's relationship with YHWH (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:5). The thrust of the argument is that YHWH is angry with Hezekiah for closing the local high places (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:7). However, this was a misunderstanding by the Assyrians because Hezekiah did exactly what was commanded in Deuteronomy which is the centralization of worship at a site which YHWH would choose (cf. Deut. 12:2-5). The high places had become sites of Ba'al and Asherah worship (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Isaiah 36:8 "come make a bargain with my master"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:8 "come make a bargain with my master" The VERB (BDB 786, KB 876) is a Hithpael IMPERATIVE denoting the offer of a political pledge (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:23; Job 17:3; Ps. 119:122). The implication is, "leave your pledge with YHWH and trust in Assyria" (and by implication, her gods). This sounds preposterous, but remember Judah had already tried to form an alliance with Egypt (cf. Isa. 36:6,9), which also involved Egyptian deities! Judah's monotheism was being tested!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

▣ "I will give you two thousand horses" This is a mocking statement based on the weakness of Judea's army. There is some historical doubt about the presence of cavalry in Judah or Assyria at this early date, therefore, many commentators say this is a reference to chariots even though the obvious language refers to cavalry.

36:9
NASB, TEV  "official"
NKJV, NRSV  "captain"
NJB  "soldiers"
REB, Peshitta  "servants"
LXX  "governor"
JPSOA  "deputy"

The term (BDB 808, cf, 2 Kgs. 18:24; see NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 603) may refer to the recently appointed governor of the defeated Judean walled cities. Each of these local governmental officials had a small military contingent. Apparently Lachish became the headquarters of this Assyrian administrator.

Therefore, the sarcastic claim of Rabshakeh was that Jerusalem could not even defend itself against a regional, local militia, much less the Assyrian army.

entries.title: Isaiah 36:10 "Have I now come up without the Lord's approval"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:10 "Have I now come up without the Lord's approval" This verse is a statement by the Assyrians that

  1. they did not consult Judah's God
  2. God was even on their side!

How they knew of the prophecies concerning God's choosing of Assyria to judge Israel, Isa. 10:5-7, is uncertain. Some believe it is a half-truth related to Isal 37:26.

This verse seems to contradict itself.

  1. "without ... approval," literally "apart from" (BDB 116)
  2. "the Lord said to me"

Obviously Assyria (i.e. Sennacherib) is flaunting itself against the will of YHWH and His people!

entries.title: Isaiah 36:11 "Aramaic. . .Judean"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:11 "Aramaic. . .Judean" Aramaic (BDB 74) was the diplomatic language of the ANE and "Judean" should be translated "Hebrew" (BDB 397, cf. 2 Kgs. 18:26,28; 2 Chr. 32:18). The thrust of this verse is that Hezekiah's officials are asking the Assyrian representative to speak in the diplomatic language so the people of the city could not understand the threats.

entries.title: Isaiah 36:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:12 This was a threat about the problems associated with a siege (i.e. shortage of food and water, cf. 2 Kgs. 18:27) to cause fear and panic within Jerusalem. Even though Hezekiah may trust YHWH, possibly the citizens would not.

entries.title: Isaiah 36:13-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:13-16 There are several IMPERATIVES and JUSSIVES used in this message from Sennacherib through Rabshakeh (threats and promises).

  1. hear, Isa. 36:13 ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. do not let Hezekiah deceive you, Isa. 36:14 ‒ BDB 674, KB 728, NEGATED Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense, cf. Isa. 37:10; this is the same VERB used in Gen. 3:13!
  3. nor let Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord, Isa. 36:15 ‒ BDB 105, KB 120, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  4. do not listen to Hezekiah, Isa. 36:16 ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  5. make your peace with me, Isa. 36:16 ‒ BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE
  6. come out to me, Isa. 36:16 ‒ BDB 422, KB 425, Qal IMPERATIVE
  7. eat, Isa. 36:16 ‒ BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERATIVE
  8. drink, Isa. 36:16 ‒ BDB 1059, KB 1667, Qal IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Isaiah 36:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:17 Notice that Sennacherib's two promises are directed to the people from the countryside who had fled into the walled city of Jerusalem for protection. He would let them stay on their own land, but as Isa. 36:17 clarifies, only for a short while. He would spare their lives, but still they would be exiled. Even if they surrendered at this time, they would still be taken out of the land of Judah. However, Assyria killed the old and young on the spot!

entries.title: Isaiah 36:18 "Has any one of the gods of the nations delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:18 "Has any one of the gods of the nations delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria" Here is the theological challenge. The gauntlet has been thrown down and YHWH will pick it up!

The VERB "deliver" (BDB 664, KB 717) is used five times in Isa. 36:18-20. The first and last are Hiphil IMPERFECTs and the other three are Hiphil PERFECTS.

entries.title: Isaiah 36:19 "the gods of Hamath and Arpad"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:19 "the gods of Hamath and Arpad"

  1. Hamath was a city in central Syria whose king participated in the rebellion against Assyria and was crushed by Sargon II in 720 B.C. and its population deported to Samaria (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:24).
  2. Arpad was a city in northern Syria whose king participated in the rebellion against Assyria and was crushed by Tiglath-pileser III in 740 B.C.

The exact names of their deities are uncertain.

▣ "the gods of Sepharvaim" It may have been a city of northern Babylon. This was a location from which Sargon II (722-705 B.C.) sent exiles to settle in Samaria (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:24). Some scholars assume it refers to Samaria (the captured capital of Israel, 722 B.C.).

From 2 Kgs. 17:31 we know that the fertility gods they worshiped by child sacrifice were "Adrammelech" and "Anammelech." The first name is also the name of one of Sennacherib's sons who assassinated him (cf. Isa. 37:38). How they are connected is uncertain.

▣ "have they delivered Samaria from my hand" This is interesting because Samaria's gods are listed separately from Judah's. They both worshiped YHWH, but apparently the idolatry in the north had become so bad or the Assyrian information so poor that they did not realize that they both worshiped YHWH (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:5,6,24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

entries.title: Isaiah 36:22 "with their clothes torn"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:22 "with their clothes torn" See SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES.

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Isaiah 37:1 "he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:1 "he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth" These are signs of mourning.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "the house of the Lord" This refers to the temple in Jerusalem. Exactly what area of the temple he entered is uncertain. Only priests and Levites had access to the sacred buildings. However, there was a special area set aside for the monarch to be as close as possible and view the activities of festival rituals.

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
